title: Accessicook
honestNotes: This is everyday American home cooking.
Deep frying is left out on purpose for safety.
A few breads start from store-bought dough.
The recipes have not been individually kitchen-tested and the files have not been formally screen-reader tested.
Written with AI assistance and reviewed for consistency.

entries.title: How to Use This Book with VoiceOver, NVDA, and a Braille Display

blocks.text: Accessicook is a plain-text cookbook written so a blind or low-vision cook, and a sighted helper if you have one, can follow the same page. Every recipe uses the same heading order, short numbered steps, and doneness cues you can hear, smell, feel, or measure, plus visual cues a helper can speak out loud.
This chapter explains how to move through the files, how a recipe is organized, and how to cook from a phone, computer, or braille display without getting lost at the stove.
The book lives in a folder called Accessicook. Inside it you will find:
README.txt, which is the best place to start
INDEX.txt, an alphabetical list and a list by category, with file paths
CONTENTS.txt, the full table of contents, including these teaching chapters
Accessicook-all-recipes.txt, one large file with every chapter and recipe in order, useful if you want to search a single document or copy the book to a notetaker
Numbered category folders, such as 01-breakfast and 02-mains, each holding individual recipe files
File names start with a number so they sort in a sensible order. Recipe file names are descriptive, for example 01-omelette.txt.
All files are plain UTF-8 text. There are no tables, no images, and no steps that depend on color alone. You can open them in a text editor, in Books or a similar app, or on a braille display.

VoiceOver on iPhone, iPad, or Mac, and NVDA or JAWS on Windows, will read the files straight through. Headings are written in capital letters on their own lines, such as STEPS and SAFETY. Some apps will not treat those lines as official headings in a heading list. If that happens, use find and search for a word like STEPS, INGREDIENTS, or SAFETY, or read the short sections in order.
Temperatures are written as "165 degrees F" so they are spoken clearly. Fractions are written in ordinary recipe form, with a short spoken cue when needed, such as "1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon)."

If you use a phone at the stove, set it back from the burners, use a stand or a raised lip so it cannot slide forward, and pause the reader when you need both hands. A talking timer or a voice assistant is safer for timing than handling a phone over a hot pan. A braille display can sit on the counter away from water and heat.
Every recipe follows this order:
A short introduction
Servings, total time, and difficulty
Equipment, including accessible tools when they help
Ingredients, with tactile tips for measuring and identifying them
A short "Before you start" note
Numbered steps
How to tell when it is done, with non-visual cues and visual cues for a helper
Safety
Tips and variations
Leftovers
Sources

Read the introduction, time, and safety section once before you cook, especially the first time. Then set out equipment and ingredients before you turn on any heat. Work the numbered steps in order. Use the tips after you know the basic method.

If you are cooking with an in-home care worker or another partner, agree on roles before the heat goes on. One useful split is: the cook who knows the recipe leads, the helper reads the next step out loud, handles a visual check when the recipe asks for one, and spots hot pans. The helper should not silently take over a step. Ask for a specific check, such as "Does the chicken look opaque, and what is the thermometer reading?" rather than "Is it done?"
Both of you should hear the thermometer temperature. If you disagree, measure again in a second spot.
For more on working together, see the README in this book.

In the combined file, search for the recipe title, or for ACCESSICOOK followed by the title. In the index, search for the dish you want and then open the path listed next to it. If you remember only the category, open that folder and move through the file names.

These pages are written as cooking lessons for adults. They describe what food feels, sounds, and smells like when it is going well and when it is not. They do not assume you can see the pan, and they do not talk down to you.

You do not need a special kitchen to cook from this book. You do need a layout you can trust, a few habits that keep heat and knives predictable, and labels on the things you cannot identify by shape or smell. This chapter is a setup guide. You can change a kitchen over a weekend, then improve it as you cook.

Keep the cutting board, knives, mixing bowls, measuring tools, salt, oil, timers, and thermometers in the same places every time. A consistent layout is faster and safer than searching with a burner on.

Store heavy pans on a low, sturdy shelf. Keep spices and everyday oils where you can reach them without stretching over a hot stove. If you share the kitchen with a helper, agree on the layout and put it back the same way after cleaning.

Before you cook, move mail, devices, and extra dishes off the work surface. Clutter is how pans get bumped and knives get found the hard way. Leave one clear landing zone for hot pans, and do not use that zone for anything else while you cook.

Use bump dots, tactile marking pens, braille labels, or a talking labeler on spice jars, oil bottles, and pantry staples that feel similar. Mark the oven and stove settings you use most often, such as medium heat, 350, 375, 400, and 425 degrees F. If the knobs are smooth, one raised dot at each of those positions is enough.
A talking scale reduces the number of similar-feeling cups you have to keep track of. A liquid level indicator beeps or vibrates as a cup or pot fills.

Create a raw-meat zone and a ready-food zone. Use one cutting board and one set of tools for raw meat and poultry, and a different board for bread, vegetables, cheese, and cooked food. If you have only one board, wash it with soap and hot water, and wash your hands, before it touches anything that will not be cooked again.
Put a damp dish towel or a non-slip mat under the cutting board. Keep a trash bowl on the raw zone for wrappers and trimmings so you are not crossing the kitchen with chicken packaging.

Wear short sleeves or roll long sleeves above the elbow. Avoid loose cuffs, dangling jewelry, and long loose hair that can catch a handle or dip into a pan. Tie back anything that hangs. Use long oven mitts, not damp towels, on hot pans.

sections.title: Lighting and Contrast, for Low Vision and Helpers

blocks.text: If you have some usable vision, or if you cook with a sighted helper, high-contrast tools help: a dark board for light foods, a light board for dark foods, and a well-lit, uncluttered counter. This book does not rely on that contrast, but it is useful when it is available.
You can cook most of this book with:
A talking or instant-read thermometer
A tactile or talking timer
Measuring spoons and cups with tactile markings, plus a liquid level indicator
A cut-resistant glove
Long oven mitts
A splatter screen
One stable cutting board and one sharp chef's knife
A large pot, a heavy skillet or Dutch oven, a rimmed baking sheet, and an 8-inch nonstick skillet
Add a talking scale, a box grater or pre-grated cheese, a colander, tongs, and a wooden spoon as you go. Adaptive tools are covered in more detail in the next chapter.

entries.title: Adaptive Tools and Where to Find Them

blocks.text: The right tools do not cook the meal for you, but they make measuring, timing, and doneness much more reliable. This chapter lists the tools used most often in Accessicook, what they do, and how to think about buying them. You do not need every item on day one.

A talking or large-display instant-read thermometer is the most important safety tool in this book. Use it for meat, poultry, egg dishes, casseroles, and leftovers. A fry or probe thermometer is worth adding if you will heat oil.
A talking or tactile timer keeps you from burning food when you cannot watch a clock. A phone timer works if the phone stays away from the heat and you can hear it.

A talking kitchen scale measures flour, meat, and cheese without a stack of similar cups. Tactile or large-print measuring cups and spoons still matter for liquids and small amounts. An electronic liquid level indicator hangs on the rim of a cup, bowl, or pot and beeps or vibrates as the liquid rises.
Bump dots, Hi-Mark or similar tactile pens, braille labels, and talking labelers all work on jars and appliance knobs. Use whatever system you will actually maintain.

A cut-resistant glove goes on the hand that holds the food, not the knife hand. Long oven mitts protect wrists and forearms in the oven. A splatter screen cuts down grease burns on a skillet. A lid that fits your main pot should live within reach in case of a grease flare-up. Cool-touch oven rack guards, if you can find them, reduce forearm burns when you reach into the oven.

A sharp chef's knife is safer than a dull one, because it is less likely to slip. A vegetable peeler is safer than peeling with a knife. A pizza cutter or a rocking knife can be easier than a long slicing stroke when you are learning. A pair of tongs, a wooden spoon, and a heat-safe spatula will get you through most of this book. A double spatula, sometimes sold as a "safety food turner," helps flip fish or an egg without chasing it around the pan.

Specialty products are sold by blindness organizations and independent living stores, including the National Federation of the Blind Independence Market and many state or private agencies. Ordinary kitchen stores and large retailers also sell talking thermometers, timers, scales, cut-resistant gloves, splatter screens, and long mitts. A tool does not have to be marketed as "adaptive" to be useful.
If cost is a barrier, start with a thermometer, a timer, one tactile set of measuring spoons, a cut-resistant glove, and bump dots. Add the rest as you need them.

Replace the batteries in talking tools before they fail in the middle of a recipe. Dry thermometers and liquid level indicators as the package directs. Keep knives sharp. Wash cut-resistant gloves as the maker allows; some are machine washable, and some are not.

entries.title: Knife Skills, the Claw Grip, and Cut-Resistant Gloves

blocks.text: Most recipes in this book ask you to cut something: an onion, a chicken breast, a loaf of bread. A calm, repeatable method matters more than speed. This chapter covers a stable board, the claw grip, a cut-resistant glove, and a few safer alternatives when a large knife is not the right tool.

Put a damp dish towel or a non-slip mat under a sturdy cutting board so it cannot slide. Give yourself enough counter space that your elbows are not pinned to your sides. Use a board reserved for raw meat when you are cutting meat or poultry, or wash the board and your hands thoroughly before they touch ready-to-eat food.

The hand that holds the food is the claw hand. Tuck your fingertips under and curl your fingers so the fingertips are behind the knuckles, with the thumb tucked behind as well. The side of the knife blade rests against those knuckles, which act as a fence. The fingertips stay back and out of the way.

The other hand holds the knife with a secure grip on the handle. Confirm the sharp edge is down by feeling the spine, which is the dull top of the blade, before you start. Cut down and slightly forward, then move the claw hand backward a little at a time. Do not rush. Let the knife finish one cut before you set up the next.

A cut-resistant glove on the claw hand adds a layer of protection while you learn, and many experienced cooks keep wearing one for raw poultry and slippery foods. It is not a reason to be careless with the blade. The glove does not belong on the knife hand.

Feel the item, then set it on a flat, stable side if it has one. Cut a thin slice off a round food such as an onion or potato to make a flat face, then rest that face on the board so the food cannot roll. For garlic, you can loosen the paper skin by pressing the clove under the flat of the knife, with your hand on the blade spine, never on the sharp edge.
Move trimmings out of the work area so you do not cut through a pile of scraps. If the knife feels like it is slipping, stop, dry the handle, and dry the food.

sections.title: When Not to Use a Chef's Knife

blocks.text: A vegetable peeler is the better tool for peeling carrots and potatoes. Work away from your body and rotate the food. Kitchen shears are useful for snipping herbs, cutting raw bacon, and opening packages. A pizza cutter can slice a sandwich or a quesadilla. If chopping an onion is the step that stalls you, a hand chopper or already-diced onion from the store is a fair substitution.

sections.title: Keeping Knives Safe When You Are Not Cutting

blocks.text: Set a knife down with the blade facing away from the edge of the counter. Do not drop it into a sink full of soapy water, where it cannot be seen or felt safely. Wash it individually, dry it, and put it back in its block, sheath, or magnetic strip.

This chapter draws on standard culinary teaching, including the claw-grip guidance used in professional training materials such as the Institute of Child Nutrition's knife-skills resources, and on common adaptive-kitchen practice.

entries.title: Measuring by Touch, Sound, and Weight

blocks.text: Accurate measuring makes baking rise and keeps seasoning under control. You can measure well without seeing the line on a cup. This chapter covers dry measures, liquid measures, spoons, scales, and a few tricks for salt, oil, and spices.

Use individual or nesting dry measuring cups with raised, large-print, or braille markings. To fill a dry cup, spoon the ingredient in and level it with a straight edge, such as the back of a knife, feeling for the rim of the cup. Do not pack flour. Brown sugar is the usual exception: pack it until it holds the shape of the cup when you turn it out.

If two cups feel similar, mark them with bump dots or keep only one set, stored in order. A talking scale is often easier for flour, sugar, and oats. When a recipe in this book gives cups, you can use a standard conversion if you prefer weight, such as about 120 grams for 1 cup of unsifted all-purpose flour, but not every ingredient weighs the same per cup, so use a reliable conversion for that ingredient.

Use a liquid measuring cup, which has a pouring spout, together with an electronic liquid level indicator. Clip or hang the indicator on the rim and pour slowly until it beeps or vibrates at the level you want. You can also pour over a kitchen sink or a tray to catch spills, and dip a clean finger just over the rim to feel when a cup is nearly full, but the indicator is more precise and more sanitary for stocks and milk.
For a small amount, such as 1 tablespoon of oil or soy sauce, tactile measuring spoons are easier than a cup.

Tactile or well-marked spoons let you feel 1/4, 1/2, and 1 teaspoon, and 1 tablespoon. Fill the spoon and level dry spices with a finger or a straight edge. For liquids, fill to the brim but do not overflow. Wash the spoon between a strong spice such as cayenne and a mild one such as sugar, or keep two spoons in play.

Many savory recipes in this book give an amount of salt and then tell you to taste a cooled bite at the end. If you are learning, measure the salt. A pinch is roughly 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). When you are comfortable, you can salt from a small dish rather than over the pan, which prevents a stuck shaker lid from dumping a load into the food.
Oil can be measured in a spoon or poured in a slow count you practice once with a spoon nearby. For frying, though, measure, because the amount of oil affects safety.

Taste only food that is safe to taste: not raw meat, not raw eggs, not raw batter or dough with eggs or flour, and not a boiling spoonful that will burn you. Cool a small spoonful, then taste and adjust salt, acid, or heat.

The stove is where most weeknight cooking happens, and it is also where most burns happen. This chapter covers finding a burner, setting a pan down, judging heat without watching a flame, and working on a smooth flat-top range.

sections.title: Find the Burner Before You Turn It on

blocks.text: Position the pan on a cold burner first, then turn the heat on. Stand square to the front of the stove. Keep pot handles turned inward, but not over another burner.

To find a burner without placing your hand on a hot surface, use a long wooden spoon as a feeler, or learn a "safety zone" heat check: keep your hand at least midriff height, lower it slowly, and feel for rising heat rather than touching the grate or the glass. Some cooks mark the center of each burner on a wooden spoon with tactile tape, measuring once from the front edge of the stove.
Medium heat is the default in many of these recipes. On many electric and flat-top stoves, the middle of the knob is a useful tactile mark. The pan tells you more than the knob does:
A drop of water should sizzle and skitter on a hot, empty skillet, then dry quickly, when you are preheating for searing.
Butter should melt, then foam, and smell nutty, not acrid or burnt.
Oil should flow easily and smell hot, not sharp or smoky. If oil smokes, the pan is too hot. Take it off the heat.
A gentle simmer sounds like small, regular bubbles. A boil is louder and more rattling. A hard, spattering boil usually means you should turn the heat down.
If food smells scorched, remove the pan from the heat first, then decide what to do. Turning the food is easier once the burner is not still blasting.

Fill a pot no more than halfway to two-thirds full. You can feel the water line with a clean finger before the heat is on, or use a liquid level indicator on the rim. Add salt after the water is hot if you like, keeping your face back from steam. Add pasta or vegetables carefully so the water does not splash. If a pot sounds like it is boiling over, turn the heat down and, if needed, slide it off the burner.
Turn the heat off before you move a full, heavy pot. If a pot of water is too heavy to lift safely, cook a smaller amount, or scoop some water out with a mug before you drain.

Use flat-bottomed, stable pans. Keep the glass clear of paper, food wrappers, and plastic. The surface stays hot after the burner is off; treat the whole top with caution until it has cooled. Always turn the heat off before you move a pan. Wipe spills after the surface is cool enough, following the maker's directions, because sugar syrups can damage some glass tops.

If you cook with gas, learn how your starter sounds and how the knob feels when the burner is lit. If you smell gas and the burner is not lit, turn it off, do not use a flame or unplug anything, and follow your local gas-safety procedure. Confirm the flame is actually on before you walk away, using heat, sound, and, for a helper, a visual check.
Hot oil, bacon, popcorn, and empty pans on high heat need you to stay in the kitchen. Set a timer even when you think you will remember.

The oven gives you even heat and free hands once the food is in, but the racks, the door, and the pans are serious burn hazards. This chapter covers rack position, preheating, putting food in and taking it out, and judging doneness without staring through the window.

Place oven racks before you preheat. A middle rack is the default in this book unless a recipe says otherwise. For many sheet-pan meals and cookies, the center is best. For a pie that needs a browner bottom, a slightly lower rack can help. For a casserole that browns on top, a slightly higher rack can help.
Feel the rack positions when the oven is cold. Count the slots from the bottom so you can repeat the same setting. If you need to move a rack, do it before the oven is hot.

Preheat unless the recipe, or a package such as some turkey bacon, says to start in a cold oven. Many ovens beep or chime when they reach temperature; learn that sound, and still give the oven a couple of extra minutes if your oven runs cool. A tactile mark or bump dot on 350, 375, 400, and 425 degrees F will cover most of this book.
Decide where the hot pan will land before you open the door. Clear that space and set out long, dry oven mitts.

Stand to the side as you open the door so the first roll of steam does not hit your face. Pull the rack partly out with mitts, set or remove the pan, and close the door. Do not reach deep into a hot oven with bare forearms.
If you cannot tell whether the pan is centered, ask a helper to confirm, or feel the rack edges with a mitted hand and locate the pan relative to the rack, not by reaching over the food.
Use a talking timer every time something is in the oven. Set it when the food goes in, not after you think of it.

A thermometer is the right tool for meat, poultry, casseroles, and leftovers. For baked goods, use time, aroma, and touch: a cake often springs back lightly in the center, a toothpick or skewer comes out without wet batter (a few moist crumbs can be fine), and the kitchen smells baked, not raw and floury or sharp and burnt. A sighted helper can add color cues, such as golden brown, but color alone is not enough for meat.
If you open the door to check, do it quickly so the oven does not cool too much, and start with a thermometer or a touch test rather than a long look.
Turn the oven off. Leave hot pans on the reserved landing zone. Tell anyone else in the home that a hot pan is there. Let the oven cool before you wipe it.

A microwave is one of the most useful tools in an accessible kitchen. It reheats leftovers, steams vegetables, makes mug cakes, and cooks a baked potato. It also heats unevenly, and the containers get hotter than people expect. This chapter covers safe containers, even heating, and how to check that food is actually hot enough.

Use microwave-safe glass, ceramic, or labeled microwave-safe plastic. Do not put metal, including gold-rimmed dishes and twisted metal ties, in the microwave. If you are not sure a container is safe, choose glass.

Cover food so it does not spatter, but leave a vent for steam. A microwave-safe lid, a plate, or a slightly loose wrapper all work. The cover and the dish will be hot. Use a dry mitt or a thick cloth, and lift the cover away from your face.

Microwaves have cold spots. Stir soups, sauces, and leftovers halfway through. If your microwave has no turntable, rotate the dish once or twice. After cooking, let the food stand for a minute or two; cooking continues during that time, especially in dense foods.

Leftovers, casseroles, and anything with meat or poultry should be reheated to 165 degrees F. Check in more than one spot with a food thermometer, including the center. If one area is cooler, stir and heat longer. Sauces, soups, and gravies should return to a boil.
Mug cakes and mug eggs are done by the cues in those recipes, usually a set center. If a mug feels only warm at the bottom and molten in the middle, it is not done.

Plain water can occasionally become superheated in a microwave and then boil over when you move the cup. Use a microwave-safe container, do not overheat plain water, and consider placing a wooden stir stick in the cup when you heat water for tea. Stand back when you uncover any liquid.
Clean splatters when the oven is cool. A dirty microwave heats unevenly and smells like the last sauce that exploded.

If the keypad is flat, add bump dots to Start, Stop, Add 30 seconds, and the buttons you use most. Some microwaves have an audible confirmation; learn yours. A talking assistant can also time a manual cook if the microwave itself is hard to program.

An air fryer is a small, intense convection oven. It can crisp leftover pizza, cook frozen fries, roast vegetables, and finish chicken without heating a full oven. It also runs very hot, the basket is a burn hazard, and crowding the basket gives you steamed, soft food instead of crisp food.

Air fryers vary. A time that works in one basket will be too long in another. The first time you cook a food, start at the low end of the time range, shake or turn once, and check early. Keep a short braille or text note of the times that work in your machine.
Read, or have a helper read, your model's booklet for maximum fill level, preheat instructions, and whether the basket and crisper plate are dishwasher safe.

Many recipes in this book tell you whether to preheat. If they do, preheat with the basket in, using a timer. If you oil the food, a thin brush of oil is often safer for nonstick coatings than some aerosol sprays. Check your manual.

Load food in a single layer with a little space between pieces whenever you want crispness. Cook in batches rather than piling. Pull the basket out by the handle and set it on a reserved heat-safe landing zone. Shake the basket or turn the food with tongs, then return it. Never reach into the well of the air fryer with a bare hand.

Use the same USDA temperatures you use in the oven: 165 degrees F for poultry and leftovers, 160 for ground beef, 145 plus a 3-minute rest for whole-muscle beef, pork, and lamb, and 145 for fish. Check more than one piece, especially pieces from the center of the basket.

The air fryer housing, the basket, and the steam that puffs out when you open it can all burn you. Keep the machine back from the wall, on a stable, heat-safe surface, with space around it. Do not set it under cabinets that can be damaged by hot exhaust. Unplug it when you are finished and let it cool before you wash the basket.

Fatty foods such as bacon can smoke. Check your manual; some makers recommend a little water in the drawer, or a lower temperature. Stay in the kitchen the first time you cook a fatty food. If you smell heavy smoke, stop, unplug, and let the machine cool, then clean out grease.
Grease left in the drawer will smoke the next time. Wash the basket and plate after they are cool. Wipe the interior only when the machine is unplugged and cool.

You cannot see, smell, or taste the bacteria that cause many foodborne illnesses. Safe cooking in this book rests on four USDA rules: Clean, Separate, Cook, and Chill. This chapter is the reference page for temperatures and leftovers. The individual recipes repeat the numbers that apply to that dish.

Wash your hands with soap and water before you cook, after you handle raw meat, poultry, eggs, or flour, after you use the restroom, and before you serve. Wash cutting boards, knives, thermometers, and counters with soap and hot water after they touch raw meat or eggs.

Keep raw meat and poultry and their juices away from foods that will not be cooked again, including bread, salad, fruit, and cooked meat. Use a separate board, or wash the board thoroughly between tasks. Do not put cooked chicken back on the plate that held it raw unless that plate has been washed.

sections.title: Cook to a Safe Internal Temperature

blocks.text: Use a food thermometer in the center of the thickest part, without touching bone or the pan. USDA minimums used in this book are:
All poultry, including chicken pieces, turkey, ground poultry, and turkey bacon: 165 degrees F
Ground beef, ground pork, and other ground meats: 160 degrees F
Beef, pork, lamb, and veal steaks, chops, and roasts: 145 degrees F, then rest at least 3 minutes
Fish: 145 degrees F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily
Shrimp, lobster, and crab: cook until the flesh is pearly, opaque, and firm
Eggs: cook until the yolk and white are firm
Egg dishes, such as casseroles, quiches, and the omelettes in this book: 160 degrees F
Leftovers and casseroles: 165 degrees F
Fresh or uncooked ham: 145 degrees F, then rest at least 3 minutes
Fully cooked ham, to reheat: 140 degrees F if it was packaged in a USDA-inspected plant, otherwise 165 degrees F

Color is not a reliable test. Cured bacon and some ground meat can stay pink after they are safe. Poultry can look white before it is 165 degrees F, or still look slightly pink after it is. Trust the thermometer.

Bacteria multiply quickly between 40 and 140 degrees F, a range often called the Danger Zone. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Cool large pots in shallow containers. Keep the refrigerator at 40 degrees F or below.
Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days, or freeze them. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies to a boil.
Thaw meat and poultry in the refrigerator, in cold water in a leak-proof bag, or in the microwave if you will cook the food right away. Do not thaw on the counter at room temperature.

sections.title: When You Should Be Extra Careful

blocks.text: Pregnant people, young children, older adults, and anyone with a weaker immune system should be especially careful about following these temperatures, and should avoid undercooked eggs, undercooked meat, and unpasteurized juices or dairy unless a doctor has given different advice. This book defaults to fully cooked eggs and to USDA temperatures.
Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service:
https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/safe-temperature-chart/
Cook to a Safe Minimum Internal Temperature, FoodSafety.gov:
https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures
Leftovers and Food Safety, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service:
https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/leftovers-and-food-safety
Keep Food Safe! Food Safety Basics, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service:
https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/steps-keep-food-safe

A cookbook is only useful if you can find the ingredients again tomorrow. This chapter covers shopping, getting things home safely, labeling them so you can identify them, and storing them so they stay safe to eat.

If you shop in a store, a consistent route helps: produce, pantry, then cold and frozen foods last so they spend less time warming up. A helper, a store associate, or a sighted-assistance app can confirm package sizes, expiration dates, and whether fruit is ripe or bruised. If you shop online or with a delivery service, save a usual list and check the substitutions before they arrive.

For meat and poultry, feel that packages are cold and not leaking. Put them in a separate bag so juices cannot drip onto bread or produce. Frozen food should feel solid, not slushy. Dairy should feel cold.
Go home promptly, especially in hot weather. Refrigerate or freeze perishable food within 2 hours, or within 1 hour if it is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use an insulated bag if the trip is long.

When groceries come out of the bag, label anything you will not know by shape, size, or smell. Talking labelers, braille labels, bump dots, rubber bands (for example, one band for mild salsa and two for hot), and large-print tape all work. Label leftovers with the name and the date. A day-of-the-week bump system is enough if you do not use a print date.
Keep the system simple enough that you will actually use it. A helper can apply labels as you put food away, and you can check that you can identify each item yourself.
Refrigerator: 40 degrees F or below. Store raw meat and poultry on a low shelf in a pan or on a plate so they cannot drip onto other food.
Freezer: 0 degrees F or below. Wrap food well and label it. Frozen leftovers are safest for quality if you use them within 3 to 4 months, though they stay safe longer if kept frozen solid.
Pantry: cool, dry, and consistent. Once you open sauces, salsas, and many condiments, read or have a helper read the label; some must be refrigerated after opening.
Eggs: keep them in the refrigerator, not on the counter.
Leftovers: 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, then freeze or discard.
If you are not sure how long something has been in the refrigerator, and it is a perishable leftover older than 4 days, throw it out. When in doubt, throw it out.

Do not use cans that are bulging, leaking, or badly dented at a seam. Do not use jars with a popped lid or a broken seal. If a package of raw meat is leaking, you can still cook the meat if it was kept cold and smells normal for raw meat, but clean any juices from the refrigerator right away.

Cleanup is part of cooking, not an afterthought. A clear sink and a known place for knives prevent cuts. A clean board and thermometer prevent the next meal from picking up bacteria from the last one. This chapter is a short, practical closing routine.

Wash knives one at a time, by themselves, not loose in a sink full of soapy water. Set the knife on the counter, wash the blade with the sharp edge turned away from you, dry it, and put it away in a block, sheath, or magnetic strip. The same rule applies to vegetable peelers, box graters, and food-processor blades.

Wash boards, tongs, and thermometers with soap and hot water after they touch raw meat, poultry, or eggs. If you used a board for raw chicken, do not slice bread on it until it has been washed. Some plastic boards can go in the dishwasher; wooden boards are usually hand-washed and dried upright.

sections.title: The Stove, Oven, and Air Fryer

blocks.text: Turn burners and the oven off before you clean around them. Let pans, air-fryer baskets, and oven racks cool until they are safe to handle. Wipe grease while it is still slightly warm if you can do that safely, because cold, hard grease is harder to remove, but never wipe a burner that is still on. Pour cooled bacon grease or frying oil into a jar, not down the sink.
Wipe splatters when the microwave is cool. A bowl of water heated until it steams can loosen dried food; use a mitt, and do not move a bubbling bowl carelessly.

Wipe floor spills as soon as you can so they are not a slip hazard, especially oil and other grease. If oil spills on the floor, tell anyone else in the home, and stay off that spot until it is clean.
Tie bags before they overflow. Chicken trays and raw-meat wrappers should go straight to the trash so juices are not left on the counter. Wash your hands after handling trash.

A good last pass is: heat off, knives put away, boards washed, food in the refrigerator, hot pans on a known landing zone, and your thermometer rinsed and back in its home. If you are cooking with a helper, do this check together out loud.

If you are returning to cooking, or teaching a helper how you like to work, it helps to practice a few small skills before you take on a long braise or a sheet of cookies. This chapter is a five-day practice plan. Each day has a small task and an optional meal from this book. Skip a day or change the order if you need to. The point is confidence, not speed.

sections.title: Day 1: The Kitchen and a Piece of Toast

blocks.text: Walk the kitchen and name, out loud, the home of the board, the knife, the thermometer, the timer, the salt, the oil, and the mitts. Add bump dots to one stove setting and one oven setting if you have not already. Then make toast the way you prefer: toaster, toaster oven, or skillet.

Cues: the kitchen smells toasted, not burnt. The bread feels firmer and drier. A helper can look for an even golden color. Optional meal: avocado toast, cinnamon toast, or a peanut butter and jelly sandwich from the snacks chapter, if you already have the ingredients.

sections.title: Day 2: Boiling Water and a Simple Side

blocks.text: Practice filling a pot no more than two-thirds full, finding the burner, and bringing water to a boil. Listen for the change from quiet to a rolling bubble, and feel the steam from a safe height, not by putting your hand over the pot. Cook corn on the cob, steamed broccoli, or stovetop rice from the sides chapter, or just boil the water, turn it off, and let it cool if you only want the skill.
Practice turning the heat off before you move the pot.

Make scrambled eggs or the omelette from the breakfast chapter. Practice cracking eggs into a small bowl first, beating them, and cooking until they are set and, for the omelette, 160 degrees F. This is also a good day to practice the claw grip by cutting a piece of butter or a slice of bread, not a pile of onions.
Optional add-on: the bacon recipe, or a simple cheese toast, if you want a fuller breakfast.

Use the pasta primer in the pasta chapter. Practice a full pot of boiling water, stirring the pasta so it does not clump, saving a cup of pasta water, draining safely, and dressing the pasta with butter and cheese or with marinara. If you have a helper, have them watch the pot for boil-overs while you handle the timer and the doneness bite test.
Optional full meal: spaghetti with meat sauce, if you are ready to brown ground beef and use the 160 degree F check, or fettuccine Alfredo if you want a cream sauce instead.

Bake a sheet of cookies, a pan of cornbread, baked chicken breasts, or oven bacon. Practice setting the rack while the oven is cold, preheating, using long mitts, pulling the rack out, and using a timer. For chicken, practice the 165 degree F thermometer check in more than one piece. For baked goods, practice the toothpick or spring-back test and the smell of a baked, not raw, center.

After this week, pick meals you actually want to eat. Good early projects from this book include grilled cheese, pancakes, chili, baked potatoes, chicken nuggets, and a fruit crisp. Save deep frying, candy, and large holiday roasts until the everyday habits feel automatic.

If a recipe goes poorly, that is data, not a verdict. Note whether the heat was too high, the pieces were uneven, or a step was skipped, and try the same recipe once more before you decide it is not for you.

entries.title: Omelette

blocks.text: An omelette is beaten eggs cooked quickly in butter in a small skillet, then folded into a soft, savory oval. It is one of the fastest real meals you can make, and it is also a skill recipe: the pan is hot, the timing is short, and your hands and ears tell you more than a clock does.

Classic restaurant omelettes are often left slightly creamy in the center. This page aims for a fully set omelette that meets USDA guidance for egg dishes: 160 degrees F in the center, with no liquid raw egg remaining. The result is a little firmer than a traditional French omelette, and it is the safer standard for a teaching cookbook. Once you know the motions, you can make one in a few minutes on a busy morning.

1 omelette (a hearty breakfast or a light meal). Double the eggs and use a 10-inch skillet only after you are comfortable with the basic method. It is easier to make two separate omelettes than one large one.
About 10 to 15 minutes, including setup. The cooking itself takes about 2 to 4 minutes.
Intermediate at first, then easy with practice. The technique is simple, but it happens quickly. Read the whole recipe once before you heat the pan.
An 8 inch nonstick skillet with sloped sides and a handle you can hold securely. A well-seasoned omelette pan also works. A sticky pan will fight you.
A medium mixing bowl
A fork or a small whisk
A heat-safe silicone or rubber spatula (a fork can work in a nonstick pan if you are gentle)
A talking or instant-read thermometer
A tactile or talking timer, useful as a backup, though you will cook mostly by feel and sound
Measuring spoons with tactile markings
A plate, set next to the stove before you start
Optional: a small bowl for cracked eggs, and a grater if you are adding cheese
Long sleeves rolled above the elbow, so they cannot catch the handle or dip into the pan
3 large eggs
1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon, a small pinch) salt, or to taste
A few grindings of black pepper, or a pinch
1 tablespoon unsalted butter
1 tablespoon water or milk, optional, for a slightly more tender curd
Optional fillings, already prepared and at room temperature or gently warmed, about 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) total so the omelette still folds:
Shredded cheese, such as cheddar or Swiss
Cooked, crumbled bacon or diced ham that has already been heated
Finely chopped tender herbs, such as chives or parsley
A spoonful of cooked vegetables that are already soft and not wet

A raw egg in the shell is oval, smooth, and cool. Crack each egg on a flat counter or the rim of a small bowl, then drop it into that small bowl and feel for shell fragments with a spoon before you add it to the mixing bowl. A stray piece of shell feels hard and sharp against the spoon or your clean finger.
Beaten eggs feel uniformly slick and slightly thick, with no separate slippery whites floating among the yolks. Salt is crystalline. Butter is firm when cold; it will melt and then foam in the pan.

If you add cheese, pre-shredded cheese is easy to feel and measure. If you grate your own, a talking scale or a 1/4-cup measure both work. Keep fillings dry. Wet tomatoes or leftover vegetables will make the eggs watery and harder to set.
This recipe uses raw eggs. Use clean, uncracked eggs from the refrigerator, and cook them through as written.

This dish moves quickly. Set the plate by the stove. Beat the eggs, measure the butter, and have any fillings ready before the pan gets hot. If you are new to the motion of folding and sliding the omelette out, you can practice once with the empty, cold pan and a dry plate: tilt the pan over the plate and turn it as if you were unmolding the eggs. Then start cooking.
Use a burner that you can stand square to, and turn the handle of the skillet to the side, inward, so you cannot bump it.
Crack the eggs into a bowl.
Add the salt, pepper, and the optional water or milk.
Beat with a fork or whisk just until the yolks and whites are combined and the mixture feels even. You do not need a frothy foam. Overbeating can make the omelette tough.
Set the 8 inch skillet over medium or just-under-medium heat.
Add the butter and swirl or tilt the pan so the butter coats the bottom and a little of the sides.

Wait until the butter melts, foams, and then settles, and you can hear a soft, lively sizzle. The butter should smell nutty but not browned or acrid. That is your cue that the pan is ready. If the butter smells burnt or the foam goes straight to a sharp, dark smell, take the pan off the heat, wipe it out with a paper towel once it is cool enough to handle, and start again with fresh butter at a slightly lower heat.
Pour the eggs into the pan. They should sizzle gently, not violently.

Right away, stir with the spatula or a fork, keeping the tool moving around the bottom of the pan and shaking the pan gently with your other hand. Soft curds will start to form. At first the mixture still sloshes like a liquid. Within a minute or so, it will feel thicker, like very soft, wet scrambled eggs that are starting to hold together.

When the eggs are mostly set but the top still feels slightly moist, stop stirring and spread the eggs into an even layer. The top should no longer flow like raw egg, though it may still feel a little damp.
If you are using fillings, sprinkle them over one half of the omelette now.

Give the pan another 15 to 30 seconds on the heat so the bottom firms enough to fold. Fold means lift one edge and lay it over the other half. If the bottom starts to smell browned or sharp, the heat is too high. Lift the pan off the burner for a few seconds.

Check the doneness cues in the next section. If the center is still under 160 degrees F or still feels liquid, cook a little longer over lower heat, or finish with a lid on the pan for 15 to 30 seconds so steam can set the top without browning the bottom. Then check again.
To fold, tilt the pan and use the spatula to lift one edge of the omelette and fold it over the other half, making a half-moon.
Let it sit for a few seconds so the fold holds.
Hold the plate next to the skillet, tilt the pan, and slide or invert the omelette onto the plate, seam side down if you can. Serve right away.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The omelette is done when the center is set, with no liquid egg remaining, and a thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 160 degrees F. The surface should feel moist but not wet or slippery with raw egg. The omelette should smell gently cooked and buttery, not sulfurous or scorched.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The omelette should look pale yellow, set, and moist, with no shiny pools of raw egg on top and no large brown scorch patches on the bottom unless the heat was too high. When folded, it should hold a half-moon or oval shape. If you cut it, the center should look cooked and opaque, not liquid and translucent. A thermometer in the thickest part should read 160 degrees F.
These visual cues are for a sighted partner. They do not replace the thermometer or the non-visual cues in the steps. Call them out loud so both of you are working from the same information.

The omelette should look pale yellow, set, and moist, with no shiny pools of raw egg on top and no large brown scorch patches on the bottom unless the heat was too high. When folded, it should hold a half-moon or oval shape. If you cut it, the center should look cooked and opaque, not liquid and translucent. A thermometer in the thickest part should read 160 degrees F.
Raw eggs can carry bacteria. Wash your hands, the bowl, and the fork after you beat the eggs, and cook the omelette to 160 degrees F. Do not taste raw beaten egg.

The skillet handle and the pan itself get hot. Keep the handle turned inward, but not over another burner. Use a dry mitt if the handle heats up. Oil and butter can spatter; stand back when the eggs go in, and do not flick water into the pan.

If you add meat fillings, they should already be cooked. Leftover meat or bacon belongs in the omelette only after it has been cooked and, if it was refrigerated, reheated or at least brought into the hot pan with the eggs until the whole omelette reaches 160 degrees F.
Clean the skillet after cooking. For a nonstick pan, wipe it out or wash it gently once it has cooled a little. Do not leave raw egg sitting in the pan.

Heat control is the whole skill. If the eggs set on the bottom in a few seconds and smell browned, the pan is too hot. If they sit there with no sizzle and no curds after a minute, the pan is too cool. Adjust and try again. Eggs are inexpensive, and a second attempt is part of learning.
Cheese omelette: Add the cheese just before you fold, so it softens but does not scorch on the pan.
Western or Denver-style: Fold in a small amount of already-cooked diced pepper, onion, and ham. Cook the vegetables first in a separate pan until they are soft, then add them as a filling.
Herb omelette: Stir chopped chives, parsley, or dill into the beaten eggs.
Larger appetite: Make a second omelette rather than crowding six eggs into the same 8 inch pan.

If the omelette sticks: The pan is not nonstick enough, or it was not buttered well, or the heat was too high. Do not scrape aggressively. Loosen what you can with a spatula, scramble the rest, and still cook it to 160 degrees F. It will still taste good, even if it is not a neat fold.
Omelettes are best eaten immediately. If you do have leftovers, refrigerate them within 2 hours and eat them within 3 to 4 days. Reheat until the center reaches 165 degrees F.

The method in this page is written in original language, informed by classic omelette technique and by USDA egg-safety temperatures. The doneness target is set to the USDA figure for egg dishes, which is firmer than some classic French recipes.

entries.title: Bacon

blocks.text: This page covers two breakfast staples that look similar in the package and cook in similar pans, but they are not the same food. Regular bacon is cured pork belly. It is fatty, it renders a lot of grease, and it is thin enough that a thermometer is often hard to use. Turkey bacon is made from turkey. It is leaner, it can stick, and it is poultry, so it needs to reach 165 degrees F whenever you can get a reliable reading.

Both are usually sold uncooked and need to be cooked thoroughly before you eat them. Neither one should be judged by color alone. Cured pork bacon can stay pink even when it is fully cooked, and turkey bacon can brown before the interior is hot enough. You will go by texture, sound, smell, time, and, for turkey bacon, a thermometer.

The oven method is the easiest to control and the least spattery. The skillet method is faster for a few slices and teaches you the sound of fat rendering. Both methods are included for each kind of bacon.

About 4 servings. Use 8 to 12 slices of pork bacon, or 8 to 12 slices of turkey bacon, depending on appetite and how crisp you like it. The two kinds should be cooked in separate pans or at separate times, not mixed, because their fat, timing, and safe temperatures differ.
Skillet: about 15 to 20 minutes, including turning.
Oven, pork bacon: about 20 to 25 minutes at 400 degrees F, including a few minutes to preheat.
Oven, turkey bacon: about 20 to 25 minutes at 375 degrees F.
Beginner to intermediate. The steps are simple. The hazards are hot grease, spatters, and, with turkey bacon, making sure poultry is fully cooked.
A large, heavy skillet, for the stovetop method (cast iron or a heavy nonstick both work)
A rimmed baking sheet, for the oven method
Foil or parchment, to line the baking sheet
A wire rack that fits the baking sheet, optional, so fat can drip away
Tongs
A splatter screen
Long oven mitts
A tactile or talking timer
A talking or instant-read meat thermometer, especially for turkey bacon
A plate lined with paper towels or a clean brown paper bag, for draining
A heat-safe jar or metal can, for cooled grease (never pour grease down the sink)
Optional: a lid that fits the skillet, kept nearby in case of a grease flare-up
Optional: a little oil or cooking spray, for turkey bacon, which is lean and can stick
8 to 12 slices regular pork bacon (standard or thick-cut)
or 8 to 12 slices turkey bacon
Cooking spray or about 1 teaspoon oil, for turkey bacon only, if your pan or sheet tends to stick

Do not cook the two kinds in the same pan at the same time. If you want both on the same plate, cook them one after the other and keep the cooked bacon warm in a low oven, about 200 degrees F, on a rack or paper-towel-lined plate.

In the package, both products are thin, cool, and flexible, with slices that can be peeled apart. Pork bacon usually feels fattier and more slippery, with firmer streaks of fat along a slice. Thick-cut pork bacon is obviously thicker and takes longer. Turkey bacon often feels leaner, drier, and a little more uniform, and it may have a slightly tighter, rubbery bend when raw.
If the slices are stuck together, peel them apart slowly while they are still cold. If they tear, you can still cook the pieces; they will just be smaller.

Read the package with a reader app or a helper the first time you buy a new brand. Some turkey bacon is labeled with skillet and oven times. Those times are a starting point. You will still finish by texture and, when possible, temperature.
Keep raw bacon on a plate so its juices do not run onto bread, fruit, or anything that will not be cooked.

Clear a landing space for a hot pan or baking sheet. Set out tongs, a splatter screen, and the paper-towel-lined plate. If you are using the oven, place the rack in the center of the oven before you preheat, and line the baking sheet.
Do not leave bacon cooking unattended. Grease can pop, and thin slices can go from done to burnt in a short time.
If you are cooking pork bacon, plan now for the leftover grease. Let it cool in the pan, then pour it into a heat-safe jar, not down the drain.
Skillet method (pork)

Lay the slices in a cold skillet in a single layer. The slices can touch slightly but should not be stacked. Starting in a cold pan lets the fat render more evenly and can reduce aggressive spatters. Render means the fat melts out of the meat slowly.
Turn the heat to medium.
After a minute or two you will hear a gentle sizzle, then a steadier frying sound as fat melts into the pan. Place a splatter screen over the skillet.

Cook, turning every couple of minutes with tongs, for about 8 to 12 minutes for regular slices, or 12 to 16 minutes for thick-cut. Time varies by stove and by how crisp you want the bacon. Use the doneness cues in the next section.
Transfer the slices to the paper-towel-lined plate to drain. They will crisp a little more as they cool.
Turn off the heat. Let the grease cool before you move the pan or pour it off.
Oven method (pork)
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F. Heat the oven, sometimes called preheat, means bring it to that temperature before the food goes in.

Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil or parchment. For easier cleanup and slightly drier bacon, set a wire rack in the pan and lay the slices on the rack. Otherwise, lay the slices directly on the lined pan in a single layer, not stacked.

Bake 15 to 20 minutes, until the slices feel firm and crisp, with the same texture and smell cues as the skillet method. You usually do not need to turn oven bacon, especially on a rack. If you are cooking directly on the pan and the bottoms feel greasy and soft at 12 minutes, you can turn the slices once with tongs, using long mitts and pulling the rack partly out.
Remove the pan with long mitts.
Transfer the bacon to paper towels.
Let the fat cool in the pan before you discard or save it.

Turkey bacon is poultry. USDA guidance is to cook all poultry to 165 degrees F. Slices are thin, so a single slice can be hard to probe. Use one or more of these methods: fold a slice loosely and insert the thermometer tip into the thickest part without touching the pan; stack two cooked slices briefly and check the center; or, if the product is thicker, check a slice from the side. If you cannot get a trustworthy reading, cook until the slices are hot all the way through, firm, and crisp, and extend the time rather than serving them soft in the middle.
Skillet method (turkey)
If your skillet is not very nonstick, add a thin film of oil or a mist of cooking spray.
Lay the turkey bacon in a single layer. You can start in a cold skillet, as many turkey-bacon packages recommend, or in a skillet already at medium heat. Either way, do not crowd the pan.

Cook over medium heat, turning often, for about 7 to 9 minutes, or until the slices are done as described in the next section. Turkey bacon has less fat, so it can go from pale and flexible to dry and brittle quickly. Stay with the pan and use a splatter screen. There will be less grease than with pork, but there can still be some spatter.
Drain on paper towels and serve.
Oven method (turkey)

Heat the oven to 375 degrees F. Some brands say not to preheat and to put the pan into a cold oven. If your package says that, follow it and start your timer when you turn the oven on, then still finish by texture and temperature. If there is no special instruction, heating the oven first is fine.
Line a baking sheet with foil and coat it lightly with cooking spray, or use a lightly oiled rack.
Lay the slices in a single layer.
Bake about 16 to 19 minutes, until the slices are crisp to your taste and a thermometer reading, if you can get one, is 165 degrees F. Turning is usually not necessary.
Remove the pan with long mitts and drain the bacon on paper towels.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues for pork bacon: The slices go from floppy and raw-feeling to firmer, then to crisp. When you lift a slice with tongs, it should hold its shape and feel rigid along the edges, not limp and heavy with unrendered fat. The sizzle changes. At first it is uneven and can sputter as water leaves the meat. As the bacon finishes, the sound becomes a drier, steadier fry, then quiets as less moisture remains. The kitchen should smell like cooked, smoky pork, not sour or burnt. A sharp, acrid smell means the pan is too hot or the bacon is scorching. Reduce the heat. A thermometer is often impractical on a thin slice, because there is not enough depth for the probe. If you use thick-cut bacon and can insert the tip sideways into a folded slice without touching the pan, cook until the bacon is crisp throughout. Color is not a reliable test. Cured bacon may remain pink after it is fully cooked. Cook pork bacon until it is thoroughly done and crisp to your taste. Do not stop at a soft, under-rendered, raw-feeling center.

Non-visual cues for turkey bacon: The slices should feel firm and heated through, with no cool, raw, or pasty center when you press or cut one. A thermometer should read 165 degrees F in the thickest area you can measure. The edges should feel drier and more rigid. You can cook it to a softer chew or to a crisp snap, but it should not feel undercooked and rubbery-cool in the middle. The smell should be cooked and savory, like turkey and smoke, not raw poultry.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: Pork bacon usually turns a deep golden to reddish brown and looks crisp and rendered, but curing can leave some pink even when it is fully cooked, so color alone is not a safety test. The fat should look clear and melted, not thick and raw-white in the middle of a slice. Turkey bacon should look evenly browned and cooked through, with no dull, raw, rubbery center. Because turkey bacon is poultry, confirm 165 degrees F whenever you can get a thermometer reading.
These visual cues are for a sighted partner. They do not replace the thermometer or the non-visual cues in the steps. Call them out loud so both of you are working from the same information.

Pork bacon usually turns a deep golden to reddish brown and looks crisp and rendered, but curing can leave some pink even when it is fully cooked, so color alone is not a safety test. The fat should look clear and melted, not thick and raw-white in the middle of a slice. Turkey bacon should look evenly browned and cooked through, with no dull, raw, rubbery center. Because turkey bacon is poultry, confirm 165 degrees F whenever you can get a thermometer reading.

Raw pork bacon and raw turkey bacon should be treated like other raw meat and poultry. Wash your hands, tongs, the plate that held the raw slices, and the counter with soap and hot water before you touch bread, fruit, cooked food, or your face.
Hot grease is the main injury risk. Use a splatter screen. Keep your face and forearms back when you turn slices. Wear short sleeves or rolled sleeves. Keep children and pets away from the stove.
If grease catches fire, turn off the heat and slide a lid over the pan to smother the flame. Do not throw water on a grease fire. Do not carry a flaming pan to the sink.

The oven pan and the rendered fat are both hot enough to burn. Use long mitts. Set the pan on a reserved landing space. Let fat cool before you pour it into a jar. Do not pour grease down the sink; it can solidify in the pipes.

Do not leave raw bacon out on the counter. Keep it refrigerated at 40 degrees F or below, and use opened packages within about 7 days, or freeze them. Cooked bacon should not sit out more than 2 hours (1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F).
Crispness: Bacon continues to firm as it cools for a minute or two on paper towels. If you want it very crisp, cook a little longer, but stay close at the end.
Thick-cut pork bacon: Give it more time, and use the oven if you want more even results with less turning.

Microwave: This works in a pinch for a few slices. Place slices in a single layer on a microwave-safe plate lined with paper towels, cover with another towel, and cook in short bursts, turning or rotating as your oven requires, until the texture cues above are met. Times vary widely. Watch for steam and for paper that can overheat. Turkey bacon still needs to be fully hot throughout.

Air fryer: A single layer at 350 to 375 degrees F often takes about 6 to 10 minutes for pork and about 8 to 10 minutes for turkey, turning once if your basket tends to cook unevenly. Check early. Finish turkey bacon at 165 degrees F when you can measure it.
Breakfast plate: These methods pair well with the omelette sample in this folder. Cook the bacon first, then the omelette, so the eggs get your full attention.

Saving pork bacon fat: Strained, cooled bacon fat can be stored in the refrigerator in a labeled jar and used later to fry eggs or potatoes. Treat it like other perishable fat and keep it refrigerated.
Refrigerate cooked bacon within 2 hours, wrapped or in a container, for 3 to 4 days, or freeze it. Reheat until it is steaming hot and, for leftover turkey bacon, until it reaches 165 degrees F.

The methods and safety notes in this page are written in original language, informed by published bacon-cooking methods, manufacturer heating directions for turkey bacon, and USDA food-safety guidance.

entries.servings: About 4 servings. Use 8 to 12 slices of pork bacon, or 8 to 12 slices of turkey bacon, depending on appetite and how crisp you like it. The two kinds should be cooked in separate pans or at separate times, not mixed, because their fat, timing, and safe temperatures differ.

Skillet: about 15 to 20 minutes, including turning.
Oven, pork bacon: about 20 to 25 minutes at 400 degrees F, including a few minutes to preheat.
Oven, turkey bacon: about 20 to 25 minutes at 375 degrees F.
entries.difficulty: Beginner to intermediate. The steps are simple. The hazards are hot grease, spatters, and, with turkey bacon, making sure poultry is fully cooked.

blocks.text: Toast topped with mashed avocado, salt, and an optional firm-cooked egg. It is a fast savory breakfast.
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 ripe avocado
1 or 2 slices bread
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, or to taste
A squeeze of lemon or lime juice, optional
1 large egg, optional, cooked until firm
Black pepper, optional
A ripe avocado yields gently when pressed and feels slightly soft, not mushy and not hard as a rock. The flesh inside should feel creamy, not stringy and brown all the way through.

If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Toast the bread until it feels dry and smells toasted.
Cut the avocado in half around the pit.
Twist the halves apart.
Carefully pop out the pit with a spoon. Do not strike the pit with a knife.
Scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Mash it with a fork.
Add salt and lemon if you like.
Spread the mash on the toast.
Top with a firm-cooked egg if you want one, cooked to the cues in Fried Eggs Cooked Through.
Serve at once.

Spoon the cream over the top.
Add salt and pepper.
Set the dishes on a baking sheet.

Let the dishes cool 1 minute.
Use mitts.
Serve in the dishes.

In a second bowl, mix the milk, egg, melted butter, and vanilla.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix.
Stir in the fruit.
Spread the mix in the pan.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until the center feels set and a thermometer reads 160 degrees F.
Cool 10 minutes.
Cut into squares.
Serve warm.

blocks.text: A Southern breakfast of split biscuits topped with a milk gravy made from breakfast sausage drippings. Bake the biscuits from the Baked Goods chapter, or use good store-bought biscuits.
About 35 minutes, if the biscuits are already baked
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
8 baked biscuits
1 pound pork breakfast sausage
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) all-purpose flour
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) milk
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
Salt, to taste
The gravy should feel smooth and coat a spoon, not pasty and not as thin as milk. Flour lumps feel hard in the spoon if you have not stirred enough.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cook the sausage in a skillet over medium heat, breaking it up, until it is 160 degrees F.
Leave the drippings in the pan.
Sprinkle the flour over the sausage.
Stir 1 minute, until the raw flour smell fades.
Pour in the milk slowly, stirring the whole time.
Simmer, stirring, 3 to 6 minutes, until the gravy thickens and coats a spoon. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Add the pepper.
Taste a cooled spoonful and add salt only if it needs it.
Split the biscuits.
Spoon the hot gravy over them.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The gravy should feel smooth and silky on a spoon. The sausage must be 160 degrees F before you add the milk. You should smell cooked pork and pepper, not raw flour.

Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The gravy should look opaque and pale, and it should coat a spoon. The sausage should be brown, with no pink.
Cook sausage to 160 degrees F. The gravy is very hot and can spatter as it thickens. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, and bring gravy back to a bubble. Cook ground pork to 160 degrees F.
If the gravy is too thick, add a splash of milk. If it is too thin, simmer a few minutes more. Turkey sausage can be used, but cook it to 165 degrees F, and you may need a little oil in the pan.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The muffin should look lightly browned. The egg should look set. The cheese should look melted.
Cook eggs until firm. Cook bacon or sausage fully before they go in the sandwich. Reheat leftover meat to 165 degrees F. Cook egg dishes to 160 degrees F. There should be no liquid raw egg left.
You can cook the eggs in a greased jar lid ring in the pan if you want a neat round shape. A biscuit from the Baked Goods chapter also works here.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Pork or turkey breakfast sausage cooked in a skillet as patties or links until it reaches a safe temperature. Pork sausage should reach 160 degrees F. Turkey sausage should reach 165 degrees F.
4, about 8 patties
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound breakfast sausage, as patties or links, pork or turkey
A little oil, only if the sausage is very lean
Raw sausage feels soft and cold. Patties should be even in thickness. Links are already shaped. Keep raw sausage on a plate so juices do not run across the counter.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat a skillet over medium heat.
Add a film of oil only if the sausage is lean turkey or if the pan is very dry.
Add the patties or links in a single layer.
Cook, turning now and then, 8 to 12 minutes, depending on thickness.
Check a patty or the end of a link with a thermometer.
Pork should read 160 degrees F.
Turkey should read 165 degrees F.
The juices should run clear, not pink and thick, and the meat should feel firm, not pasty.
Drain on a plate lined with a paper towel. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Serve hot.

A one-pan breakfast of potatoes, cooked sausage or vegetables, and eggs finished on top until the eggs are set.
About 40 minutes
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound potatoes, cut into 1/2 inch (half inch) cubes
2 tablespoons oil
8 ounces breakfast sausage, or 1 cup leftover cooked vegetables
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
4 large eggs
1/2 cup (half a cup) shredded cheese, optional
Black pepper
The potatoes should be tender before the eggs go on, or the eggs will overcook while you wait for the potatoes.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
If you are using raw sausage, cook it until it is 160 degrees F for pork, or 165 degrees F for turkey, then break it up and move it to a plate.
Add the potatoes and salt to the pan.
Cook 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then, until they are tender and crisp in spots.
Return the sausage, or add the leftover vegetables, and heat until steaming.
Make 4 small wells in the pan.
Crack an egg into each well.
Cover and cook until the eggs are set, 160 degrees F, about 5 to 8 minutes.
Sprinkle cheese on top if you like.
Serve from the skillet, which will be very hot.

entries.title: Chia Pudding

blocks.text: A no-cook pudding made by soaking chia seeds in milk until they swell and thicken. It is a cold breakfast or a simple dessert.
About 10 minutes of work, plus at least 2 hours in the refrigerator
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) chia seeds
1 cup milk, or a milk alternative
1 tablespoon maple syrup or honey
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) vanilla extract, optional
Fruit, for serving
Dry chia seeds feel like tiny, hard ovals. After soaking they feel gelatinous and slippery, and the pudding should feel thick like yogurt, not watery, and not a solid block of dry seeds.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the chia, milk, sweetener, and vanilla in a jar.
Wait 5 minutes, then stir again so the seeds do not sit in a clump at the bottom.
Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours, or overnight.
Stir.
Add a splash of milk if it is too thick.
Serve cold, with fruit if you like.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The seeds should feel soft-gelled, not hard. The mix should smell fresh and milky, not sour.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The pudding should look thick and even, with no dry layer of seeds at the bottom and no standing liquid on top after you stir.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The pudding should look thick and even, with no dry layer of seeds at the bottom and no standing liquid on top after you stir.
Keep it refrigerated and eat it within 3 days. If it smells sour, throw it out. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Cocoa powder or mashed banana can be stirred in before chilling. If you dislike the seed texture, blend the pudding until it is smooth.

blocks.text: Toast with butter, sugar, and cinnamon. You can make it in a toaster oven, a skillet, or under a broiler, which is the top heating element in an oven. This version uses a skillet or a toaster oven, which is easier to control.
1 to 2
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
2 slices bread
1 tablespoon butter, softened
2 teaspoons sugar
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) cinnamon
The butter should be soft enough to spread without tearing the bread. The cinnamon sugar should feel sandy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the sugar and cinnamon in a small bowl.
Toast the bread lightly, or leave it untoasted if you will finish it in a skillet.
Spread the butter on the bread.
Sprinkle the cinnamon sugar on top.
For a toaster oven, toast again until the sugar feels melted and the bread smells caramelized, often 2 to 4 minutes.
For a skillet, place the bread butter-side up over medium-low heat and cover for 2 to 3 minutes, until the bottom is crisp and the topping is warm.
Let it cool 30 seconds. The sugar can burn your mouth.
Serve.

Sugar burns quickly. Stay with the toaster oven or skillet. The topping is very hot at first. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Mix a small jar of cinnamon sugar to keep on hand. A 4 to 1 mix of sugar to cinnamon is a good start.

2 tablespoons oil or butter
1 medium onion, diced
3 cups cooked potatoes, cubed, or 1 pound potatoes, cubed and already cooked until tender
2 cups chopped cooked corned beef
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper
Salt, only if needed, because corned beef is salty
4 large eggs, optional
Corned beef feels firm and a little oily, with visible fat streaks. The hash should feel crispy in spots, not wet and stewed.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
Add the onion.
Cook 4 to 5 minutes, until it feels soft.
Add the potatoes and corned beef.
Season with pepper.
Press the mix into the pan.
Cook 4 to 5 minutes without stirring, until the bottom feels browned and crisp.
Turn sections and brown the other side.
Taste a cooled bite before you add salt.
If you want eggs, make wells and cook them covered until they are set, 160 degrees F.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: You should hear a sizzle, not a steam hiss. The bottom should feel crusty. Corned beef should be hot all the way through. Leftover meat in the hash should reach 165 degrees F.

For steaks, roasts, and other whole pieces of beef, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. If this dish is a slow stew, keep cooking until the meat is also tender.
Canned corned beef works if you do not have leftovers. Do not stir too often or you will lose the crust.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) water or milk, or a mix
1/2 cup (half a cup) Cream of Wheat or plain farina
A pinch of salt
1 tablespoon butter or brown sugar, optional
Dry farina feels finer than grits, like very fine sand. The finished cereal should feel silky, not lumpy and not pasty.

Bring the liquid and salt to a boil.
Slowly whisk in the farina. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk until the mixture looks even.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring, 2 to 3 minutes, until it is thick and smooth.
Stir in butter or sugar if you like.
Serve at once.
