entries.title: Chicken Nuggets

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

These baked chicken nuggets are bite-size pieces of boneless chicken with a crisp breadcrumb coating, meant for lunch, a casual supper, or a plate of snacks. They are cousins of the boneless wings in the Misc chapter, but they are not tossed in hot sauce. Bake them until a thermometer in the center of a thick nugget reads 165 degrees F. An air-fryer method is included as a variation.
4 as a lunch, or 6 as a snack
About 40 minutes
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
Two shallow bowls or pie plates for breading
Tongs or a fork
A wire rack for the pan, optional
An air fryer, optional, for the variation
1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) boneless, skinless chicken breasts or thighs
1 teaspoon salt, divided
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) paprika, optional
1/2 cup (half a cup) all-purpose flour
2 large eggs
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) dry breadcrumbs or panko
Oil spray, or 2 tablespoons oil for brushing
Dipping sauces, such as ketchup, barbecue sauce, or honey mustard, for serving

Chicken breasts feel smooth and firm, with a thicker middle; thighs are a bit looser and more even in thickness. Cut the meat into chunks about 1 to 1 1/2 inches, roughly the size of a large walnut or the first two joints of a finger, so they cook at the same rate. Flour feels silky. Breadcrumbs feel coarser and dry. The breaded nuggets should feel dry and sandy on the outside, with no slick, bare spots.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F and set a rack in the middle.
Line a baking sheet with parchment or foil, set a rack on it if you have one, and oil the surface lightly.
Cut the chicken into even 1 to 1 1/2 inch (one to one and a half inch) pieces.
Pat them dry and toss with 1/2 teaspoon salt, the pepper, garlic powder, and paprika.
Set up three bowls: flour mixed with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt; beaten eggs; and breadcrumbs.
Using one hand for wet and one for dry if you can, dip each piece in flour, then egg, then breadcrumbs, pressing so the crumbs stick.
Set the pieces on the prepared pan with space between them.
Spray or brush the tops lightly with oil.
Bake 10 minutes, then turn the pieces and bake 6 to 10 minutes more.
Check doneness in the center of two or three of the thickest nuggets.
They are done at 165 degrees F.
If any are under, return the pan for 2 to 3 minutes and check again.
Serve hot with dipping sauce.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The coating should feel firm and a little crisp, and the meat should feel springy, not squishy. You should smell cooked chicken and toasted crumbs, not raw meat. A thermometer in the center of the thickest piece must read 165 degrees F.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The coating should look golden and dry, not pale and pasty or dark brown. When you cut a thick nugget, the chicken should be opaque and white or very light tan all the way through, with no raw pink or glassy look, and the juices should run clear.

When you cut a thick nugget, the chicken should be opaque and white or very light tan all the way through, with no raw pink or glassy look, and the juices should run clear.

Use a raw-poultry board and wash your hands, the knife, and any tongs that touched raw chicken before you handle sauces or plates. Do not taste raw egg or raw flour from the breading bowls. 2 to 4
About 15 minutes

Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings

A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
4 cups water plus 1 teaspoon instant dashi powder, or 4 cups low-sodium vegetable broth
3 tablespoons miso paste, white or yellow
1/2 cup (half a cup) soft tofu, cut into small cubes
1 green onion, thinly sliced
Optional: a small handful of dried wakame seaweed, soaked and drained
Miso paste is thick, salty, and fragrant. Dissolve it in a little hot broth first so you do not have lumps. Tofu cubes should be soft and small enough for a spoon.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Bring the water and dashi, or the broth, to a simmer. Simmer means small, gentle bubbles.
If you are using seaweed, add it now.
Lower the heat so the pot is hot but not boiling hard.
Whisk the miso with a ladle of hot broth in a small bowl until smooth, then stir it back into the pot. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk until the mixture looks even.
Add the tofu and heat 1 minute, without boiling hard.
Add the green onion.
Serve at once.

The pot is hot. Taste before you add salt. Miso is already salty. Use clean bowls. Reheat leftovers gently, and try not to boil them hard. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
White miso is milder than red miso. Add cooked mushrooms if you like. Instant dashi is a powder or packet in many grocery stores.

Thinly sliced beef cooked with onions, then piled into a roll with melted cheese. Use shaved steak or very thinly sliced sirloin. The USDA minimum for whole-muscle beef is 145 degrees F with a 3-minute rest, but thin slices in a sandwich are often cooked further, until no longer red and raw-feeling. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
About 30 minutes
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound shaved steak or very thinly sliced beef
1 tablespoon oil
1 medium onion, thinly sliced
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
4 slices provolone or American cheese, or 1/2 cup (half a cup) cheese sauce
2 hoagie rolls, split
Shaved steak feels thin and floppy. It cooks fast. Keep the pieces moving so they do not steam into a clump.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
Add the onion and a pinch of salt. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Cook 6 to 8 minutes, until it feels soft and smells sweet.
Push the onion to the side.
Add the beef and the remaining salt.
Cook, stirring and breaking up the meat, until it is browned and a thermometer in a thicker piece reads at least 145 degrees F, and the meat no longer feels raw and slimy.
Lay the cheese over the meat.
Cover 30 to 60 seconds, until the cheese feels melted.
Pile the mix into the rolls.
Serve at once.

Heat the oil or butter in a large pot over medium heat.

Heat gently. Do not boil hard after the milk goes in.
Taste a cooled spoonful and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot.

entries.title: Beef Tips over Mashed Potatoes and Gravy

blocks.text: This is a slow, savory braise: bite-size pieces of beef simmered in a brown gravy until they go from chewy to tender, served over buttery mashed potatoes. It is a good teaching recipe for two skills at once, browning meat and then cooking it gently in liquid, plus a straightforward pot of mashed potatoes.

The beef is done when a fork or the tip of a knife slides into a piece with little resistance, not merely when it has reached the USDA minimum temperature. Stew-size pieces of beef are safely cooked at 145 degrees F with a 3-minute rest, but they will still be tough at that point. You will keep simmering until the meat is tender, which takes well over an hour.
4 generous main-dish servings (6 smaller ones)
About 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours, including 30 minutes of prep. Most of that time is hands-off simmering. The mashed potatoes take about 30 minutes and can be made near the end of the braise.
Intermediate. There is knife work, a hot Dutch oven, and two pots going near the end. The method itself is steady and forgiving.
A large cutting board, with a damp towel underneath so it cannot slide
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove
A heavy Dutch oven or a wide, heavy pot with a lid
A second large pot, for the potatoes
A colander, for draining potatoes
A potato masher or ricer
A wooden spoon or heat-safe spatula
Tongs
A talking or instant-read meat thermometer
A tactile or talking timer
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator
Long oven mitts or sturdy pot holders
A ladle or large spoon, for serving
Optional: a talking kitchen scale, for the beef and potatoes
Optional: a vegetable peeler
For the beef tips and gravy
2 to 2 1/2 pounds (two to two and a half pounds) beef chuck roast, cut into 1 to 1 1/2 inch (one to one and a half inch) pieces, or the same weight of already-cut stew beef
1 1/2 teaspoons (one and a half teaspoons) kosher salt, or 1 teaspoon table salt, plus more later if needed
1 teaspoon black pepper
1 teaspoon dried thyme, or 2 teaspoons fresh thyme leaves
2 tablespoons vegetable oil, or another neutral oil, divided
2 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 medium yellow onion, diced
3 garlic cloves, minced
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) all-purpose flour
3 cups low-sodium beef broth
1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce
1 tablespoon soy sauce, optional but helpful for a deeper, savory gravy
2 tablespoons chopped fresh parsley, optional, for serving
For the mashed potatoes
2 pounds Yukon Gold or russet potatoes
1 tablespoon salt, for the cooking water, plus more to taste
4 tablespoons unsalted butter
1/2 cup (half a cup) whole milk or half-and-half, warmed
Black pepper, to taste

Chuck roast feels well marbled: you will notice softer fat seams running through firmer muscle. Stew beef is already in cubes, which saves cutting time, though the pieces can be uneven. Trim off only large, hard chunks of fat or silver skin; some fat is useful for flavor.

An onion is round and papery. After you cut off the root and stem ends and peel away the dry skin, the flesh is slick and layered. Garlic cloves are smaller, with a tighter paper skin that slips off more easily if you crush the clove lightly under the flat of the knife (press down on the blade spine, never on the sharp edge).

Flour is fine and dry. Beef broth is thin and smells meaty. Worcestershire sauce is thin, dark, and sharp, with a tamarind and anchovy smell. Soy sauce is salty and rounded. Keep both bottles labeled.

Yukon Gold potatoes are medium, smooth, and slightly thin-skinned. Russets are larger, with a rougher, drier skin. Either works. After peeling, the surface is damp and slightly starchy. Warm the milk in a small pan or in the microwave until it feels hot to a clean finger held just above the surface, or until a thermometer reads about 120 to 140 degrees F. Cold milk makes the mash gluey and cools it too fast.
Measure broth with a liquid cup and a liquid level indicator so you can hear when you near 3 cups.

Pat the beef dry and season it before you heat the pot. Dice the onion and mince the garlic, and set them aside in small bowls. Measure the flour, broth, Worcestershire, and soy sauce so they are ready when the onions are cooked. Clear a landing space for the hot pot. If your stove has more than one burner, plan to keep the potatoes on a back or side burner so you are not reaching over the Dutch oven.

If you are starting with a roast, place it on the board and cut it into roughly even cubes, about 1 to 1 1/2 inches (one to one and a half inches). Use the claw grip and a cut-resistant glove. A cube about the size of a large walnut or the first joint of your thumb is a good guide. If the beef is already cubed, skip the cutting.
Toss the beef in a bowl with the salt, pepper, and thyme until the pieces feel evenly dusted.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the Dutch oven over medium-high heat until the oil smells hot and a single piece of beef sizzles firmly when it touches the surface.
Add only enough beef to make a single layer with space between the pieces. If you crowd the pot, the meat will steam and will not brown.
Sear without moving the pieces for 2 to 3 minutes, until they release easily and smell deeply browned, not just steamed. Sear means cook the surface in a hot pan until it browns.
Turn and brown a second side the same way.
Transfer that batch to a plate and repeat with the remaining oil and beef. The bottom of the pot should have browned bits stuck to it. Those will flavor the gravy.
Reduce the heat to medium.
Add the butter and the diced onion to the pot. Dice means cut into small, even cubes.
Stir, scraping the bottom, and cook 3 to 5 minutes, until the onion feels softer, smells sweet, and no longer tastes raw and sharp if you test a cooled piece.
Add the garlic and cook about 30 seconds, until it is fragrant. Do not let the garlic stay on the hot surface long enough to smell bitter or sharp in a burnt way.
Sprinkle the flour over the onions.
Stir for about 1 minute, until the flour coats the onions and leaves a thin film on the bottom of the pot and the raw flour smell fades.

Slowly pour in the broth while you stir or whisk, scraping the bottom so the browned bits dissolve and no dry lumps of flour remain. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk. You can feel lumps with the back of a spoon. Press and stir until the liquid is smooth.
Stir in the Worcestershire and soy sauce.
Return the beef and any juices from the plate to the pot.
Bring the liquid up until you hear a steady boil, then reduce the heat so the pot stays at a gentle simmer. Simmer means small, regular bubbles, not a hard, rattling boil.
Cover and cook for 1 hour, stirring every 20 minutes or so and making sure nothing is sticking. A talking timer helps here.

After 1 hour, uncover the pot and keep simmering 45 minutes to 1 hour more, stirring now and then, until the beef is very tender and the gravy has thickened. Use the doneness cues in the next section.
Taste a cooled spoonful of gravy and add a pinch of salt only if it needs it. Low-sodium broth and soy sauce already contribute salt.
While the beef finishes, peel the potatoes if you like a smoother mash. A peeler is safer than a knife. Work away from your body and rotate the potato.
Cut them into roughly even chunks, about 1 1/2 to 2 inches (one and a half to two inches), so they cook at the same rate.

Put them in the second pot, add cold water to cover by about 1 inch, and add the 1 tablespoon of salt. Feel with a clean finger or a spoon for the water line before you turn on the heat, or use a liquid level indicator at the pot rim.
Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a moderate boil so the pot does not splash.
Cook 15 to 20 minutes, until a piece is done. Use the potato cues in the next section.
Drain the potatoes well in a colander, then return them to the hot pot for a minute so leftover steam can escape.
Add the butter and the warmed milk.
Mash until the mixture feels smooth enough for your taste, with no hard lumps. Do not beat it long after it is smooth, or it can turn gluey.
Taste a cooled bite and add salt and pepper as needed. Cover to keep warm.
Spoon a bed of mashed potatoes into a bowl or plate and ladle the beef and gravy over the top. Sprinkle with parsley if you are using it. Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues for the beef and gravy: A fork or the tip of a knife should slide into a piece of beef with little resistance. The meat should give and start to shred when you press it, not bounce back like a rubber eraser. A thermometer in the center of a piece will be well above 145 degrees F by this point. That minimum is for safety on whole-muscle beef. Tenderness is the real finishing cue for this dish. The gravy should feel silky and coat the back of a spoon. When you draw a finger (carefully, the spoon will be hot) or the edge of another spoon through that coating, it should leave a brief, clear trail. If the gravy is still thin and watery at the end, simmer a few more minutes uncovered. If it is too thick and pasty, stir in a splash of broth or water. The kitchen should smell browned, meaty, and savory, not sour or raw.

Non-visual cues for the potatoes: A fork or skewer should slide into the center of a chunk with no grit or hard core. The chunk should mash easily when pressed against the side of the pot. A thermometer in the center of a large chunk will often read around 205 to 210 degrees F when the potato is fully soft. The pieces may show slight cracks at the edges and will smell plainly of cooked potato, not raw and earthy.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The beef should look browned on the outside and dull and cooked inside, and it should come apart easily. The gravy should look brown and slightly thick, not watery and not pasty. The mashed potatoes should look fluffy and even, not gluey and shiny, and not dry with hard lumps.
These visual cues are for a sighted partner. They do not replace the thermometer or the non-visual cues in the steps. Call them out loud so both of you are working from the same information.

The beef should be browned on the outside, not gray and steamed. In the finished gravy, the meat should look dull and cooked, not red or raw in the center. The gravy should be a medium-brown and thick enough to coat a spoon, not the color of weak broth. The mashed potatoes should look fluffy and even, with no hard, translucent lumps of undercooked potato.

Use the claw grip and a cut-resistant glove when you cut raw beef and when you cut potatoes. Keep raw beef and its juices away from the potatoes, butter, milk, and serving dishes until the beef is fully cooked. Wash the board, knife, and your hands with soap and hot water after cutting the meat.

The Dutch oven, its lid, and the potato pot will be very hot, and the gravy can bubble and spit as it thickens. Keep handles turned inward, use long mitts or sturdy pot holders, and lift the lid away from your face so steam does not roll toward you.
Never fill the potato pot so full that it boils over. If a boil sounds suddenly louder and you hear water hitting the burner, reduce the heat.
Refrigerate leftovers promptly, as described below. A big pot of gravy cools slowly, so divide it into shallow containers.
Better browning: Dry beef and uncrowded batches matter more than high heat. If the pot sounds like it is steaming instead of sizzling, wait, or brown fewer pieces at a time.
No soy sauce: You can leave it out. The gravy will still work. A teaspoon of tomato paste cooked with the flour is another way to deepen the flavor.

Mushrooms or carrots: Add sliced mushrooms after the onion softens, and cook until they give off liquid and start to shrink, or add thick carrot coins with the broth. They should be tender by the time the beef is tender.

Make-ahead: The beef and gravy often taste even better the next day. Reheat gently on the stove until the gravy bubbles and the beef is hot in the center, at least 165 degrees F if you are reheating leftovers. Add a splash of broth if the gravy has tightened in the refrigerator. The potatoes are best freshly mashed, but they can be reheated with a little extra milk.
Other starches: The same beef and gravy are good over egg noodles or rice if you want to skip the potatoes.
Refrigerate within 2 hours, in shallow containers, for 3 to 4 days, or freeze the beef and gravy for up to 3 to 4 months. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring gravy back to a bubble on the stove.
The method and amounts in this page are written in original language, informed by published beef-tips and mashed-potato recipes and by USDA temperatures for beef and leftovers.

entries.title: Spaghetti with Meat Sauce

blocks.text: Spaghetti with meat sauce is a weeknight staple: a pot of ground beef simmered with onion, garlic, tomato paste, and crushed tomatoes, tossed with long pasta and a little of the starchy cooking water. It is a good teaching recipe for browning ground meat, judging a simmer by sound, and cooking pasta to a firm, pleasant bite without looking at it.
This is an American-style meat sauce, not a long Sunday Bolognese. It is ready in under an hour, and the sauce can be made ahead.
4 to 6
About 45 to 55 minutes, including 15 minutes of prep and a 15- to 20-minute simmer.
Beginner to intermediate. The knife work is simple, and the timing is relaxed, but you will manage two pots and a pot of boiling water.
A cutting board, with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove
A wide, heavy pot or a deep skillet with tall sides, for the sauce
A large pot, for the pasta
A colander
A wooden spoon or heat-safe spatula
A measuring cup for scooping out pasta water
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator
Measuring spoons with tactile markings
A talking or instant-read meat thermometer
A tactile or talking timer
Long oven mitts or sturdy pot holders
Tongs or a pasta fork, for turning and serving the spaghetti
A ladle
Optional: a talking kitchen scale, and a box grater or a bowl of pre-grated Parmesan
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, finely diced
3 garlic cloves, minced
1 pound ground beef (85 or 90 percent lean is a good middle ground)
1 teaspoon salt, divided, plus more for the pasta water
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
2 tablespoons tomato paste
1 teaspoon dried oregano
1 teaspoon dried basil, or 2 teaspoons Italian seasoning in place of the oregano and basil
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) red pepper flakes, optional
1 can (28 ounces) crushed tomatoes
1/2 cup (half a cup) water or low-sodium beef broth, if the sauce gets tighter than you like
1 pound dried spaghetti
1/2 cup (half a cup) grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
A little chopped fresh basil or parsley, optional

Ground beef is cool, damp, and packed. Keep it on a plate until it goes in the pot. Onion and garlic are described in the beef-tips recipe in this folder: peel the papery skins, use the claw grip, and keep the pieces fairly small so they soften quickly. If chopping onion is uncomfortable at first, a food chopper or already-diced onion from the store is fine.

Tomato paste is thick, sticky, and concentrated, usually from a small can or tube. Crushed tomatoes are wet and slightly chunky in the can; use a liquid level indicator only if you transfer them to a cup, or simply empty the whole can into the pot. Dried oregano and basil are leafy and fragrant; Italian seasoning is a blend with a similar smell. Parmesan is dry, granular, and salty. Pre-grated cheese is the easiest to measure by the handful or with a 1/2-cup measure.
Dried spaghetti is a tight, long bundle. Before the water is hot, you can feel how much of the box you are using. For 1 pound, use the full standard box.

Salt for pasta water should be generous. A common teaching cue is that the water should taste plainly salty, like seawater, once the salt dissolves. Add the salt after the water is hot, so it dissolves quickly, and keep your face away from the steam.

Dice the onion and mince the garlic first, then wash your hands and set those bowls aside. Measure the tomato paste, herbs, and cheese. Open the can of tomatoes and set it near the stove. Fill the pasta pot with water before you start the sauce, but do not turn it on until the sauce is simmering, unless you are comfortable managing both at once.

Clear space for draining pasta. Set the colander in the sink before the pot of water boils. Make sure you can carry or slide the heavy pot safely, or use a smaller pot and cook the spaghetti in two batches if a full pot is hard to lift.
Heat the olive oil in the wide pot over medium heat until it smells hot and flows easily when you tilt the pot.
Add the onion and a pinch of the salt.
Cook, stirring often, 4 to 6 minutes, until the onion feels soft, smells sweet, and no longer tastes sharp and raw if you try a cooled piece.
Add the garlic and cook about 30 seconds, until it is fragrant. If the garlic starts to smell bitter or sharp in a burnt way, reduce the heat.
Add the ground beef, the remaining salt, and the pepper.

Break the meat into small pieces with the spoon as it cooks. At first the beef is soft and pasty. As it cooks, it will firm up, smell savory, and stop feeling raw and slick. Keep stirring so the pieces brown rather than steam in a solid cake.
Cook until a thermometer in several pieces reads 160 degrees F, and no soft, raw-feeling meat remains. This usually takes 6 to 8 minutes.

If a lot of fat has collected in the pot and you prefer a less greasy sauce, push the meat to one side and spoon off some of the fat, or carefully tilt the pot and spoon from the edge. Leave a little fat for flavor.
Stir in the tomato paste, oregano, basil, and red pepper flakes if you are using them.
Cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens slightly in smell, from bright and raw-tomato to deeper and caramelized. This step takes the canned edge off the sauce.
Pour in the crushed tomatoes and stir, scraping the bottom of the pot.
Bring the sauce up until you hear a gentle bubble, then reduce the heat to maintain a steady, quiet simmer, not a splattering boil. Simmer means small, gentle bubbles.
Set a talking timer for 15 minutes. Stir now and then so the sauce does not stick. Use the sauce cues in the next section.
You can keep the sauce on very low heat while the pasta cooks. If it starts to spit, turn the heat down and partly cover the pot, leaving a gap so steam can escape.
While the sauce simmers, bring the large pot of water to a rolling boil. You will hear a full, rolling bubble, and steam will rise strongly from the surface.
Add the salt, then add the spaghetti.
Fan the noodles with tongs or a spoon as they soften so they slide under the water and do not set in a stiff clump. Stir in the first 30 seconds, then once or twice more.

Cook according to the package time, then start testing about 1 minute earlier. To test, lift a strand, blow on it or hold it until it is cool enough, and bite it. Al dente pasta is fully flexible, cooked through, and still slightly firm in the center, with no hard, chalky, raw core. Al dente means "to the tooth," or tender with a slight firmness in the center. If you cut a cooled strand, you should feel even resistance, not a brittle middle.

Before you drain, dip a heat-safe mug or measuring cup into the pot and save about 1 cup of the starchy pasta water. The water will be hot. Use a mitt and set the cup back from the edge of the counter.
Drain the pasta in the colander.
Add the drained spaghetti to the sauce, or return the pasta to its pot and ladle the sauce over it.
Add about 1/2 cup (half a cup) of the reserved pasta water and the Parmesan. Reserved pasta water is the starchy cooking water you saved, and it helps the sauce cling to the noodles.
Toss with tongs until the noodles feel evenly coated and the sauce clings rather than sitting in a puddle at the bottom. If it seems dry or sticky, add more pasta water a little at a time.
Serve hot, with more Parmesan and herbs if you like.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The ground beef is safely done when a thermometer in several pieces reads 160 degrees F, and no soft, raw-feeling meat remains. After 15 to 20 minutes, the sauce should feel thicker. A spoon drawn through it should leave a brief trail, and it should mound a little on the spoon rather than running off like juice. The raw, tinny smell of canned tomato should have rounded into something sweeter and cooked. Taste a cooled spoonful and add salt only if it needs it. Parmesan at the end will add more salt. If the sauce gets too tight and pasty, stir in a splash of water or broth. If it is still thin at 20 minutes, simmer a few minutes more, uncovered. The pasta should feel fully flexible, cooked through, and still slightly firm in the center, with no hard, chalky, raw core.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The beef should look browned and broken into small pieces, with no raw pink remaining. The sauce should look thick enough to coat a spoon, not watery and not pasty. The pasta should look evenly coated, not dry and not sitting in a puddle of sauce.
These visual cues are for a sighted partner. They do not replace the thermometer or the non-visual cues in the steps. Call them out loud so both of you are working from the same information.

The ground beef should be brown all the way through, with no pink, raw-looking spots. The sauce should look thick and slightly glossy, not thin and watery, and it should cling to the pasta. Cooked spaghetti should look flexible and slightly pale in the very center when you bite or cut a strand, not chalky white and stiff, and not falling apart. A thermometer in the browned beef should read 160 degrees F before you simmer it in the sauce; once mixed, leftovers must be reheated to 165 degrees F.

Ground beef must reach 160 degrees F. Use a thermometer in several spots, because a pan of ground meat does not always cook evenly. Wash your hands, the board, the knife, the package plate, and the spoon if it touched raw beef, with soap and hot water before you handle the cheese, the colander, or serving dishes.

Boiling pasta water is a burn hazard. Fill the pot no more than halfway to two-thirds full so it cannot boil over. Add the pasta carefully so the water does not splash. Keep handles turned inward. When you drain, stand back from the steam, and do not try to pour from a pot that is too heavy. If lifting a full pot is hard, use a mug or a small colander scoop to remove some water first, or cook only half a pound at a time.
Tomato sauce can bubble and spit as it thickens. Stir with a long spoon, and use a splatter screen or a partly set lid if needed.
Raw pasta water and sauce are both hot enough to burn. Keep the reserved-water cup where it cannot be knocked over.

Make-ahead sauce: The meat sauce can be refrigerated for 3 to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 to 4 months. Reheat it to a bubble, then toss with freshly cooked pasta and a splash of pasta water. Leftover combined spaghetti also keeps, though the noodles will be softer.
No red pepper: Leave out the flakes for a milder sauce.

Other meats: Ground turkey or a mix of beef and Italian sausage also works. Ground turkey is poultry and should reach 165 degrees F. Sausage should be cooked through, with no raw, pasty center; if it is a ground-meat sausage, use 160 degrees F for pork or beef sausage, or 165 for poultry sausage.
Extra vegetables: Finely chopped carrot or celery can go in with the onion. Let them soften before you add the beef. A handful of baby spinach can wilt in the sauce at the end.
Other pasta shapes: Rigatoni, penne, or linguine all carry this sauce well. Use the same doneness test.

If the pasta sticks: It needed more water, more stirring at the start, or a little more oil in a very starchy pot. Do not rinse the pasta for this recipe; the surface starch helps the sauce cling, and reserved pasta water is part of the method.

Refrigerate within 2 hours, in shallow containers, for 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. A splash of water in the pan or microwave keeps the noodles from drying out. Reheat sauce on the stove until it bubbles.
The method and amounts in this page are written in original language, informed by published weeknight meat-sauce and spaghetti recipes and by USDA temperatures for ground beef and leftovers.

entries.title: Baby Back Ribs

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

Baby back ribs become tender when they cook low and slow, wrapped so they steam in their own juices, then finish unwrapped with sauce so the outside turns sticky and glazed. This is an oven method, which is easier to control than a grill. The USDA minimum for pork is 145 degrees F with a 3-minute rest, but ribs are not really done until the meat is tender and starts to give on the bone. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
About 3 to 3 1/2 hours, mostly unattended oven time
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
Heavy-duty foil
A large roasting pan or rimmed baking sheet with a rack if you have one
Tongs
A small bowl for the rub
A brush or a spoon for the sauce
2 racks baby back pork ribs, about 1 1/2 to 2 pounds (one and a half to two pounds) each, or about 3 to 4 pounds total
2 tablespoons brown sugar
1 tablespoon paprika
2 teaspoons kosher salt, or 1 1/4 teaspoons (one and a quarter teaspoons) table salt
1 teaspoon black pepper
1 teaspoon garlic powder
1 teaspoon onion powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) chili powder or cayenne, optional
1 cup barbecue sauce, plus more for serving

A rack of baby back ribs is curved and flexible, with a row of bones you can feel under a layer of meat. One side often has a thin, slippery membrane. If it is still on, you can loosen a corner with a knife tip and pull it off with a paper towel for better texture. The rub should feel like damp sand once it is mixed, and it should coat the meat in a thin, even crust.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 275 degrees F.
Set a rack in the lower-middle position while the oven is still cold.
Line a roasting pan or a rimmed baking sheet with foil.
If needed, remove the membrane from the bone side of each rack: slide a knife tip under a corner, grip the skin with a paper towel, and pull.
Pat the ribs dry.
Mix the brown sugar, paprika, salt, pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, and optional chili powder.
Rub the mixture over both sides of the ribs until the meat feels evenly coated.
Set the racks meat-side up on the pan.
Wrap the pan tightly in foil so steam stays in.
Bake for 2 hours 15 minutes to 2 hours 30 minutes.

Carefully open the foil away from your face, watching for steam. The meat should have pulled back a little from the bone ends and should give when you press it. A thermometer in the thickest meat, not touching bone, will usually read well above 145 degrees F at this point.
If the meat still feels tight and rubbery, rewrap and bake 20 to 30 minutes more.
Brush the top with barbecue sauce.
Return the ribs unwrapped and bake 15 to 25 minutes more, until the sauce feels tacky and set, not wet and runny.
Rest 10 minutes, then cut between the bones with a knife or kitchen shears and serve with more sauce.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The meat should feel tender when pressed and should tear with only a little effort. A bone should twist slightly in its socket. The kitchen will smell rich, porky, and sweet-smoky from the sauce, not raw or scorched. A thermometer in the thickest meat, off the bone, should be at least 145 degrees F; tenderness is the real finishing cue.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The finished ribs should look glazed and a little browned at the edges, with meat that has shrunk back from the bone ends. The sauce should look sticky, not watery. If you twist a bone, it should start to move in the meat without the rack falling completely apart unless you want them extra soft.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The finished ribs should look glazed and a little browned at the edges, with meat that has shrunk back from the bone ends. The sauce should look sticky, not watery. If you twist a bone, it should start to move in the meat without the rack falling completely apart unless you want them extra soft.

Raw pork juices belong on the raw-meat board only. Wash your hands, the knife, and the board before you handle the sauce brush or serving platter. Use long mitts; the foil-wrapped pan holds a lot of steam. Open foil away from your face. If you finish the ribs on a grill instead of in the oven, keep them over controlled heat so the sauce does not flare and burn. For pork chops, ribs, and roasts, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. For ribs or pulled pork, also cook until the meat is tender.

For spicier ribs, add more cayenne to the rub or use a hot barbecue sauce. For a drier, less sticky finish, sauce only at the table. You can cook the wrapped stage a day ahead, refrigerate the racks, and finish with sauce at 350 degrees F until hot and glazed, checking that leftovers reach 165 degrees F if they were fully cooked and chilled. An air fryer is too small for a full rack; use the oven for this recipe.

Cut leftover ribs off the bone before storing so they cool faster. Reheat, covered, in a 300 degree F oven or in a covered skillet with a splash of water until the meat is 165 degrees F. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Lamb Chops

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

Lamb chops cook quickly in a hot skillet and taste strongly of the meat itself, so a simple seasoning of salt, pepper, garlic, and herbs is enough. The USDA minimum for lamb chops is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat. At that temperature the center may still look slightly pink, which is expected and safe when the thermometer confirms the number.
2 to 4, depending on the size of the chops (about 4 loin chops or 6 to 8 smaller rib chops)
About 25 minutes, plus 20 minutes to take the chill off the meat
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
Tongs
A plate for resting the chops
Foil, to tent the meat while it rests
4 lamb loin chops, about 1 inch thick, or 6 to 8 rib chops of similar thickness, about 1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) total
1 teaspoon kosher salt, or 3/4 teaspoon (three-quarters of a teaspoon) table salt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
1 teaspoon dried rosemary or thyme, or 2 teaspoons chopped fresh
2 garlic cloves, minced, or 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 tablespoon unsalted butter, optional, for finishing
Lemon wedges, optional, for serving

Loin chops feel like small T-bone steaks, with a bone in the middle and meat on both sides. Rib chops have a long bone handle and a round eye of meat. They should feel cold and slightly damp, and the fat along the edge should feel firm. Let them sit out 15 to 20 minutes so they are not ice-cold in the center, but do not leave raw meat out longer than needed.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Pat the chops dry.
Mix the salt, pepper, rosemary or thyme, and garlic, and rub it over both sides of the meat.
Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until the oil smells hot and a corner of a chop sizzles firmly when it touches the pan.
Lay the chops in the pan in a single layer, leaving space between them.
Cook, without moving them, for 3 to 4 minutes, until they release easily from the pan and smell browned, not steamed.
Turn the chops and cook 3 to 5 minutes more, depending on thickness.
Start checking temperature at 3 minutes on the second side.
Insert a thermometer into the thickest part of the meat, from the side if you can, without touching bone.
When the thermometer reads 145 degrees F, transfer the chops to a plate.
Add the optional butter to the hot pan and spoon the melted butter over the chops, or skip this step.
Tent loosely with foil and rest at least 3 minutes, then serve with lemon if you like.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A firm sizzle means the pan is hot enough; a steaming sound means it is crowded or too cool. Done chops feel springy-firm, not soft and raw, and not hard like overcooked meat. The fat should smell browned and savory, not scorched. A thermometer in the thickest meat, off the bone, should read 145 degrees F, then the chops should rest at least 3 minutes.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The outside should be browned, with some darker, caramelized spots in the fat. At 145 degrees F the center may still look lightly pink, which is normal for lamb at the USDA minimum. There should be no cool, raw, dark-red look in the middle, and the juices should run only faintly pink or clear, not thick and bloody.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The outside should be browned, with some darker, caramelized spots in the fat. At 145 degrees F the center may still look lightly pink, which is normal for lamb at the USDA minimum. There should be no cool, raw, dark-red look in the middle, and the juices should run only faintly pink or clear, not thick and bloody.

Use the claw grip only if you are trimming fat; many chops need no cutting before they go in the pan. Wash your hands and tongs after they touch raw lamb. The skillet and spattering fat are burn hazards; use a splatter screen and turn handles inward. Do not press hard on the chops or you will squeeze out juices and encourage flare-ups. For lamb chops and roasts, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. The center may still look slightly pink at this temperature.

If the chops are much thicker than 1 inch, finish them in a 400 degree F oven after searing both sides, still to 145 degrees F. For a mint finish, stir a little chopped mint into the butter before you spoon it on. Shoulder chops are often cheaper and a bit chewier; they can take another minute or two per side.

Leftover lamb is good sliced cold in a salad or warmed gently. Reheat to 165 degrees F if you are serving it hot. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: A Simple Pasta Primer

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

This is the basic method for cooking dried pasta, then dressing it with butter and cheese. Once you can do this, you can use the same pot method for spaghetti with meat sauce, Alfredo, and the other pasta suppers in this book. The main skills are a safe pot of boiling water, a doneness bite test, and saving a little of the cooking water before you drain. Drain means pour off the liquid.
2 to 4, depending on how much pasta you cook
About 20 to 25 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
A colander
Tongs or a pasta fork
A heat-safe mug or measuring cup
Long oven mitts or sturdy pot holders
A liquid level indicator, optional
8 ounces dried pasta, such as spaghetti, penne, or another shape you like, for 2 servings, or 1 pound for 4 servings
1 tablespoon salt, for the pasta water
2 tablespoons unsalted butter, or 2 tablespoons olive oil
1/2 cup (half a cup) grated Parmesan cheese, plus more if you like
Black pepper, to taste

Dried pasta feels hard and smooth. A standard 1 pound box is a tight bundle or a full box of short shapes. Butter is firm when cold. Parmesan feels dry and grainy. The cooking water will be hot, so use a mitt when you dip out a cup of it.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Fill a large pot no more than two-thirds full with water.
Set the pot on the burner, then turn the heat to high.
Bring the water to a rolling boil. A rolling boil means large bubbles break hard across the surface and you can hear a steady roar of steam.
Add the salt.
Add the pasta.
Fan long noodles with tongs as they soften so they slide under the water.
Stir in the first 30 seconds so the pasta does not clump.
Start testing 1 minute before the package time.
Lift a piece, let it cool, and bite it.
Stop cooking when the pasta is al dente. Al dente means it is tender but still slightly firm in the center, with no hard, chalky core.
Dip a heat-safe mug into the pot and save about 1 cup of the cooking water.
Use a mitt. This is reserved pasta water, meaning starchy water you will use to loosen the sauce. Reserved pasta water is a cup of the starchy cooking water you save before you drain the pot.
Turn off the heat.
Drain the pasta in a colander in the sink.
Stand back from the steam.
Return the pasta to the pot.
Add the butter or oil, about 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) of the reserved pasta water, the cheese, and the pepper.
Toss until the pasta feels coated.
Add a little more pasta water if it feels dry or sticky.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A rolling boil is loud and steamy. Done pasta bends easily and feels slightly firm in the center when you bite it, not hard and raw, and not mushy. The dressed pasta should feel silky and evenly coated.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The water should be bubbling hard before the pasta goes in. Cooked pasta should look flexible, not stiff. A bitten piece may look slightly paler in the very center, but it should not look chalky white or raw. The butter and cheese should cling to the noodles, not sit in a puddle.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The water should be bubbling hard before the pasta goes in. Cooked pasta should look flexible, not stiff. A bitten piece may look slightly paler in the very center, but it should not look chalky white or raw. The butter and cheese should cling to the noodles, not sit in a puddle.

Boiling water can burn you. Do not fill the pot to the top. Turn the heat off before you move a full pot. If the pot is too heavy, dip out some water first, or cook only 8 ounces at a time. Keep handles turned inward. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

Salt the water so it tastes plainly salty, like seawater, once the salt dissolves. Do not rinse the pasta. The surface starch helps sauce cling. Use this same boiling method for the other pasta recipes in the Supper chapter.

Leftover buttered pasta will firm up in the fridge. Reheat it with a splash of water until it is steaming hot, at least 165 degrees F if you added perishable toppings. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Fettuccine Alfredo is long pasta in a smooth sauce of butter, cream, and Parmesan cheese. This version does not use raw egg, which keeps the method simpler and safer. The sauce should stay gentle and hot, not a hard boil, so the cheese stays smooth.
About 30 minutes
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A colander
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
Tongs
A heat-safe mug
Long oven mitts or pot holders
1 pound dried fettuccine, or another long pasta
1 tablespoon salt, for the pasta water
4 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 cup heavy cream
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) finely grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for serving
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper, or to taste
A pinch of salt, if the cheese is not very salty
Optional: cooked chicken or cooked shrimp, already heated, for serving on top

Fettuccine feels like flat, wide ribbons. Heavy cream is thick and coats a cup. Finely grated Parmesan feels like damp sand, not long shreds, and melts more evenly. If you add chicken or shrimp, they should already be fully cooked and hot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Fill a large pot no more than two-thirds full with water and bring it to a rolling boil.
Add the salt, then add the fettuccine.
Cook, stirring now and then, until the pasta is al dente. Al dente means tender but still slightly firm in the center.
Save 1 cup of the pasta cooking water, then drain the pasta. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Turn off the pasta pot.
Melt the butter in a wide skillet over medium-low heat.
Add the cream.

Warm it until it is steaming and just barely bubbling at the edges. This gentle heat is a simmer, meaning small bubbles, not a hard boil. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Lower the heat.
Add the Parmesan a handful at a time, stirring until it melts.
Add the pepper.
Add the drained pasta to the skillet.

Toss, adding splashes of reserved pasta water, until the sauce coats the noodles and feels silky, not pasty and not watery. Reserved pasta water is a cup of the starchy cooking water you save before you drain the pot.
Taste a cooled bite and add a pinch of salt only if it needs it. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve at once, with more cheese if you like.
Add already-cooked hot chicken or shrimp now, if you are using them.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look smooth, pale, and glossy. It should cling to the noodles. It should not look grainy, oily, or like a thin puddle in the pan. The pasta should look flexible, not stiff.

Boiling pasta water can burn you. Stand back from steam when you drain. Keep the cream sauce at a gentle heat so it does not boil over. If you add chicken, it should already have been cooked to 165 degrees F. If you add shrimp, they should already be opaque and firm. Leftovers must be reheated to 165 degrees F. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.

Grate the cheese yourself if you can. Pre-grated cheese sometimes makes a grainy sauce. If the sauce tightens too much, add more pasta water. If you want garlic, cook 1 minced clove in the butter for 30 seconds before you add the cream. Mince means cut into very small pieces.

This is a pot of classic beef and bean chili: browned ground beef, onion, garlic, tomatoes, beans, and chili powder, simmered until the flavors come together. It is a good supper on its own, with rice, or with cornbread from the Baked Goods chapter. The ground beef must reach 160 degrees F before you simmer it with the tomatoes.
About 1 hour, including a 30-minute simmer
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
A can opener
A wooden spoon
1 tablespoon oil
1 medium yellow onion, diced
3 garlic cloves, minced
1 pound ground beef
1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
2 tablespoons chili powder
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) paprika or smoked paprika
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) cayenne pepper, optional
1 can (15 ounces) tomato sauce, or 1 can (14 1/2 ounces) diced tomatoes plus 1/2 cup (half a cup) water
1 can (15 ounces) kidney beans or pinto beans, drained and rinsed
1/2 cup (half a cup) water, if the chili gets thicker than you like
Optional toppings: shredded cheese, chopped onion, or sour cream

Ground beef is cool, damp, and packed. An onion is papery on the outside and slick inside after you peel it. Dice means cut into small, even cubes. Chili powder smells warm and earthy. Beans are soft and slippery once they are rinsed. Drain and rinse them in a colander so the can liquid does not make the chili taste metallic. Drain means pour off the liquid.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Dice the onion. Dice means cut into small, even cubes.
Mince the garlic. Mince means cut into very small pieces.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the onion and a pinch of salt. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Cook, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes, until the onion feels soft and smells sweet.
Add the garlic.
Cook about 30 seconds, until it is fragrant.
Add the ground beef and the remaining salt.
Break it into small pieces as it cooks.
Cook until the beef is brown and a thermometer in several pieces reads 160 degrees F. This usually takes 6 to 8 minutes.
Stir in the chili powder, cumin, paprika, and cayenne, if you are using it.
Cook 30 seconds so the spices smell toasty.
Add the tomato sauce or tomatoes, and the beans.
Bring the pot to a simmer. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cook uncovered 20 to 30 minutes, stirring now and then so it does not stick.
If the chili gets too thick, add a splash of water.
If it is still thin, simmer a few minutes more.
Taste a cooled spoonful and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot, with toppings if you like.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The beef should feel firm and crumble into pieces, not pasty and raw. A thermometer should read 160 degrees F in the meat before it simmers in the sauce. Finished chili should mound on a spoon and smell warm, tomatoey, and spicy, not raw or tinny.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The beef should be brown all the way through, with no pink, before you add the tomatoes. The finished chili should look thick, not like soup, and the oil may shine a little on the surface. The beans should look whole and hot.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. The finished chili should look thick, not like soup, and the oil may shine a little on the surface. The beans should look whole and hot.

Wash your hands, the board, and the spoon after they touch raw ground beef. Keep toppings such as cheese and sour cream cold until you serve. Reheat leftover chili to 165 degrees F, or until it bubbles throughout. Cook ground beef to 160 degrees F.

For a milder chili, skip the cayenne and start with 1 tablespoon chili powder. For no beans, leave them out and add an extra half pound of beef, still cooked to 160 degrees F. For a vegetarian pot, see Vegetarian Chili in this chapter and skip this beef version. Chili often tastes even better the next day.

blocks.text: A fully cooked ham reheated in the oven, often with a simple glaze. Most supermarket hams are already cooked and only need to be heated through. Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look thick and golden or red-gold, depending on the tomatoes and curry powder, and the chickpeas should look hot and coated, not dry and not lost in a watery broth.

The pot is hot. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Taste before adding a lot of salt, because canned chickpeas and broth vary. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A squeeze of lemon at the end brightens the pot. Leftovers are even better the next day. Serve with rice or warm flatbread.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A pot of corned beef brisket simmered until tender, with cabbage and other vegetables added near the end. Packaged corned beef is already cured and often comes with a spice packet. Tenderness, not just temperature, is the finishing cue, though leftovers should later be reheated to 165 degrees F.
About 3 hours, mostly simmering
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 corned beef brisket, about 3 to 4 pounds, with spice packet if included
Water, to cover the meat by about 1 inch
6 carrots, cut into large pieces
8 small potatoes, or 3 large potatoes, cut into chunks
1 small head cabbage, cut into wedges

The brisket is a thick, firm, often vacuum-packed piece of meat. After a long simmer it should feel tender when pierced, and a slice should shred a little under a fork, not feel like a rubber eraser. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Rinse the brisket if the package says to, then put it in a large pot and cover it with water by about 1 inch.
Add the spice packet.
Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer. Simmer means small, gentle bubbles, not a hard, rattling boil.
Cover and cook about 2 1/2 hours, until a fork goes in with less resistance than at the start.
Add the potatoes and carrots.
Simmer 15 minutes.
Add the cabbage wedges.
Simmer 15 to 20 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender and the meat is easy to pierce.
Lift the meat out and rest it 10 minutes. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Slice it across the grain, meaning across the long fibers, so it is easier to chew.
Serve with the vegetables and a little of the broth.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A fork should slide into the meat and into a potato with little resistance. The kitchen should smell salty, spicy, and savory. Cabbage should feel tender.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The meat should look dull pink from curing, which can remain even when it is fully cooked, so do not use color alone. The vegetables should look tender, not raw in the center, and not falling into mush unless you like them very soft.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The meat should look dull pink from curing, which can remain even when it is fully cooked, so do not use color alone. The vegetables should look tender, not raw in the center, and not falling into mush unless you like them very soft.

Use a large, stable pot. The water is hot. Lift the meat with large forks or a sturdy spatula, and use mitts. Cool leftovers quickly. Reheat to 165 degrees F. For steaks, roasts, and other whole pieces of beef, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. If this dish is a slow stew, keep cooking until the meat is also tender.
Save some leftover meat for hash in the Breakfast chapter. If the broth is too salty, serve the meat with a little mustard rather than a lot of the cooking liquid.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A baked dish of seasoned ground beef and vegetables in gravy, topped with mashed potatoes and browned in the oven. If you use lamb, some people call it shepherd's pie. This version is beef, which is cottage pie. The beef must reach 160 degrees F before it is baked, and the finished center should be 165 degrees F if you are reheating leftovers later. For a first bake of freshly cooked filling, heat it until the top is browned and the filling is bubbling hot.
About 1 hour
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 tablespoon oil
1 pound ground beef
1 onion, diced
2 carrots, diced
1 cup frozen peas
2 tablespoons flour
1 cup beef broth
1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce, optional
1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
4 cups mashed potatoes, from the Misc chapter or leftovers
The filling should feel loose and gravy-like, not dry, before the potatoes go on. The potato topping should be spread to the edges so it is a lid.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Grease the baking dish if the ingredients include butter or oil for the dish.
Cook the onion, carrot, and beef in oil until the beef is 160 degrees F.
Stir in the flour, then the broth, Worcestershire, salt, and peas.
Simmer until slightly thick. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Spread in a baking dish.
Cover with mashed potatoes, going all the way to the edges.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes.
The filling should be bubbling at the edges, and the top should feel hot and slightly browned.
If the filling was made ahead, the center should reach 165 degrees F.
Rest 5 to 10 minutes so the dish can settle, then serve. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The beef must be 160 degrees F as you cook the filling. The finished pie should be bubbling hot throughout. You should smell browned potatoes and savory gravy. A thermometer in the center should read at least 165 degrees F if the filling was made ahead and chilled.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look golden with browned spots. The filling should be bubbling at the edges.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look golden with browned spots. The filling should be bubbling at the edges.
Wash hands after raw beef. The dish is very hot. Use mitts. Cool leftovers in the dish or in shallow containers, then reheat to 165 degrees F. Cook ground beef to 160 degrees F.
Leftover mashed potatoes work perfectly. A fork dragged over the top makes ridges that brown nicely for a sighted helper to check.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. entries.title: Crab Cakes

blocks.text: Patties of crab meat, crumbs, and a little egg, cooked in a skillet until browned and hot in the center. The egg binder should reach 160 degrees F. Use lump crab if you can, and handle the mix gently so the lumps stay intact.
4, about 8 small cakes
About 30 minutes, plus brief chilling if the mix is soft
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound lump crab meat, picked over for shells
1 large egg
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) mayonnaise
1/2 cup (half a cup) breadcrumbs, plus more if the mix is wet
1 teaspoon mustard or Worcestershire sauce
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, or to taste
2 tablespoons oil or butter, for the pan
Feel through the crab for hard shell pieces before you mix. The mix should just hold a cake. Too many crumbs make it pasty. Too few and it falls apart.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the egg, mayonnaise, mustard or Worcestershire, and salt.
Gently fold in the crab and crumbs. Fold means turn the mixture over itself gently.
Shape 8 small cakes.
If they feel very soft, chill 15 to 20 minutes.
Heat the oil or butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook the cakes 3 to 5 minutes per side, until they feel browned and the centers are hot, 160 degrees F because of the egg.
Serve with lemon or a simple sauce.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The centers should be hot, 160 degrees F. You should smell toasted crumbs and sweet crab, not burning butter or a sour seafood smell. If you find a shell piece while eating, stop and remove it.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cakes should look golden brown, and the centers should look set, not wet and loose.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cakes should look golden brown, and the centers should look set, not wet and loose.

Pick through the crab carefully. The oil will spatter. Use a splatter screen. Because of the egg, heat the centers to 160 degrees F. Keep leftover cakes refrigerated and reheat to 165 degrees F. Cook fish to 145 degrees F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes, meaning it comes apart easily with a fork.
These are rich, so smaller cakes are easier to handle and cook through. A little lemon in a yogurt sauce is plenty of accompaniment.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Slices of eggplant baked with marinara and cheese until the eggplant is tender and the center is bubbling hot. Salting and roasting or baking the eggplant first keeps the dish from getting watery and greasy. This is a meatless supper.
About 1 hour 15 minutes
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
2 medium eggplants, sliced into 1/2 inch (half inch) rounds
1 teaspoon salt, for sweating the eggplant, plus more for the sauce layers
2 tablespoons oil
3 cups marinara sauce
2 cups shredded mozzarella cheese
1/2 cup (half a cup) grated Parmesan cheese

Eggplant feels spongy when raw. After salting and baking, it should feel more flexible and less full of water. The finished dish should feel tender all the way through a slice, not tough and raw in the middle.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease the baking dish if the ingredients include butter or oil for the dish.
Salt the eggplant slices and let them sit 20 minutes, then pat them dry.
Brush with oil and bake or roast until they feel flexible, about 20 minutes at 400 degrees F.
In a baking dish, layer sauce, eggplant, and cheeses, repeating, and finish with cheese.
Bake 25 to 35 minutes after the dish is layered.
The dish should be bubbling at the edges, the cheese should feel melted, and a slice of eggplant should feel tender all the way through.
Rest 5 to 10 minutes so the dish can settle, then serve. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A slice should feel tender all the way through. The dish should be bubbling hot in the center, 165 degrees F if it was assembled ahead. You should smell roasted eggplant, tomato, and cheese, not burning cheese.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look bubbly, with melted, lightly browned cheese. The eggplant slices should look collapsed and tender, not pale and stiff.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look bubbly, with melted, lightly browned cheese. The eggplant slices should look collapsed and tender, not pale and stiff.

The baking dish is very hot. Use mitts. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. If you bread and fry the eggplant instead, use the same hot-oil cautions as in other fried variations in this book, and consider the baked method first. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Salting the slices, letting them sit 20 minutes, then patting them dry, helps a lot. You can roast the slices at 400 degrees F for 20 minutes before you layer the casserole.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Baked or pan-cooked fish in warm tortillas with a crisp slaw and a simple sauce. Cook the fish to 145 degrees F, or until it flakes. This is a lighter taco night than the ground-beef tacos in this chapter.
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) mild white fish fillets
1 tablespoon oil
1 teaspoon chili powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
8 small corn or flour tortillas
2 cups coleslaw or shredded cabbage
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sour cream mixed with 1 teaspoon lime juice, or salsa
The fish should flake into large, moist pieces for filling tacos. Warm tortillas are less likely to crack. Keep the slaw crisp and relatively dry.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Toss the fish with oil, chili powder, and salt.
Bake at 400 degrees F for 12 to 18 minutes, or cook in a skillet over medium heat, until the fish is 145 degrees F or flakes easily.
Warm the tortillas until they feel flexible.
Flake the fish into large pieces.
Fill the tortillas with fish, slaw, and sauce.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: Fish should be 145 degrees F or flaky and opaque. Tortillas should feel warm and soft. You should smell chili, lime, and cooked fish, not a sour off smell.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The fish should look opaque and flake into moist pieces, not look wet and raw or dry and crumbly. The slaw should look crisp.

Wash the board after raw fish. If you use leftover fish, reheat it to 165 degrees F or serve it cold and fully cooked, kept refrigerated until assembly. Cook fish to 145 degrees F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes, meaning it comes apart easily with a fork.
A squeeze of lime on the fish just before serving helps. See Coleslaw in the Misc chapter if you want a homemade slaw.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.
