Shrimp cooked quickly in butter and garlic. This is a fast supper over rice, pasta, or grits. The shrimp are done when they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled.
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound raw shrimp, peeled and deveined
3 tablespoons unsalted butter
3 garlic cloves, minced
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
A pinch of red pepper flakes, optional
1 tablespoon lemon juice
Pat the shrimp dry so they sear. Mince the garlic into very small pieces so it flavors the butter without lingering as harsh, half-raw chunks. Mince means cut into very small pieces.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Pat the shrimp dry.
Season them with salt.
Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Add the garlic and optional red pepper flakes.
Cook 30 seconds, until fragrant, not brown and bitter.
Add the shrimp in a single layer.
Cook 1 to 2 minutes per side, until they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled.
Add the lemon juice.
Taste a cooled shrimp and add salt if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The shrimp should feel firm and springy, and they should smell like garlic, butter, and sweet shrimp, not ammonia or burning garlic.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The shrimp should look opaque and pearly or pink, not gray and raw, and they should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. The garlic should look pale gold, not dark brown.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The shrimp should look opaque and pearly or pink, not gray and raw, and they should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. The garlic should look pale gold, not dark brown.

Keep raw shrimp cold, then wash the board. Garlic burns fast. Do not walk away. Overcooked shrimp get tough. Cook shrimp until the flesh is pearly, opaque, and firm. It should curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean it is overcooked.
Serve over rice, pasta, or the Shrimp and Grits idea by spooning these shrimp over the Grits from the Breakfast chapter. A little chopped parsley is a good finish.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A one-pan supper of ground turkey, vegetables, and a simple seasoning or sauce, served over rice or in tortillas. The turkey must reach 165 degrees F.
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 tablespoon oil
1 pound ground turkey
1 onion, diced
1 bell pepper, diced, or 2 cups other cut vegetables
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon chili powder or Italian seasoning
1 can (14 1/2 ounces) diced tomatoes, or 1/2 cup (half a cup) salsa
Optional: 1 cup shredded cheese, or cooked rice, for serving

Ground turkey feels sticky and pale when raw. It should turn firm and crumbly as it cooks, and a thermometer should read 165 degrees F in several places, because a skillet of ground meat does not always cook evenly.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
Add the onion and pepper.
Cook 4 to 5 minutes, until they feel soft.
Add the turkey, salt, and seasoning.
Cook, breaking it up, until it is 165 degrees F and no longer pasty and raw, about 8 minutes.
Add the garlic.
Cook 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes or salsa.
Simmer 5 minutes. Simmer means small, gentle bubbles.
Taste a cooled bite and add salt if it needs it.
Add cheese if you like, then serve with rice or tortillas.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A thermometer must read 165 degrees F in several spots. The mix should smell savory, like onion and cooked turkey, not raw meat.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The turkey should be opaque and browned in spots, with no raw pink. The vegetables should look soft. The mix should look moist, not dry and gray, and not watery.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The turkey should be opaque and browned in spots, with no raw pink. The vegetables should look soft. The mix should look moist, not dry and gray, and not watery.

entries.title: Pot Roast

blocks.text: A large cut of beef, usually chuck, browned and then cooked slowly with broth and vegetables until it is tender. The USDA minimum is 145 degrees F with a 3-minute rest, but pot roast is not really done until a fork slides in easily, which takes much longer. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
About 3 to 3 1/2 hours, mostly unattended simmering
Intermediate

2 teaspoons salt
1 teaspoon black pepper
2 tablespoons oil
1 onion, cut into wedges
4 carrots, cut into large pieces
2 potatoes, cut into large chunks, optional
2 cups beef broth
1 tablespoon tomato paste or Worcestershire sauce, optional

Chuck feels well marbled, with fat seams running through the meat. Early in cooking it will feel tough. When it is done, a fork should slide in with little resistance and the meat should start to shred.

Heat the oven to 325 degrees F, or plan to simmer on the stove. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Pat the beef dry.
Season it with salt and pepper.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat.
Brown the roast 3 to 4 minutes per side, until it smells deeply browned.
Move it out for a moment if the pot is crowded.
Add the onion.
Cook 2 minutes.
Add the broth and optional tomato paste or Worcestershire, scraping up the browned bits.
Return the beef to the pot. The liquid should come partway up the sides, not cover it completely.
Cover.
Cook in the oven, or at a gentle simmer on the stove, 2 hours.
Add the carrots and potatoes.
Cover and cook 45 to 60 minutes more, until the meat is fork-tender and the vegetables are soft.
Rest the meat 10 minutes.
Slice or shred it.
Serve with the vegetables and juices.

Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat. This is an oven method.

The shoulder is a large, well-marbled cut. Early on it will feel tough. When it is done, two forks should shred it with little effort, and a bone, if present, should twist and start to come free.

Cover tightly with a lid or foil.

Rest 15 minutes.
Pull the meat into shreds with two forks, discarding large pieces of fat and the bone if there is one.
Toss with barbecue sauce if you like, or serve the sauce on the side.
Serve on buns or with sides.

Patties made from canned salmon, egg, and crumbs, cooked in a skillet until they are browned and hot in the center, 145 degrees F for fish, or 165 degrees F if you are using leftover cooked salmon that has been chilled and you are reheating it in the patty. Canned salmon is already cooked, so you are mainly heating the patties through and setting the egg binder, which should reach 160 degrees F.
About 25 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
2 cans (6 to 7 ounces each) salmon, drained
1 large egg
1/2 cup (half a cup) breadcrumbs or crushed crackers
2 tablespoons diced onion or green onion, optional
1 tablespoon lemon juice or mustard
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste, because canned salmon can be salty
2 tablespoons oil, for the pan

Drain the salmon well and flake it, removing large, hard bones if you prefer, though the soft bones are edible. Drain means pour off the liquid. The mix should hold a patty, not feel wet and loose, and not dry and crumbly.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the salmon, egg, crumbs, onion, lemon or mustard, and salt.
Shape 8 small patties.
If the mix is too wet, add a spoon of crumbs.
If it is too dry, add a teaspoon of water or another bit of egg.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook the patties 3 to 5 minutes per side, until they feel browned and firm, and the center is hot, 160 degrees F because of the egg.
Drain on a plate lined with a paper towel.
Serve with lemon or a simple sauce.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The centers should feel hot and set, 160 degrees F. You should smell toasted crumbs and salmon, not burning oil or a sour fish smell.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The patties should look golden brown on both sides, and the center should look set, not wet and raw with liquid egg.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The patties should look golden brown on both sides, and the center should look set, not wet and raw with liquid egg.

The canning liquid is messy, so drain over the sink. The oil will spatter. Use a splatter screen. Because of the egg, treat the centers as an egg dish and heat them to 160 degrees F. Cook fish to 145 degrees F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes, meaning it comes apart easily with a fork.

These are good with a yogurt-dill sauce or with the Ranch Dip in the Misc chapter. Leftover cooked salmon can replace canned, and the patties should then be heated to 165 degrees F if that salmon was leftover and chilled.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Italian sausages cooked with sliced bell peppers and onions until the sausages are done and the vegetables are tender. For pork or beef sausages that are sold raw, cook to 160 degrees F. For poultry sausages, cook to 165 degrees F. Some sausages are sold fully cooked and only need to be heated through, still to 165 degrees F if they are leftovers or poultry.
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound Italian sausage links, sweet or hot
2 tablespoons oil
2 bell peppers, sliced
1 onion, sliced
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) Italian seasoning or black pepper
Optional: 1/2 cup (half a cup) tomato sauce, or toasted rolls, for serving
Raw sausages feel soft and even. As they cook they feel firmer. Check temperature in the end of a link, in the center of the meat, not just on the surface.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium heat.
Add the sausages.
Brown them 5 to 6 minutes, turning, then move them to a plate if the pan is crowded.
Add the peppers, onion, and salt.
Cook 8 to 10 minutes, until they feel soft and smell sweet.
Return the sausages.
Add seasoning, and tomato sauce if you like.
Cover and cook 8 to 12 minutes more, until pork or beef sausages are 160 degrees F, or poultry sausages are 165 degrees F, and the vegetables are tender.
Serve on plates or in rolls.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: Pork or beef sausage must be 160 degrees F. Poultry sausage must be 165 degrees F. Peppers and onions should feel soft and sweet-smelling. You should smell browned sausage and peppers, not burning.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sausages should look browned, and the peppers should look soft and slightly browned, not raw and stiff. A cut sausage should not look raw and pasty in the center, but a thermometer is the test.

Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sausages should look browned, and the peppers should look soft and slightly browned, not raw and stiff. A cut sausage should not look raw and pasty in the center, but a thermometer is the test.

Check the package to see if the sausage is raw or fully cooked. Raw sausage needs the full temperature check. The skillet will spatter. Use a splatter screen. For pork chops, ribs, and roasts, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. For ribs or pulled pork, also cook until the meat is tender.
This is good over pasta or in a hoagie roll. If the sausages brown too fast, lower the heat and finish with the lid on.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Chicken pieces and cut vegetables roasted together on one pan. Cut the vegetables so they cook in the same time as the chicken, and confirm the chicken is 165 degrees F before you serve.
About 45 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) boneless chicken thighs or breasts, cut into large chunks, or 4 small thighs
4 cups cut vegetables, such as potatoes, carrots, broccoli, or bell peppers
2 tablespoons oil
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon dried herbs or paprika
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
Cut dense vegetables such as potatoes smaller than the chicken pieces, so they get tender in time. Leave a little space on the pan so everything roasts instead of steaming.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Set a rack in the middle while the oven is cold.
Pat the food dry.
Season it as the ingredients describe.
Toss the chicken and vegetables separately with oil, salt, pepper, and herbs, then spread them on a lined pan.
If you can, keep the chicken in one area so you can check temperature easily.
Set the food in the pan in a single layer, or as described.
Roast 25 to 35 minutes. Roast means cook uncovered in the hot oven.
Turn the pieces once halfway through.
The thickest chicken piece must read 165 degrees F.
A vegetable cube should mash or pierce easily.
Rest the chicken 5 minutes, then serve with the vegetables. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Serve.

Use a raw-poultry board and keep raw chicken off the vegetable cutting area, or cut vegetables first and wash the board. Use mitts. The pan is very hot. Cook all poultry to 165 degrees F. Measure in the thickest part. Do not let the thermometer tip touch bone or the pan.
If some vegetables brown too fast, take them off early and let the chicken finish. Broccoli cooks faster than potatoes, so add it in the last 15 minutes if you mix them.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. entries.title: Sheet-Pan Pizza

blocks.text: A rectangular pizza baked on a sheet pan, using store-bought dough to keep this weeknight-friendly. The crust should feel set and lightly crisp, and any meat toppings should be already cooked or be toppings that cook through in the oven, such as fully cooked sausage.
4 to 6
About 40 minutes, plus dough rest if you make dough, or 25 minutes with store-bought dough
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 pound pizza dough, store-bought, at room temperature for 20 minutes
2 tablespoons oil, for the pan and the crust
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) pizza sauce or marinara
2 cups shredded mozzarella cheese
Toppings you like, such as cooked sausage, sliced peppers, or olives

Let the dough sit out so it is easier to stretch. Oiled fingers help. The dough should feel elastic, not ice-cold and tight, and not so warm that it tears into holes you cannot pinch shut. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 450 degrees F.
Oil a sheet pan.
Press or stretch the dough to fit the pan.
If it shrinks back, wait 5 minutes and try again.
Brush the dough with a little oil.
Add sauce, then cheese, then toppings.
Keep toppings lighter in the center so the middle can cook.
Bake 12 to 18 minutes, until the crust feels set and lightly crisp, and the cheese is melted and bubbling.
Rest 3 minutes, then cut and serve. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Use a cutter or a knife, and a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the pizza steady if you need it.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The crust should feel set and lightly crisp, not doughy and raw in the center. You should smell toasted dough, tomato, and cheese, not burning. The pan will be extremely hot.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The crust should look golden at the edges. The cheese should look melted and lightly browned in spots, not pale and stretchy-raw, and not black.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The crust should look golden at the edges. The cheese should look melted and lightly browned in spots, not pale and stretchy-raw, and not black.

Use mitts. If you use meat toppings, they should be already cooked, or be ingredients that can reach a safe temperature in this short bake. Reheat leftover pizza to 165 degrees F. See Midnight Snacks for a leftover pizza reheat method. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Cornmeal or extra oil on the pan helps the crust not stick. If the center stays pale and soft, move the pan to a lower rack for a few minutes.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Creamy grits topped with shrimp cooked in a savory sauce, sometimes with bacon or sausage. Make the Grits from the Breakfast chapter, or follow the short method below, then cook the shrimp at the end so they do not sit and get tough.
About 40 minutes
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 cup regular grits, cooked as in the Breakfast chapter, with butter and optional cheese
1 pound raw shrimp, peeled and deveined
1 tablespoon oil or bacon drippings
2 garlic cloves, minced
1/2 cup (half a cup) broth
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
Optional: 4 slices cooked bacon, crumbled, or a pinch of red pepper flakes
Time it so the grits are creamy and hot when the shrimp are just done. The shrimp should feel firm, opaque, and loosely curled. The grits should feel smooth, not lumpy and not stiff.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cook the grits as in the Breakfast chapter, and keep them warm over very low heat, adding a splash of water if they tighten.
Pat the shrimp dry.
Season them with salt.
Heat the oil or drippings in a skillet over medium heat.
Add the garlic and cook 30 seconds.
Add the shrimp.
Cook 1 to 2 minutes per side, until they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled.
Add the broth and optional red pepper flakes.
Simmer 1 minute. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Add bacon if you are using it.
Spoon the grits into bowls.
Top with the shrimp and sauce.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: Grits should feel silky and hot. Shrimp should feel firm and smell sweet, buttery, and garlicky, not ammonia-like or burnt.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The grits should look creamy. The shrimp should look opaque and loosely curled, not gray, and not tight and small from overcooking.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The grits should look creamy. The shrimp should look opaque and loosely curled, not gray, and not tight and small from overcooking.

Cook bacon fully if you use it. Keep raw shrimp cold, then wash the board. Do not overcook the shrimp. The bowls will be hot. Cook shrimp until the flesh is pearly, opaque, and firm. It should curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean it is overcooked.
Cheddar in the grits makes this more filling. If the grits sit, they thicken a lot. Whisk in hot water or milk to loosen them. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk until the mixture looks even.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Shrimp and vegetables cooked quickly in a hot pan with a simple sauce. Shrimp cook very fast. They are done when they are opaque, pearly, and firm, and they curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean they are overcooked.
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 pound raw shrimp, peeled and deveined
2 tablespoons oil, divided
4 cups cut vegetables, such as bell pepper, snap peas, or broccoli
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) stir-fry sauce, or 3 tablespoons soy sauce mixed with 1 tablespoon honey and 1 minced garlic clove
Rice, for serving
Raw shrimp feel slightly translucent and soft. Deveined means the dark vein along the back has been removed. Done shrimp feel firm and springy, not mushy, and not tough as rubber.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cut the protein and vegetables into pieces about the same size so they cook evenly.
Mix the sauce ingredients in a small bowl.
Pat the protein dry.
Season it with the salt, if listed.
Heat the oil in a large skillet or wok over medium-high heat until it smells hot and a piece of vegetable sizzles at once.
Cook the shrimp in 1 tablespoon oil 1 to 2 minutes per side, until they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled, then move them to a plate so they do not overcook while the vegetables finish.
Move the protein to a plate if the pan is crowded.
Add a little more oil if the pan is dry.
Add the firmer vegetables first.
Stir and cook until the vegetables are tender-crisp, meaning they are hot and slightly bent but not mushy.
Return the protein to the pan.
Add the sauce.
Stir until the sauce thickens slightly and coats everything, 1 to 2 minutes.
Serve hot over rice if you like.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The shrimp should feel firm and opaque, and they should smell sweet and briny, not ammonia-like or sour. If they smell off before cooking, throw them out. Vegetables should feel tender-crisp.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The shrimp should look opaque and pink or pearly, not gray and translucent. They should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. The vegetables should look bright.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The shrimp should look opaque and pink or pearly, not gray and translucent. They should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. The vegetables should look bright.

Wash the board after raw shrimp, and keep them cold until they go in the pan. Do not overcook. The pan is very hot. Cook shrimp until the flesh is pearly, opaque, and firm. It should curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean it is overcooked.

If the shrimp are frozen, thaw them in the refrigerator, then pat them dry so they sear instead of steam. Add shrimp near the end if your vegetables need more time, because shrimp can be done in 3 to 5 minutes.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. 1 onion, diced
1 bell pepper, diced
2 garlic cloves, minced
2 tablespoons chili powder
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
1 can (28 ounces) diced or crushed tomatoes
2 cans (15 ounces each) beans, drained and rinsed
1 cup corn, optional
Optional toppings: cheese, sour cream, or chopped onion
The chili should feel thick and stew-like, similar to beef chili, with tender vegetables and beans you can feel in a spoonful.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Dice the onion and any other vegetables listed. Dice means cut into small, even cubes.
Mince the garlic. Mince means cut into very small pieces.
Heat the oil or butter in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the onion and pepper, and cook until they feel soft, about 5 to 7 minutes.
Add the garlic, chili powder, cumin, and salt, and cook 30 seconds, until the spices smell toasty.
Add the tomatoes, beans, and optional corn.
Bring the pot to a simmer. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.

Taste and add salt if it needs it.
Serve with toppings.
Taste a cooled spoonful and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot.

blocks.text: Sliced apples baked in a double crust until the fruit is tender and the juices are bubbling. Use a store-bought crust if you want to skip making dough, or see Pie Crust in this chapter. Toss the apples with sugar and spice, then bake until you can hear or see the filling bubble, and a knife slides easily into an apple slice.
8 servings
About 1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients

2 pie crusts, store-bought or homemade, for a 9 inch pie
6 cups peeled, sliced apples, about 2 to 2 1/2 pounds (two to two and a half pounds)
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) sugar
2 tablespoons flour, or 1 tablespoon cornstarch
1 teaspoon cinnamon
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
1 tablespoon lemon juice
1 tablespoon butter, cut into small pieces
1 tablespoon milk, for brushing the top, optional

Apple slices should be about 1/4 inch (a quarter inch) thick, and even, so they cook at the same rate. After baking, a knife or skewer should slide into the apples easily, and the juices should feel thick, not watery, once the pie cools. The crust should feel golden and set, not pale and soft.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Place a baking sheet on a lower rack to catch drips.
Toss the apples with the sugar, flour or cornstarch, cinnamon, salt, and lemon juice.
Fit one crust into a 9 inch pie pan.
Add the apples and dot them with the butter.
Set the second crust on top.
Trim the edges, pinch them together, and cut 3 or 4 slits in the top so steam can escape. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Brush the top with milk if you like.

Bake 20 minutes, then reduce the oven to 375 degrees F and bake 30 to 40 minutes more, until the crust feels golden and set, and the filling is bubbling through the slits. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
If the edges brown too fast, cover them with a ring of foil.
Cool at least 2 hours before you slice, so the juices thicken.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The crust should feel golden and set. You should hear or sense bubbling under the top crust near the end of baking. A knife should slide into the apples easily. You should smell cooked apple, cinnamon, and toasted crust, not raw dough or burning sugar.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The crust should look golden brown, not pale. Filling should bubble visibly through the slits near the end. After cooling, a slice should hold together, with tender, not raw, apples.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The crust should look golden brown, not pale. Filling should bubble visibly through the slits near the end. After cooling, a slice should hold together, with tender, not raw, apples.

Use a stable board and a cut-resistant glove if you peel and slice many apples. Use mitts. The filling is extremely hot, like molten sugar. Cool before you slice. Set the pie on a sheet pan to catch drips, and keep foil away from the oven wall. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

A mix of tart and sweet apples tastes better than one kind alone. If the bottom crust stays pale, you can start the pie on the lower rack. Leftovers keep, covered, at room temperature 1 day, or refrigerated 3 to 4 days. Reheat slices until the filling is steaming hot if you want them warm.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Baked Cheesecake

blocks.text: A creamy baked cheesecake on a graham-cracker crust. The filling is mostly cream cheese, sugar, and eggs, and it must reach a set, not-liquid center. Cook egg dishes to 160 degrees F, but a cheesecake is also judged by a slight jiggle in the very center, which finishes setting as it chills. Chill several hours before you slice it.
12 servings
About 1 hour 30 minutes, plus several hours of chilling
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) graham-cracker crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar, for the crust
5 tablespoons melted butter
24 ounces cream cheese, softened
1 cup sugar, for the filling
3 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1/2 cup (half a cup) sour cream, optional, for a slightly tangier filling

Softened cream cheese should feel smooth and spreadable, not cold and lumpy. After baking, the edges should feel set, and the very center should jiggle slightly like firm gelatin, not like liquid. After a full chill, a slice should feel creamy and hold its shape.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 325 degrees F.
Mix the crumbs, 3 tablespoons sugar, and melted butter until the mix feels like damp sand.
Press it firmly into the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan, or a deep 9 inch cake pan lined with parchment.
Bake the crust 8 to 10 minutes, then cool slightly.
Beat the cream cheese and 1 cup sugar until the mix feels smooth, with no lumps.
Add the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla and optional sour cream, and mix just until even.
Too much beating can add air and cause cracks.
Pour the filling over the crust.
Bake 45 to 60 minutes, until the edges feel set and the center still jiggles slightly. The surface should not look wet and liquid.
If you use a thermometer, the center should be near 150 to 160 degrees F.
Turn off the oven.
Crack the door and let the cake sit 30 minutes, then cool on a rack.
Refrigerate at least 4 hours, or overnight, before you release the pan and slice.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The edges should feel set. The center should jiggle slightly, not slosh. You should smell baked dairy, vanilla, and toasted crust, not raw egg or burning. After chilling, a slice should feel creamy and firm enough to cut.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look mostly set, maybe with a small pale center, and not browned like a cake. A little crack can happen and is all right. After chilling, a slice should look creamy and hold its shape, not slump into a puddle.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look mostly set, maybe with a small pale center, and not browned like a cake. A little crack can happen and is all right. After chilling, a slice should look creamy and hold its shape, not slump into a puddle.

Do not taste raw filling. It contains raw eggs. Use mitts. A springform pan can leak, so set it on a sheet pan. Cool, then refrigerate within 2 hours. Keep the cake refrigerated, and do not leave slices out more than 2 hours. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

Run a thin knife around the edge after baking to reduce cracking as it cools. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. A pan of hot water on a lower rack can help the cake bake more gently. Serve plain or with fruit.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Tender, flaky biscuits for breakfast, supper, or strawberry shortcake. Cut in means rub or mash cold butter into the flour until the mix feels like coarse crumbs with some pea-size pieces. Those pieces of butter make steam and flakes in the oven. Handle the dough as little as you can.
8 to 10 biscuits
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for the board
1 tablespoon baking powder
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon sugar, optional
6 tablespoons cold unsalted butter, cut into small cubes
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) cold milk, plus 1 or 2 tablespoons more if needed

The butter should feel cold and firm, not greasy and soft. After you cut it in, you should still feel small pieces of butter. The dough should feel soft and a little shaggy, not smooth like bread dough. Baked biscuits should feel light, with a set, slightly crisp top and a tender interior.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Line a baking sheet with parchment.
Mix the flour, baking powder, salt, and optional sugar.
Cut in the cold butter with a pastry cutter, two knives, or your fingertips, until the mix feels like coarse crumbs with some pea-size bits.
Add the milk.
Stir just until a soft dough forms.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured board.
Fold it over itself 3 or 4 times, then pat it to about 3/4 inch (three-quarters of an inch) thick. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air.
Cut biscuits with a cutter or the rim of a glass, pressing straight down without twisting.
Twisting can seal the edges and reduce the rise. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
Set the rounds on the sheet, close together for softer sides, or spaced apart for crisper sides.
Bake 12 to 16 minutes, until the tops feel set and lightly crisp, and the biscuits have risen.
Serve warm, or cool on a rack.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The tops should feel set and lightly crisp. You should smell butter and toasted flour, not raw dough. The center of a biscuit should feel cooked and fluffy, not wet.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The tops should look golden, and the sides should look risen in layers, not squat and pale. The insides should look fluffy, not wet and doughy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The tops should look golden, and the sides should look risen in layers, not squat and pale. The insides should look fluffy, not wet and doughy.

Do not taste raw dough. Use mitts. A cutter has a sharp edge. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

If you do not want to cut rounds, pat the dough into a square and cut 8 to 9 squares with a knife. Leftover biscuits reheat well at 300 degrees F for 5 to 8 minutes, or split and toasted. See Biscuits and Sausage Gravy in the Breakfast chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A moist loaf made with very ripe bananas. Quick bread means a loaf that rises with baking soda or baking powder, not yeast, so there is no rising time. The center takes longer than muffins, so test with a toothpick.
1 loaf, about 10 slices
About 1 hour 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) cinnamon, optional
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, melted, or oil
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) sugar
2 large eggs
3 very ripe bananas, mashed
1 teaspoon vanilla extract

The mashed bananas should feel very soft and almost liquid in spots. The baked loaf should feel springy on top, and a toothpick in the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. If the toothpick hits a melted chip, test again in another spot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a loaf pan, or line it with parchment.
Mix the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Mix the wet ingredients in a second bowl, including any mashed fruit.
Add the wet mix to the dry mix.
Stir just until combined.
Spread the batter in the pan.
Bake 55 to 70 minutes.
A toothpick in the center of the loaf should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. The top should feel set and the center should not feel wet.
Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn the loaf out to finish cooling.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The top should feel set. The center should not feel wet or collapse under light pressure. You should smell banana and toasted sugar, not raw flour. A toothpick in the center should come out with a few moist crumbs.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look browned and slightly cracked, which is common. A toothpick in the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look browned and slightly cracked, which is common. Do not taste raw batter. Use mitts. The loaf pan is heavy and hot. Cool before you slice, or the loaf can crumble. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

One cup of chocolate chips or chopped walnuts can be stirred in. If the top browns before the center is done, tent the pan with foil, meaning rest a sheet of foil lightly on top. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat. This loaf keeps 3 days wrapped at room temperature, or freeze slices.

Ripe bananas make these muffins moist and naturally sweet. Use bananas that feel very soft and smell fragrant. This is a good use for bananas that are too soft to eat out of hand.
12 muffins
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) all-purpose flour
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) sugar
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) cinnamon, optional
3 very ripe bananas, mashed, about 1 1/4 cups (one and a quarter cups)
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) oil or melted butter
1 large egg
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Ripe bananas should feel very soft and may have brown spots on the peel. The mashed fruit should feel almost like a thick puree. The baked muffins should feel springy on top.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a muffin pan, or line it with paper cups.
Mix the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Mix the wet ingredients in a second bowl.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix.
Stir just until you no longer feel dry flour. A few lumps are fine.
Spoon the batter into the cups, filling each about two-thirds full.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes.
A toothpick in the center of a muffin should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. The tops should feel set and springy.
Cool in the pan 5 minutes, then move the muffins out so they do not steam and get soggy.

entries.title: Berry Crumble

blocks.text: Mixed berries baked under a simple crumb topping. Frozen berries work well and do not need to be thawed. A little cornstarch helps the juices thicken.
6 servings
About 45 minutes, plus a short cooling time
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
5 cups mixed berries, fresh or frozen
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sugar, plus more to taste if the berries are very tart
2 tablespoons cornstarch
1 tablespoon lemon juice
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) all-purpose flour
1/2 cup (half a cup) packed brown sugar
1/2 cup (half a cup) rolled oats, optional
1/2 cup (half a cup) cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
A pinch of salt

The topping should feel like damp crumbs. After baking, the berries should feel very soft, the juices should feel slightly thick, not watery, once the crumble cools a little, and the topping should feel crisp.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease an 8 inch square pan or a similar baking dish.
Toss the berries with the sugar, cornstarch, and lemon juice.
Spread them in the dish.
Mix the flour, brown sugar, optional oats, and salt.
Cut in the butter until the mix feels like damp crumbs. Cut in means rub or mash the butter into the dry mix.
Sprinkle the topping over the berries.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes, until the topping feels crisp and the juices are bubbling thickly at the edges.
Cool at least 15 minutes before you serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The topping should feel crisp, not wet and raw. You should hear bubbling. You should smell cooked berries and toasted topping, not raw flour. The fruit will be extremely hot.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The topping should look golden. The juices should look bubbly and slightly glossy, not thin and watery. The berries should look collapsed.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The topping should look golden. The juices should look bubbly and slightly glossy, not thin and watery. The berries should look collapsed.

Use mitts. Berry filling is like molten sugar and can burn your mouth. Cool at least 15 minutes. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.
Serve with ice cream or Whipped Cream from the Misc chapter. If the berries are very juicy, add an extra teaspoon of cornstarch.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Chewy bar cookies that taste like a brown-sugar cookie in a pan. They are the vanilla cousin of brownies. Do not overbake, or they will be dry instead of chewy.
16 squares
About 40 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 cup unsalted butter, melted
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) packed brown sugar
2 large eggs
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 cup chocolate chips or chopped white chocolate, optional

The batter will feel thick. A toothpick in the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter, and not completely dry. The edges should feel set, and the center should feel slightly soft. It will firm as it cools.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease the pan, or line it with parchment, leaving a little overhang as a handle.
Mix the melted butter and brown sugar until even.
Add the eggs and vanilla, and mix well.
Add the flour, baking powder, and salt, and stir just until you no longer feel dry flour.
Stir in the chocolate chips, if using.
Spread the batter or dough evenly in the pan.
Bake 22 to 28 minutes.
A toothpick in the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. The edges should feel set, and the center should feel slightly soft.
Cool in the pan before you cut, unless the recipe tips say otherwise.

A classic muffin with fresh or frozen blueberries. Stir the batter only until the flour disappears, or the muffins can turn tough. Frozen berries can go in without thawing.
12 muffins
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour
1/2 cup (half a cup) sugar
2 teaspoons baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 cup milk
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) oil or melted butter
1 large egg
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) blueberries, fresh or frozen

The batter should feel thick and slightly lumpy, not silky-smooth. Frozen berries will make it colder and thicker. A toothpick in the center of a baked muffin should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease a muffin pan, or line it with paper cups.
Mix the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Mix the wet ingredients in a second bowl.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix.
Stir just until you no longer feel dry flour. A few lumps are fine.
Gently fold in the blueberries. Fold means turn the batter over itself gently.
Spoon the batter into the cups, filling each about two-thirds full.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes.
A toothpick in the center of a muffin should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter. The tops should feel set and springy.
Cool in the pan 5 minutes, then move the muffins out so they do not steam and get soggy.

blocks.text: Stale or toasted bread soaked in a sweet egg custard and baked until the center is set. Cook egg dishes to 160 degrees F. This is a good way to use leftover sandwich bread or the Simple Sandwich Bread in this chapter.

About 1 hour 15 minutes, plus a short rest

4 large eggs
2 cups milk
1/2 cup (half a cup) sugar
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 teaspoon cinnamon
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
2 tablespoons butter, for the pan, plus a little more, cut into small pieces, for the top
1/2 cup (half a cup) raisins, optional

The bread should feel dry enough to soak up custard, not already soggy. After a brief soak, every cube should feel moist. After baking, the center should feel set, like a firm custard, not liquid, and a thermometer should read 160 degrees F.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Butter an 8 or 9 inch baking dish.
Spread the bread cubes in the dish, and scatter the raisins if you are using them.
Mix the eggs, milk, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, and salt until even.
Pour the custard over the bread.
Press the bread down gently so it soaks.
Let it sit 10 to 15 minutes.
Dot the top with the remaining butter.
Bake 40 to 50 minutes, until the center feels set and a thermometer in the middle reads 160 degrees F. The top should feel golden and slightly crisp in spots.
Cool at least 15 minutes before you serve.

blocks.text: A pie with a cooked chocolate pudding filling in a prebaked crust, finished with whipped cream. The pudding must come to a bubble and thicken on the stove so the eggs cook and the filling sets when it chills.
8 servings
About 40 minutes, plus several hours of chilling
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 pie crust, baked and cooled, or a graham-cracker crust
2/3 cup (two-thirds of a cup) sugar
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) cornstarch
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) unsweetened cocoa powder, or 4 ounces chopped semisweet chocolate added at the end
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) milk
3 large egg yolks
2 tablespoons butter
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
Whipped cream, for topping, from the Misc chapter or store-bought

The pudding should feel smooth and thick enough to coat a spoon, and it should bubble slowly as you stir. After a full chill, a slice should feel set and creamy, not runny. Lumps can often be stirred or strained out while the filling is still hot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the sugar, cornstarch, salt, and cocoa in a saucepan.
If you are using chopped chocolate instead of cocoa, mix only the sugar, cornstarch, and salt now.
Whisk in the milk and egg yolks until the mix feels smooth. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk so there are no lumps.
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until the mix thickens and large, slow bubbles break the surface.
Let it bubble 1 minute while you stir.
Take the pan off the heat.
Stir in the butter, vanilla, and chopped chocolate if you are using it, until the filling feels smooth.
Pour the filling into the cooled crust.
Press plastic wrap or a piece of buttered parchment onto the surface if you want to reduce a skin. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
Cool, then refrigerate at least 4 hours, until a slice holds its shape.
Top with whipped cream just before serving.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The filling should feel thick, glossy, and smooth, and you should see or feel slow bubbles as it finishes. You should smell chocolate and cooked milk, not scorched milk or raw egg. After chilling, a slice should feel set.

Do not taste the filling until it has boiled and then cooled. Stir constantly so it does not scorch. The pan and filling are very hot. Cool, then refrigerate within 2 hours. Keep the pie refrigerated. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.
A graham crust is easier than a pastry crust here. If you get lumps, pour the hot filling through a strainer. Leftover pie keeps 3 days in the refrigerator.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. entries.title: Cinnamon Rolls

blocks.text: Soft cinnamon rolls made with store-bought dough, such as pizza dough or a refrigerated roll dough, so you can skip yeast work on a first try. If your package includes its own directions, follow those times, then use the doneness cues here. A filling of butter, sugar, and cinnamon is spread on the rolled dough, then the dough is rolled up and sliced.
8 to 12 rolls
About 45 minutes with store-bought dough, or longer if the package includes a rise
Beginner

A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 pound pizza dough or 1 can refrigerated roll dough, at room temperature if it was chilled, unless the package says otherwise
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus more for the pan
1/2 cup (half a cup) packed brown sugar
1 1/2 tablespoons (one and a half tablespoons) cinnamon
Optional glaze: 1 cup powdered sugar mixed with 2 tablespoons milk and 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) vanilla extract

Softened butter should spread easily. The dough should feel elastic and not ice-cold. The baked rolls should feel set in the center, not doughy, and the filling should feel hot and melted, not wet with raw dough underneath.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F, or to the temperature on the dough package if it is different.
Grease a baking pan.
Mix the brown sugar and cinnamon in a small bowl.
On a lightly floured board, roll or pat the dough into a rectangle about 1/4 inch (a quarter inch) thick.
Spread the softened butter over the dough.
Sprinkle the cinnamon sugar evenly on top.
Roll the dough up from a long side into a log.
Pinch the seam shut. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Cut the log into 8 to 12 even slices.
Set them cut-side up in the pan, close but not tightly jammed.
Bake 18 to 25 minutes, until the tops feel set and golden, and the center roll feels cooked, not doughy.
Cool 10 minutes.
If you want a glaze, stir the powdered sugar, milk, and vanilla until smooth, then spoon it over the warm rolls.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

A tender breakfast cake with a cinnamon crumb topping, meant to be eaten with coffee, not made from coffee. The topping is a mix of butter, sugar, flour, and cinnamon that bakes into a crunchy layer.
9 to 12 servings
About 55 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, softened
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 cup sour cream or plain yogurt
For the topping: 1/2 cup (half a cup) packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup (half a cup) flour, 1 teaspoon cinnamon, and 4 tablespoons cold butter, cut into cubes

The batter should feel thick. The topping should feel like damp crumbs, with some pea-size bits of butter. A toothpick in the cake should come out with a few crumbs, not wet batter. The topping should feel crisp.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a 9 inch square pan, or a similar 9 inch pan.
Mix the topping: brown sugar, flour, and cinnamon, then cut in the cold butter until the mix feels like damp crumbs. Cut in means rub or mash the butter into the dry mix.
Set this aside.
Mix the 2 cups flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a bowl.
Beat the softened butter and sugar until fluffy.
Add the eggs and vanilla, then the sour cream, and mix until even.
Add the flour mix and stir just until you no longer feel dry flour.
Spread the batter in the pan.
Sprinkle the topping evenly over it.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes, until a toothpick in the center comes out with a few crumbs, the cake feels set, and the topping feels crisp.
Cool at least 15 minutes before you cut.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cake should feel set and springy under the topping. The topping should feel crisp, not wet and sandy. You should smell cinnamon, butter, and toasted sugar, not raw flour.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The topping should look golden and crisp. A toothpick should come out with a few crumbs, not wet batter. The cake should look risen to the topping, not sunken.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The topping should look golden and crisp. A toothpick should come out with a few crumbs, not wet batter. The cake should look risen to the topping, not sunken.

Chopped pecans can go in the topping if no one has a nut allergy. This is good slightly warm or the next morning, covered once cool.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. A slightly sweet corn muffin that sits between a dinner cornbread and a breakfast muffin. Serve with chili, soup, or butter and honey.
12 muffins
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 cup yellow cornmeal
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sugar
2 teaspoons baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 cup milk
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) oil or melted butter
1 large egg
Cornmeal feels sandy and dry, coarser than flour. The batter should feel thick but pourable. Baked muffins should feel set and a little crumbly, not wet in the center.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Grease a muffin pan, or line it with paper cups.
Mix the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Mix the wet ingredients in a second bowl.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix.
Stir just until you no longer feel dry flour. A few lumps are fine.
Spoon the batter into the cups, filling each about two-thirds full.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes.
A toothpick in the center should come out clean or with a few crumbs. The tops should feel set.
Cool in the pan 5 minutes, then move the muffins out so they do not steam and get soggy.

A skillet or pan cornbread with a tender crumb and a slightly crisp edge. This version is lightly sweet. Serve with chili, soup, or a pat of butter. See also Corn Muffins in this chapter.
9 squares
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 cup yellow cornmeal
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 cup milk
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) melted butter or oil
1 large egg

Cornmeal feels sandy. The batter should feel pourable, thicker than pancake batter but looser than muffin batter. The baked bread should feel set in the center, and a toothpick should come out clean or with a few crumbs.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Grease an 8 inch square pan, or a 9 inch skillet that can go in the oven.
Mix the flour, cornmeal, sugar, baking powder, and salt in a bowl.
Mix the milk, melted butter or oil, and egg in a second bowl.
Pour the wet mix into the dry mix.
Stir just until you no longer feel dry flour. A few lumps are fine.
Spread the batter in the pan.
Bake 18 to 24 minutes, until a toothpick in the center comes out clean or with a few crumbs, and the top feels set.
Cool 10 minutes, then cut into squares.

Tender scones made with cream, cut into wedges, and baked until the edges are lightly crisp. They are a little richer and more crumbly than biscuits. Handle the dough gently.
8 scones
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for the board
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
6 tablespoons cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) heavy cream, plus 1 tablespoon for brushing
1 teaspoon vanilla extract, optional

The dough should feel soft and a little dry, just holding together, not wet and sticky. You should still feel small bits of butter. Baked scones should feel set and lightly crisp at the edges, and tender inside, not wet in the center.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Line a baking sheet with parchment.
Mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt.
Cut in the cold butter until the mix feels like coarse crumbs with some pea-size bits. Cut in means rub or mash the butter into the flour.
Add the cream and optional vanilla.
Stir just until a dough forms.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured board.
Pat it into a circle about 3/4 inch (three-quarters of an inch) thick.
Cut the circle into 8 wedges, like a pie.
Set them on the sheet with a little space.
Brush the tops with the remaining cream.
Bake 14 to 18 minutes, until the edges feel set and lightly crisp, and the bottoms feel golden, not doughy.
Cool 10 minutes.
Serve warm or at room temperature.

entries.title: Dinner Rolls

blocks.text: Soft dinner rolls from store-bought dough, baked until the tops are golden and the centers are cooked. This is an easy way to put bread on a supper table without mixing yeast dough from scratch.
12 rolls
About 30 minutes with store-bought dough, plus any rise the package requires
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) pizza dough or frozen dinner-roll dough, thawed if frozen, following the package
2 tablespoons melted butter, plus more for the pan
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, if the dough is unsalted

The dough should feel soft and elastic, not icy and not sticky enough to be unworkable. Baked rolls should feel set and lightly golden on top, and the center of a roll should feel dry and cooked, not gummy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F, or to the temperature on the package.
Grease a baking pan.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces.
Shape each piece into a ball by pulling the edges under and pinching them at the bottom.
Set the balls in the pan, close but not crushed together.
Brush the tops with melted butter.
If the package asks for a rise, cover the pan and let the rolls sit until they feel puffy.
Bake 15 to 22 minutes, until the tops feel set and golden, and the center roll feels cooked, not gummy.
Brush with a little more butter if you like.
Cool 5 minutes and serve warm.

entries.title: Focaccia

blocks.text: A dimpled flatbread with olive oil and salt, baked until the top is golden and the interior is tender. You can start with store-bought pizza dough, or with a simple yeast dough if you are comfortable waiting for it to rise. Rise, or proof, means giving yeast dough time in a warm place so it becomes puffy. Proof means let yeast dough rest until it feels puffy and risen.
1 pan, about 12 squares
About 1 hour 30 minutes, including rise time, or less with pizza dough
Beginner to intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 pounds (one and a half pounds) pizza dough, or homemade dough that has already risen once
3 tablespoons olive oil, divided
3/4 teaspoon (three-quarters of a teaspoon) coarse salt
Optional toppings: rosemary, thinly sliced garlic, or olives

The dough should feel soft, oily, and puffy after it rests in the pan. Your fingertips should leave dimples that stay. The baked bread should feel golden and lightly crisp on top, and tender inside, not wet and raw in the middle.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Oil a 9 by 13 inch pan, or a similar sheet pan, with 1 tablespoon of the oil.
Press the dough into the pan.
If it shrinks back, wait 10 minutes and try again.
Cover and let it rest until it feels puffy, 20 to 40 minutes, or according to the dough you are using. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Dimple the dough with your fingertips, pressing to the pan in spots but not tearing it.
Drizzle the remaining oil over the top.
Sprinkle with salt and any optional toppings.
Bake 18 to 24 minutes, until the top feels golden and set, and the bottom feels lightly crisp, not soft and pale.
Cool 10 minutes, then cut into squares.
