blocks.text: A moist, dark spice cake sweetened with molasses, which is a thick, dark syrup with a slightly bitter, deep sweetness. This is a snack cake, not a cookie, and it is good plain or with whipped cream.
9 servings
About 50 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
2 teaspoons ground ginger
1 teaspoon cinnamon
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, melted, or oil
1/2 cup (half a cup) packed brown sugar
1/2 cup (half a cup) molasses
1 large egg
1 cup hot water

Molasses feels thick, sticky, and heavy. A little oil on the measuring cup can help it slide out. The batter will feel thin after you add the water. A toothpick in the baked cake should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a 9 inch square pan.
Mix the flour, baking soda, salt, ginger, and cinnamon.
In a second bowl, mix the melted butter or oil, brown sugar, molasses, and egg until even.
Add the flour mix and stir until combined.
Add the hot water carefully and stir until the batter feels smooth and thin.
Pour the batter into the pan.
Bake 30 to 38 minutes, until a toothpick in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs, and the top feels springy.
Cool in the pan at least 15 minutes before you cut.

A dusting of powdered sugar or a dollop of Whipped Cream from the Misc chapter is plenty. This cake keeps well, covered, for several days.

A rustic round loaf that rises with baking soda and buttermilk, not yeast. There is no kneading beyond a brief, light mix. Knead means press and fold dough to develop gluten, which you mostly avoid here so the bread stays tender. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air.
1 round loaf, about 12 slices
About 1 hour
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
4 cups all-purpose flour, plus a little more for the board
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon salt
1 tablespoon sugar, optional
1 3/4 cups (one and three-quarters cups) buttermilk, plus 1 or 2 tablespoons more if the dough is dry

The dough should feel shaggy and slightly sticky, but it should hold a round loaf. If it feels like a tight bread dough, you have worked it too much. The baked loaf should feel crusty outside and moist inside, and a toothpick or skewer in the center should come out clean.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Line a baking sheet with parchment, or grease a cake pan.
Mix the flour, baking soda, salt, and optional sugar in a bowl.
Add the buttermilk.
Stir just until a shaggy dough forms.
If dry flour remains, add buttermilk 1 tablespoon at a time.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured board.
Fold it over itself a few times, just until it holds together.
Shape a round loaf about 2 inches tall.
Set it on the pan.
Cut a shallow X in the top with a knife, about 1/2 inch (half an inch) deep. This helps the center bake.

Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until the crust feels firm and a skewer in the center comes out clean. The loaf should sound hollow if you tap the bottom with a knuckle, once you can handle it safely with mitts.
Cool at least 20 minutes before you slice.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The crust should feel firm. A skewer in the center should come out clean. You should smell toasted wheat, not raw flour or burning. The loaf may sound hollow when the bottom is tapped.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The loaf should look rustic and golden to light brown, with the X opened a little. The inside should look moist and even, not raw and doughy in the center.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. entries.title: Key Lime Pie

blocks.text: A tart, creamy lime pie in a graham-cracker crust. The filling is sweetened condensed milk, lime juice, and egg yolks, and it sets in a short bake, then must chill. Regular lime juice works if you cannot find Key limes.
8 servings
About 35 minutes, plus several hours of chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) graham-cracker crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
5 tablespoons melted butter
1 can (14 ounces) sweetened condensed milk
4 large egg yolks
1/2 cup (half a cup) lime juice, plus 1 teaspoon lime zest if you like

Zest is the fragrant green outer skin of the lime, not the bitter white pith. The filling should feel smooth and pourable. After baking, it should feel just set, with a slight jiggle. After chilling, a slice should feel creamy and hold its shape.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Mix the crumbs, sugar, and melted butter until the mix feels like damp sand.
Press it into a 9 inch pie pan.
Bake the crust 8 minutes, then cool slightly.
Mix the condensed milk, egg yolks, lime juice, and optional zest until even.
Pour the filling into the crust.
Bake 12 to 16 minutes, until the filling is just set and still slightly jiggly in the center, not liquid.
Cool, then refrigerate at least 3 hours, until a slice holds its shape.

Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The filling should look pale and just set, not browned and not liquid. After chilling, a slice should hold a clean edge.

Do not taste raw filling. It contains egg yolks. Use mitts. Cool, then refrigerate within 2 hours. Keep the pie refrigerated, and do not leave slices out more than 2 hours. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.
Whipped Cream from the Misc chapter is the usual topping. Bottled lime juice works, but fresh juice tastes brighter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: A buttery shortbread crust with a tart lemon filling that sets as it bakes. The filling contains eggs. Cool the bars completely, then dust them with powdered sugar if you like, and cut with a clean knife.
16 squares
About 1 hour, plus cooling

Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings

A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 cup unsalted butter, softened
1/2 cup (half a cup) powdered sugar, plus more for dusting
2 cups all-purpose flour, divided
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
4 large eggs
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) granulated sugar
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) lemon juice, plus 1 tablespoon lemon zest

Zest is the fragrant yellow outer skin of the lemon, not the bitter white pith. The crust dough should feel like damp crumbs that hold when pressed. After baking, the filling should feel set, not liquid, and a slight jiggle is all right. After cooling, a bar should cut cleanly.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a 9 by 13 inch pan, or line it with parchment.
Mix the butter, powdered sugar, 1 3/4 cups (one and three-quarters cups) of the flour, and the salt until a soft dough forms.
Press the dough evenly into the pan.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes, until the crust feels set and just barely golden.
Mix the eggs, granulated sugar, remaining 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) flour, lemon juice, and zest until even.
Pour the filling over the hot crust.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes more, until the filling feels set and only slightly jiggly in the center, not liquid.
Cool completely.
Dust with powdered sugar if you like, then cut into squares.

A clean, slightly wet knife helps you cut neat squares. Keep bars refrigerated after the first day. They freeze well.

A tender lemon loaf, sometimes finished with a simple lemon glaze, meaning a thin icing of sugar and lemon juice that sets as it cools. Zest is the fragrant yellow outer skin of the lemon, not the bitter white pith underneath.
1 loaf, about 10 slices
About 1 hour 15 minutes
Beginner

A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork

1 teaspoon baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, softened
1 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1/2 cup (half a cup) milk
2 tablespoons lemon zest, from about 2 lemons
3 tablespoons lemon juice, divided, plus 1/2 cup (half a cup) powdered sugar for an optional glaze

Zest should feel like fine, dry, fragrant shreds, not wet white pith. Softened butter should give like cool clay. The baked loaf should feel springy, and a toothpick in the center should come out with a few crumbs.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a loaf pan, or line it with parchment.
Mix the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Mix the wet ingredients in a second bowl, including any mashed fruit.
Add the wet mix to the dry mix.
Stir just until combined.
Stir in the lemon zest and 2 tablespoons of the lemon juice.
Spread the batter in the pan.
Bake 45 to 55 minutes.
A toothpick in the center should come out with a few crumbs, not wet batter. The top should feel set and springy.
Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn the loaf out to finish cooling.

entries.title: Molasses Cookies

blocks.text: Soft, spiced cookies made with molasses, which is a thick, dark syrup. They are rolled in sugar before baking, which gives a slight crunch on the outside and a chewy center.
About 24 cookies
About 30 minutes, plus a short chill if the dough is soft
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 1/4 cups (two and a quarter cups) all-purpose flour
2 teaspoons baking soda
1 teaspoon cinnamon
1 teaspoon ground ginger
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) cloves or allspice, optional
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) unsalted butter, softened
1 cup packed brown sugar
1 large egg
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) molasses
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) granulated sugar, for rolling

Molasses feels thick and sticky. A little oil in the measuring cup can help it slide. Softened butter should give like cool clay. The dough should feel soft but shapeable. If it feels sticky, chill it 20 to 30 minutes. Baked cookies should feel set at the edges and slightly soft in the centers.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.
Stir the dry ingredients in a bowl until they are combined.
In a second bowl, beat the butter and sugar until the mix feels fluffy and even. This is called creaming.
Add the eggs and vanilla, if listed.
Beat until combined.
Add the dry mix.
Stir just until you no longer feel dry flour.
Stir in the molasses with the eggs and vanilla if listed, then proceed, and roll the balls in the granulated sugar before they go on the sheet.
Roll the dough into 1 inch balls.
Place them on the sheet with space between them.
Bake 10 to 12 minutes.
Check at the early time. The edges should feel set and the centers should feel slightly soft. The tops may look crackled.
Cool on the pan 2 to 3 minutes, then move the cookies to a rack or a plate to finish cooling.

For a crisper cookie, bake 1 to 2 minutes longer. These keep well in a closed container for several days.

entries.title: Monkey Bread

blocks.text: Pull-apart pieces of dough coated in butter, sugar, and cinnamon, baked in a bundt or tube pan. This version uses refrigerated biscuit dough to keep the method short. The pieces should be cooked in the center, not doughy, and the caramel-like coating will be extremely hot at first.
8 to 10 servings
About 1 hour with refrigerated biscuit dough
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 cans refrigerated biscuit dough, 16 ounces each, or the equivalent
1 cup packed brown sugar
2 teaspoons cinnamon
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, melted
Optional glaze: 1 cup powdered sugar mixed with 2 tablespoons milk
Each biscuit piece should feel coated, not dry. After baking, a center piece should feel cooked and light, not doughy and wet. The coating should feel sticky and set, not liquid, after a short cool.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Grease a bundt pan or a tube pan very well, including the tube.
Mix the brown sugar and cinnamon in a bowl.
Cut each biscuit into 4 pieces.
Dip the pieces in the melted butter, then toss them in the cinnamon sugar, and layer them in the pan.
Drizzle any leftover butter and sugar over the top.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes, until the top feels set and golden, and a center piece feels cooked, not doughy.
If the top browns too fast, tent it with foil, meaning rest a sheet of foil lightly on top. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn the bread out onto a plate.
Cool 10 minutes more before you pull it apart.
Add glaze if you like, after it is not piping hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The top should feel set. A center piece should feel cooked, not doughy. You should smell cinnamon, butter, and toasted sugar, not raw dough or burning sugar. The coating will be extremely hot at first.

Cool at least 10 minutes in the pan, then 10 minutes more after turning out, before you pull pieces apart. A bundt pan is heavy and awkward. Use a stable landing zone. If a piece in the very center is still doughy, return the bread to the pan and bake 5 to 10 minutes more. Leftovers reheat at 300 degrees F until warm.

entries.title: No-Bake Cheesecake

blocks.text: A cream-cheese pie on a graham-cracker crust that sets in the refrigerator, not the oven. There are no eggs, so you are not baking to a temperature. The filling must chill long enough to slice cleanly.
10 to 12 servings
About 20 minutes, plus at least 4 hours of chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) graham-cracker crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar, for the crust
6 tablespoons melted butter
16 ounces cream cheese, softened
1/2 cup (half a cup) sugar, for the filling
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
1 cup heavy cream, cold, or one 8 ounce tub of whipped topping

Softened cream cheese should feel smooth, not lumpy. The filling should feel thick and fluffy before it goes into the crust. After a full chill, a slice should feel set and creamy, not soft and collapsing.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the crumbs, 3 tablespoons sugar, and melted butter until the mix feels like damp sand.
Press it firmly into a 9 inch pie pan, up the sides a little.
Chill the crust 15 minutes, or bake it at 350 degrees F for 8 minutes and cool completely if you want a firmer crust.
Beat the cream cheese, 1/2 cup (half a cup) sugar, and vanilla until the mix feels smooth.
In a second bowl, beat the cold cream until it holds a soft peak, meaning a ridge of cream stands up and then slightly folds over, or fold in the whipped topping.
Fold the cream into the cream-cheese mix. Fold means turn the mixture over itself gently so you do not knock out all the air.
Spread the filling in the crust.
Smooth the top.
Refrigerate at least 4 hours, or overnight, until a slice holds its shape.

entries.title: No-Bake Peanut Butter Cookies

blocks.text: Stovetop cookies made with sugar, milk, peanut butter, and oats. They set as they cool, with no oven. Work quickly once the sugar mix has boiled, because the mixture thickens fast.
About 24 cookies
About 20 minutes, plus 20 minutes to set
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 cups sugar
1/2 cup (half a cup) milk
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) unsweetened cocoa powder, optional
1 cup peanut butter
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
3 cups quick oats
A pinch of salt
The boiled mix is extremely hot. The finished cookies should feel firm enough to lift.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Line a baking sheet with parchment or wax paper.
Put the sugar, milk, butter, and cocoa, if using, in a pot.
Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring.
When the mix reaches a full boil, boil 1 minute, still stirring.
Take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the peanut butter, vanilla, salt, and oats until evenly coated.
Drop rounded tablespoons onto the sheet.
Let the cookies sit until they feel set, about 20 minutes.

entries.title: Peach Cobbler

blocks.text: Baked peaches with a biscuit-like topping. Cobbler means fruit baked with dollops of dough that bake up like cobblestones, not a rolled pie crust. Fresh or frozen peaches both work. If you use frozen fruit, do not thaw it fully, and add a few extra minutes.
6 to 8 servings
About 55 minutes, plus a short cooling time
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
6 cups sliced peaches, fresh or frozen, or two large cans of peaches, drained
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sugar, for the fruit, plus 1 tablespoon lemon juice
1 tablespoon cornstarch or flour
1 cup all-purpose flour, for the topping
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) sugar, for the topping
1 1/2 teaspoons (one and a half teaspoons) baking powder
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
4 tablespoons cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) milk

The topping dough should feel soft and droppable, like a thick biscuit dough. After baking, the peaches should feel tender, the juices should be bubbling, and the topping should feel set and golden, not wet and raw in the center of a biscuit.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease a 2 quart baking dish.
Toss the peaches with 1/3 cup (a third of a cup) sugar, the lemon juice, and the cornstarch or flour.
Spread them in the dish.
Mix the flour, 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) sugar, baking powder, and salt.
Cut in the butter until the mix feels like coarse crumbs. Cut in means rub or mash the butter into the flour.
Add the milk and stir just until a soft dough forms.
Drop spoonfuls of dough over the fruit.
It does not need to cover every gap.
Bake 35 to 45 minutes, until the topping feels set and golden, and the fruit is bubbling at the edges.
Cool at least 15 minutes before you serve.

A sprinkle of cinnamon in the fruit is a good extra. Serve with ice cream. Other stone fruit, such as nectarines or plums, can be used the same way.

entries.title: Pie Crust

blocks.text: A basic butter pie dough for the pies in this chapter. Keep the butter cold. Cut in means rub or mash the butter into the flour until you feel coarse crumbs with some pea-size pieces. Those pieces make a flaky crust. This page also covers baking a single crust empty, which is called baking blind, meaning you bake the crust before you add a filling that does not need a long bake.
One 9 inch double crust, or two single crusts
About 20 minutes, plus at least 30 minutes of chilling
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) all-purpose flour, plus more for rolling
1 teaspoon salt
1 tablespoon sugar, optional, for a dessert crust
1 cup cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
6 to 8 tablespoons ice water

The butter should feel cold and firm. After you cut it in, you should still feel small pieces. The dough should feel shaggy, then hold together when pressed, without feeling wet and sticky. After chilling, it should feel firm and rollable, not rock-hard and not sticky. A baked empty crust should feel dry, set, and lightly golden.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the flour, salt, and optional sugar.
Cut in the cold butter until the mix feels like coarse crumbs with some pea-size bits.
Add ice water 1 tablespoon at a time, stirring, just until the dough holds when you press it.
Divide the dough in two.
Flatten each piece into a disk.
Wrap and refrigerate at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 days.
On a floured board, roll a disk from the center out, turning it as you go, until it is about 12 inches across and about 1/8 inch (an eighth of an inch) thick for a 9 inch pan.
If it cracks, let it warm 2 or 3 minutes and pinch the crack shut. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Ease the dough into the pan without stretching it.
Trim or fold the edges, and crimp, meaning pinch a pattern around the rim. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air.
Chill 15 minutes before you fill or bake.
To bake a crust empty, line it with parchment, fill it with dry beans or pie weights, and bake at 375 degrees F for 15 minutes.
Remove the weights and parchment, then bake 8 to 12 minutes more, until the crust feels dry and lightly golden.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The dough should feel shaggy, then firm after a chill, and it should roll without sticking if it is well floured and still cool. A baked empty crust should feel dry and set, and you should smell toasted butter and flour, not raw dough or burning.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: A rolled crust should look even, without big cracks. A baked empty crust should look dry and light golden, not pale and raw, and not dark brown.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. A rolled crust should look even, without big cracks. A baked empty crust should look dry and light golden, not pale and raw, and not dark brown.

Do not taste raw dough. It contains raw flour. Use mitts when you bake. Pie weights and beans will be very hot. Cool them before you store them. A rolling pin and a board can slide, so work on a stable surface, and use a bench scraper or a spatula to lift the dough. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

If the dough gets warm and sticky, chill it again. You can freeze wrapped disks for a month and thaw them in the refrigerator. Store-bought crust is a fair shortcut when you want a pie without this step.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: A dense, buttery loaf cake. The name comes from an older formula of a pound each of butter, sugar, eggs, and flour. This is a slightly smaller home version. It keeps well and is good plain, toasted, or with fruit and whipped cream.
1 loaf, about 10 slices
About 1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
1 cup unsalted butter, softened
1 cup sugar
4 large eggs
2 teaspoons vanilla extract

Softened butter should give like cool clay, not feel melted. The batter will feel thick. A toothpick in the center of the baked cake should come out clean or with a few crumbs, and the top should feel set and slightly firm.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 325 degrees F.
Grease a loaf pan and line it with parchment if you have it.
Mix the flour, baking powder, and salt.
Beat the butter and sugar until the mix feels very fluffy and pale. This is called creaming, and it matters in this cake.
Add the eggs one at a time, beating after each, then add the vanilla.
Add the flour mix and stir just until you no longer feel dry flour.
Spread the batter in the pan and smooth the top.
Bake 60 to 75 minutes, until a toothpick in the center comes out clean or with a few crumbs, and the top feels set.
If the top browns too fast, tent it with foil, meaning rest a sheet of foil lightly on top. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.

blocks.text: A basic loaf of yeast bread for sandwiches and toast. Yeast is a living ingredient that makes dough rise, meaning the dough becomes puffy as the yeast produces gas. Knead means press, fold, and turn the dough to develop gluten, which is the structure that lets bread stretch and hold its shape. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air. This takes time, but the steps are simple.
1 loaf
About 3 hours, including rising time
Intermediate
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
3 cups all-purpose or bread flour, plus more for kneading
1 packet (2 1/4 teaspoons, or two and a quarter teaspoons) instant or active dry yeast
1 1/2 teaspoons (one and a half teaspoons) salt
1 tablespoon sugar or honey
1 cup warm water, about 105 to 110 degrees F, plus 2 tablespoons more if the dough is dry
2 tablespoons oil or melted butter, plus more for the bowl and pan

The water should feel warm, like a comfortable bath, not hot enough to hurt your finger. Dough that is too hot can harm the yeast. After kneading, the dough should feel smooth and elastic, slightly tacky but not wet. After rising, it should feel puffy and hold a dent that springs back slowly. The baked loaf should feel firm, and a thermometer in the center should read about 190 to 200 degrees F, or the loaf should sound hollow when you tap the bottom with a knuckle, using a mitt.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the flour, yeast, salt, and sugar in a bowl.
If you are using active dry yeast and the package asks you to dissolve it in water first, follow that, then add it with the water.
Add the warm water and the oil or butter.
Stir until a shaggy dough forms.
Knead on a lightly floured board 8 to 10 minutes, or in a mixer with a dough hook, until the dough feels smooth and elastic.
Add flour only a tablespoon at a time if it is too sticky to handle.
Place the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, and turn it so it is coated.
Cover the bowl.
Let it rise in a warm, draft-free place until it feels doubled and puffy, about 1 hour.
Press the air out gently.
Shape a loaf and set it in a greased loaf pan.
Cover and let it rise again until the dough feels puffy and crowns slightly over the pan, 30 to 45 minutes.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F during the last 15 minutes.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes, until the crust feels firm and golden, and the center is about 190 to 200 degrees F, or the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the bottom with a mitt on your hand.
Cool in the pan 10 minutes, then turn the loaf out and cool completely before you slice, or the crumb can compress.

entries.title: Popcorn

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

Popcorn is a late-night staple, and you can make it on the stove or in the microwave. Both methods use sound as the main doneness cue: the pops start slow, get rapid, then slow again. When the gap between pops is about 2 seconds, it is time to stop. Stovetop popcorn uses hot oil, so stay with the pot.
2 to 4, about 8 to 10 cups popped
About 10 minutes for stovetop or microwave
Beginner, with extra care around hot oil and steam
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large, heavy pot with a tight lid, for the stovetop method
A large bowl
Oven mitts
A microwave, for the bag or bowl method
A microwave-safe bowl and a microwave-safe plate, for microwave kernels
Stovetop method: 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, and 1/2 cup (half a cup) popcorn kernels
Microwave kernel method: 1/3 cup (a third of a cup) popcorn kernels, and 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) oil, optional
Or 1 bag microwave popcorn, any plain or lightly salted flavor you like
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, or to taste, or 2 tablespoons melted butter, optional

Kernels feel small, hard, and pointed at one end. They should be dry. Oil is slick and liquid. Popped corn is light, irregular, and fragile. Unpopped kernels in the bowl are still hard and should be left in the bottom when you serve, so no one bites one.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Stovetop method: Put the oil and 3 test kernels in a large, heavy pot.
Cover the pot.
Set it over medium heat.
When those 3 kernels pop, add the rest of the 1/2 cup of kernels. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Shake the pot so they sit in one layer.
Cover again, leaving the lid just slightly ajar if your pot lid allows a little steam to escape, but keep it mostly closed.
Shake the pot now and then as the popping gets going.
Use mitts. The pot and lid will be very hot.
Listen for the popping to slow to about 2 seconds between pops, then turn off the heat.
Let the pot sit 30 seconds so late kernels can finish.
Pour the popcorn into a large bowl.
Season with salt or melted butter, tossing to coat.
Microwave bag method: Place the bag in the microwave with the correct side up, following the bag if you or a helper can check the arrows.
Cook on high.
Listen, and stop the oven when pops are about 2 seconds apart, even if the package time is not up.
Let the bag sit 15 seconds.
Open it away from your face, because steam will rush out.
Microwave bowl method: Put 1/3 cup kernels in a large microwave-safe bowl.
Cover with a microwave-safe plate.
Cook on high 2 to 4 minutes, listening and stopping when pops are about 2 seconds apart.
Let it stand 30 seconds.
Uncover away from your face.
Season and serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The key cue is sound. Popping starts with a few pops, becomes rapid, then slows. Stop when you can count about 2 seconds between pops. You should smell toasted corn, not burnt oil or burnt corn. The pot, bag, or bowl will be very hot.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: Most kernels should be open, white, and fluffy. A few unpopped kernels at the bottom are normal. The popcorn should not look scorched or dark brown. A microwave bag may puff up and then settle.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. Most kernels should be open, white, and fluffy. A few unpopped kernels at the bottom are normal. The popcorn should not look scorched or dark brown. A microwave bag may puff up and then settle.

Never leave popcorn unattended. Hot oil, steam, and a hot lid can burn you. Use mitts. Open lids and bags away from your face. Do not use an empty pot on high heat. If the popcorn smells burnt, turn off the heat and leave the lid on until it cools. Do not put metal in the microwave. Stop a microwave bag early rather than letting it scorch. Unpopped kernels are a tooth hazard. Leave them in the bowl. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A little more salt or butter can be added at the table. For cinnamon sugar popcorn, toss with a teaspoon of sugar and a pinch of cinnamon while it is warm. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). If many kernels stay unpopped, the heat may have been too low, or the kernels may be old and dry.

Popcorn is best fresh. Store cooled leftovers in a loosely closed bag and eat the same day. It will go stale and does not reheat well. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Celery sticks filled with peanut butter and topped with raisins, which are the "ants." This is a no-cook snack. If anyone has a peanut allergy, use a safe seed butter or cream cheese instead.
8 to 12 pieces
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
4 celery stalks
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) peanut butter, or cream cheese
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) raisins or chocolate chips
Celery should feel firm and crisp, not limp and rubbery. After you wash it, dry it so the filling stays put. The groove in the celery is the place to spread the peanut butter.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Wash the celery and pat it dry.
Trim the ends on a stable board.
Cut each stalk into 2 or 3 shorter logs.
Spread peanut butter or cream cheese into the groove of each piece.
Press raisins or chips onto the filling in a loose line.
Serve at once, or cover and refrigerate up to 1 day.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The celery should feel crisp and should smell fresh and green, not sour. The filling should feel even and thick enough to hold the raisins. Raisins should feel soft and sticky, not rock-hard, though harder raisins still work.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The filling should look even in the groove, and the raisins should look pressed on, not rolling off a dry, thin smear.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The filling should look even in the groove, and the raisins should look pressed on, not rolling off a dry, thin smear.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Do not serve peanut butter to anyone with a peanut allergy. Wash the celery well, including the groove, where dirt can hide. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Cream cheese and dried cranberries are a good variation. Cut the celery into shorter pieces if you want an easier bite.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Fresh apple slices with peanut butter for dipping or spreading. This is a fast, filling snack with no cooking. If anyone has a peanut allergy, use a seed butter that is safe for them, or skip the spread and use cheese instead.
1 snack
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
1 apple
2 tablespoons peanut butter, or another nut or seed butter that is safe for the people eating
A pinch of cinnamon, optional
A ripe apple should feel firm, not mushy, and should smell fresh, not fermented. Slices should be even enough to dip. If the peanut butter is very stiff, stir it first.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Wash the apple.
Set it on a stable board.
Cut the apple into quarters, then cut out the core from each piece, then slice.
Use a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the apple if you need it.
Spoon the peanut butter into a small bowl, or spread it on the slices.
Add a pinch of cinnamon if you like. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve at once, because cut apples brown as they sit.
A little lemon juice on the slices can slow the browning if you need to wait a few minutes.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The apple should feel crisp and juicy, and it should smell fresh. The peanut butter should feel smooth or evenly crunchy, depending on the jar, not oily and separated without a stir, and not rancid. Rancid peanut butter smells like old oil or paint.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The slices should look pale and fresh, not brown and dry, and the peanut butter should look even and scoopable.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The slices should look pale and fresh, not brown and dry, and the peanut butter should look even and scoopable.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Do not serve peanut butter to anyone with a peanut allergy. Wash the knife after spreading if you will use it on other food. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Cheddar cheese sticks are a good substitute if peanut butter is not an option. A firm apple such as Honeycrisp or Granny Smith holds its shape for dipping.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A bowl of cereal with cold milk, written out as a late-night snack so it is easy to make in a quiet kitchen. Use a bowl with a wide, stable base, and pour the milk slowly.
1 bowl
About 2 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 to 1 1/2 cups (one to one and a half cups) dry cereal
1/2 to 3/4 cup (half to three-quarters of a cup) cold milk, or enough to come partway up the cereal

The bowl should feel stable on the counter before you pour. Start with less milk. You can always add more. The cereal should feel wet at the bottom and still slightly crisp at the top if you like contrast, or fully soaked if you prefer it soft.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Set a bowl on a clear counter.
Pour the dry cereal into the bowl.
Pour the milk slowly, aiming for the center, until you can feel or hear that the cereal is partly covered.
Eat at once, because most cereals soften as they sit.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The milk should smell fresh, not sour. The cereal should smell as you expect, not stale or cardboard-like. The bowl should feel comfortably full, not so full that it sloshes.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The milk should look high enough to moisten the cereal without flooding the bowl and making it hard to carry.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The milk should look high enough to moisten the cereal without flooding the bowl and making it hard to carry.

Use a stable bowl. Wipe drips so the bowl is not slippery. Keep milk refrigerated, and do not leave the carton out. If the milk smells sour or has curdled, throw it out. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A sliced banana or a handful of berries can go on top. If you want a dairy-free bowl, use a milk alternative you know is fresh.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A no-cook plate of cheese, crackers, and simple extras. This is useful when you do not want to turn on the stove. Keep the cheese cold until you plate it, then serve soon.
1 or 2 as a snack
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
2 ounces cheese, such as cheddar, Swiss, or a mix, sliced or cubed
A handful of crackers, about 8 to 12
Optional extras: apple slices, grapes, olives, or a few nuts if no one has a nut allergy

Cheese straight from the refrigerator is firm and easier to slice. After a few minutes on the plate it smells stronger and spreads more easily on a cracker. Feel for a clean, even slice, and keep fruit dry so the crackers do not get soggy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Slice or cube the cheese on a clean board, using a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the cheese if you need it.
Arrange the cheese, crackers, and any extras on a plate, with a little space so you can find each item by touch.
Serve at once, or cover and refrigerate if you will eat in the next hour, then bring it out just before you eat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cheese should feel cool and clean-cut, not slimy. You should smell the cheese you expect, not sourness or ammonia. Crackers should feel crisp and dry. Fruit should feel fresh, not fermented.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look evenly sliced or cubed, and the plate should look uncrowded so each item is easy to pick up.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look evenly sliced or cubed, and the plate should look uncrowded so each item is easy to pick up.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Keep perishable cheese refrigerated until serving, and do not leave the plate out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Wash the knife and board after use. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Softer cheeses can be served in a small bowl with a knife for spreading. See also Fruit and Cheese Plate in the Misc chapter for a larger version.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. A tortilla folded over cheese and cooked in a skillet until the tortilla is crisp in spots and the cheese is melted. This is a smaller, later-night version of the Quesadillas in the Lunch chapter. Keep fillings light so the quesadilla turns easily.
1 quesadilla
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
1 large flour tortilla, or 2 small tortillas
1/2 to 3/4 cup (half to three-quarters of a cup) shredded cheese
1 teaspoon oil or butter, for the pan
Optional: a little salsa or leftover cooked vegetables, kept dry
The tortilla should feel flexible, not stale and cracked. After cooking, it should feel crisp in spots, and the cheese should feel fully melted and stretchy, not still shredded in the center.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil or butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Lay the tortilla in the pan.
Sprinkle the cheese over half of it, leaving a small border.
Add any optional dry fillings.
Fold the bare half over the filling. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air.
Press gently with a spatula.
Cook 2 to 3 minutes, until the bottom feels crisp in spots and you smell toasted tortilla, not burning.
Turn and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the second side feels crisp in spots and the cheese is fully melted.
Move to a plate.
Cool 1 minute, then cut into wedges and serve.
Salsa or sour cream can go on the side.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The tortilla should feel crisp in spots. The cheese should feel fully melted. You should smell toasted flour and melted cheese, not burning. The sizzle should stay gentle.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The tortilla should look lightly golden in spots, not pale and not black. When you cut it, the cheese should look melted and stretchy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The tortilla should look lightly golden in spots, not pale and not black. When you cut it, the cheese should look melted and stretchy.

The pan is hot. Use a spatula to turn the quesadilla. Melted cheese can burn your mouth, so wait 1 minute. If you add leftover meat, heat the center to 165 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A lid helps the cheese melt. Do not overfill, or the filling will spill when you turn it.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Chili Cheese Fries

blocks.text: Oven fries or leftover fries topped with hot chili and melted cheese. Make or reheat the chili until it is 165 degrees F, then add cheese so it melts. This is a heavy, late-night plate. See Chili in the Supper chapter, and Oven Fries in this chapter.
2 to 3 as a late meal
About 20 minutes with already-cooked fries and chili, or longer if you start from scratch
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
1 recipe Oven Fries, or 4 cups cooked fries, leftover or frozen fries cooked until crisp
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) chili, leftover or canned, reheated to 165 degrees F
1 cup shredded cheddar cheese
Optional: sliced green onion or a spoon of sour cream, added at the end
The fries should feel crisp before you add the chili, because they will soften under the toppings. The chili should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F. The cheese should feel melted.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cook or reheat the fries until they feel crisp.
Set them on an oven-safe platter or a sheet pan.
Reheat the chili in a pot or in the microwave until it is 165 degrees F and bubbling.
Spoon the hot chili over the fries.
Sprinkle the cheese on top.
Heat in a 400 degree F oven 3 to 5 minutes, until the cheese is melted, or cover the platter for a minute so the residual heat melts the cheese.
Add any cold toppings.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The chili should be steaming hot, 165 degrees F. The cheese should feel melted. You should smell chili, toasted potato, and cheese, not burning. The platter will be very hot.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look melted, and the chili should look bubbling in spots. The fries will look softer under the chili, with crisper pieces at the edges.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look melted, and the chili should look bubbling in spots. The fries will look softer under the chili, with crisper pieces at the edges.

Reheat leftover chili and leftover fries to 165 degrees F. Use mitts. The plate, chili, and cheese are extremely hot. Let the dish sit 1 or 2 minutes before you eat. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.
Vegetarian chili works the same way. This does not keep well once assembled, so top only what you will eat.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Chips and Salsa

2 as a snack
About 5 minutes with store-bought salsa, or 15 minutes if you make the Salsa in the Misc chapter

Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
4 cups tortilla chips
1 cup salsa, store-bought or homemade

Chips should feel crisp and dry, not stale and leathery. Salsa should feel scoopable, with a fresh, tomato-and-onion or tomato-and-chili smell, not a fermented or off smell. If a jarred salsa fizzes in an unexpected way or the jar lid was bulging, throw it out.

If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Pour the salsa into a small bowl.
Set the chips in a basket or on a plate beside it.
Serve at once.
If you are using leftover homemade salsa, keep it cold until serving, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The chips should feel crisp and should smell like toasted corn, not stale oil. The salsa should smell fresh and tomatoey or chili-bright, not fermented or musty.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The salsa should look moist and scoopable, not dried at the edges, and the chips should look whole and crisp.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The salsa should look moist and scoopable, not dried at the edges, and the chips should look whole and crisp.

Check the salsa date and the jar. Refrigerate opened salsa. If you make homemade salsa with raw onion and tomato, treat it as a perishable dip and keep it cold. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Queso or Guacamole from the Misc chapter can join the salsa, or replace it. See also Queso and Chips in this chapter.

blocks.text: Pretzels dipped in melted chocolate and left to set. This is a no-bake sweet snack. Melt the chocolate gently so it stays smooth and does not scorch or seize, which means it turns stiff and grainy.
About 20 pretzel pieces
About 20 minutes, plus setting time
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
4 ounces chocolate chips or chopped chocolate
20 pretzel twists or rods, more or less, depending on how heavily you dip
Optional: a pinch of coarse salt, or sprinkles, for the top

Melted chocolate should feel smooth and fluid, like a thin sauce, not thick and pasty, and not burnt and dry. After setting, the coating should feel firm and slightly snap, not wet and not tacky if the room is reasonably cool.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Line a pan with parchment.
Melt the chocolate in a microwave-safe bowl in 20 to 30 second bursts, stirring after each burst, until it is almost melted, then stir until smooth.
Or set the bowl over a pot of barely simmering water, without letting the bowl touch the water, and stir until smooth. Simmering means small, gentle bubbles.
Dip each pretzel partway into the chocolate.
Let the extra drip off.
Set the pretzel on the parchment.
Add a pinch of salt or sprinkles before the chocolate sets, if you like. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Let the pretzels sit until the chocolate is firm, about 20 to 40 minutes at a cool room temperature, or 10 minutes in the refrigerator.
Store in a closed container, in a cool place, for up to a week.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The melted chocolate should feel smooth and smell like chocolate, not scorched. After setting, the coating should feel firm. The pretzels should feel crisp, not stale.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The chocolate should look smooth and even, not dull and streaky from seizing. The pretzels should look half-coated and set.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The chocolate should look smooth and even, not dull and streaky from seizing. The pretzels should look half-coated and set.

Chocolate and any bowl set over steam will be hot. Wipe moisture out of the bowl and off utensils, because a little water can make chocolate seize. If you use the microwave, use short bursts and stir, because chocolate can burn even when it does not look different at first. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
White chocolate can be used the same way, still melted gently. If the chocolate is too thick for dipping, stir in 1 teaspoon of neutral oil.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cottage cheese should smell fresh and clean, not sour in a sharp, off way, and not yeasty. If it smells or looks wrong, throw it out. Fruit should smell fresh, not fermented.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Split English muffins topped with sauce and cheese, then baked or toasted until the cheese melts and the edges are crisp. This is a late-night pizza when you do not want to make a full sheet-pan pizza. See also Leftover Pizza Reheat in this chapter, and Sheet-Pan Pizza in the Supper chapter.

About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 English muffins, split
1/2 cup (half a cup) pizza sauce or marinara
1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese
Optional toppings: sliced olives, cooked peppers, or already-cooked meat
The muffin cut-sides should feel slightly dry and toasted before you add a lot of sauce, or they can get soggy. The cheese should feel fully melted, and the muffin edges should feel crisp.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Heat the oven to 400 degrees F, or use a toaster oven.
Split the muffins and set them cut-side up on a pan.

Add a thin layer of sauce, then cheese, then any optional toppings.

entries.title: Frozen Burrito Reheat

blocks.text: A method for heating a store-bought frozen burrito until the center is hot, 165 degrees F. Follow the package when it gives a time, then confirm with a thermometer or a careful check of the center. Frozen burritos can be cold in the middle when the tortilla is already hot.
1 burrito
About 5 to 20 minutes, depending on the package and method
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A microwave-safe mug or dish
A microwave-safe cover or plate, vented
A dry mitt or thick cloth for the hot dish
1 frozen burrito

The package will tell you whether to use a microwave, oven, or both. After heating, the center filling should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F, not icy or only lukewarm. Let the burrito sit 1 or 2 minutes so the heat evens out.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Read the package for the recommended method and time, and for whether to wrap the burrito in a paper towel or foil. Do not put foil in the microwave.
For a microwave: set the burrito on a microwave-safe plate, wrap it in a paper towel if the package says to, and heat for the package time, usually 1 1/2 to 3 minutes, turning halfway if you can.
For an oven: heat the oven to the package temperature, often 350 or 375 degrees F, and bake for the package time, often 15 to 25 minutes, turning once if directed.
Check the center with a thermometer. It should read 165 degrees F.
If it does not, add short bursts of heat, 20 seconds in the microwave or 5 minutes in the oven, and check again.
Let the burrito sit 1 or 2 minutes, then unwrap carefully and eat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The center should be 165 degrees F and feel steaming hot, not icy. You should smell the filling, such as beans, cheese, or meat, not burning tortilla. Let it sit 1 or 2 minutes, because the filling holds heat.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The tortilla should look hot and slightly steamy, not scorched. A little filling may bubble at the ends. That can be a sign the center is getting hot, but the thermometer is still the test.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The tortilla should look hot and slightly steamy, not scorched. A little filling may bubble at the ends. That can be a sign the center is getting hot, but the thermometer is still the test.

Reheat to 165 degrees F. Use mitts. Steam will escape when you unwrap, so keep your face back. Never put foil in the microwave. The filling can be hotter than the tortilla. Do not eat from a burrito that is still cold in the center. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.

A microwave can leave a soft tortilla. An oven gives a firmer wrap but takes longer. A combination, microwave first, then a few minutes in a skillet or oven, is a good middle path if the package allows it.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Bread topped with butter, garlic, and cheese, then toasted until the cheese melts and the edges are crisp. This is a smaller, cheesier cousin of the Garlic Bread in the Misc chapter, meant as a late-night snack.
2 to 4 slices
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
4 slices bread, or a split roll
2 tablespoons butter, softened
1 garlic clove, minced, or 1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) garlic powder
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) shredded mozzarella or a mix of mozzarella and cheddar
A pinch of salt
Softened butter should spread without tearing the bread. Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces. The finished toast should feel crisp at the edges, and the cheese should feel fully melted.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven or toaster oven to 400 degrees F, or use a skillet over medium-low heat.
Mix the butter, garlic, and a pinch of salt. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Spread it on the bread.
Set the bread on a pan.
Sprinkle the cheese on top.
Bake 6 to 10 minutes, until the cheese is fully melted and bubbling, and the edges feel crisp.
If you use a skillet, start butter-side down for a minute, then turn, add cheese, and cover until the cheese melts.
Cool 1 minute, then serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, and the edges of the bread should look golden, not burnt.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, and the edges of the bread should look golden, not burnt.

Use mitts. The pan and melted cheese are very hot. If you use a broiler, do not walk away. Mince garlic on a stable board. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A pinch of red pepper flakes or dried oregano is a good extra. This is best eaten at once.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. A toasted cheese sandwich cooked in a skillet until the bread is crisp and the cheese is melted. Low to medium heat gives the cheese time to melt before the bread burns. This is a classic late-night meal, and it also works for lunch.
1 sandwich
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
2 slices sandwich bread
1 to 2 teaspoons butter or oil, for the bread or the pan
2 slices cheese, or 1/2 cup (half a cup) shredded cheese, such as cheddar or American

Soft butter spreads more evenly than cold butter and is less likely to tear the bread. The finished sandwich should feel crisp on the outside and fully melted and stretchy inside, not cool and still sliced in the middle.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Spread a thin layer of butter on the outside of each slice of bread, or heat a little butter or oil in a skillet over medium-low to medium heat.
Place one slice of bread in the skillet, buttered side down if you buttered the bread.
Add the cheese, then the second slice, buttered side up.
Cook 3 to 5 minutes, until the bottom feels crisp and golden, not soft and pale, and not burnt. You should hear a gentle sizzle, not a harsh scorch.
Turn the sandwich with a spatula.
Cook 3 to 5 minutes more, until the second side feels crisp and the cheese feels fully melted.
If the bread is brown before the cheese melts, lower the heat and cover the pan for a minute.
Move the sandwich to a plate.
Cool 1 minute, then cut if you like, and serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The bread should feel crisp. The cheese should feel fully melted and stretchy. You should smell toasted bread and melted cheese, not burning butter. The sizzle should stay gentle.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: Both sides should look even golden brown, not pale and not dark brown or black. When you cut or pull the sandwich, the cheese should look melted and stretchy, not still in a solid slice.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. Both sides should look even golden brown, not pale and not dark brown or black. When you cut or pull the sandwich, the cheese should look melted and stretchy, not still in a solid slice.

The pan is hot. Use a spatula, not your fingers, to turn the sandwich. Melted cheese can burn your mouth, so wait 1 minute. If you use a gas flame, keep the bread and paper towels away from the burner. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A lid helps the cheese melt. Tomato soup from the Lunch chapter is a classic partner. Add a slice of tomato or a little leftover ham, and heat until the center is hot, 165 degrees F if the filling was leftover.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A simple stovetop cocoa made with milk, cocoa powder, and sugar. Heat the milk gently so it does not scorch or boil over. This is also listed here because it is a late-night drink as often as it is a winter afternoon one.
2 mugs
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 cups milk
2 tablespoons unsweetened cocoa powder
2 tablespoons sugar, or to taste
A pinch of salt
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) vanilla extract, optional
Optional toppings: whipped cream or marshmallows

The cocoa should feel smooth, not dusty and not gritty with dry cocoa lumps. The drink should feel steaming hot, but not so hot that it burns your mouth, and it should coat the mug lightly, like thin chocolate milk that is a little richer.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Whisk the cocoa, sugar, and salt with 2 tablespoons of the milk in a small pot until the mix feels smooth, like a paste. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk so there are no lumps.
Add the remaining milk.
Stir until combined.
Heat over medium-low heat, stirring often, until the cocoa is steaming hot and you see small bubbles at the edge, not a rolling boil.
Take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the optional vanilla.
Pour into mugs.
Add toppings if you like.
Let it sit 1 minute, then drink.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cocoa should feel smooth and steaming hot, not gritty. You should smell chocolate and milk, not scorched milk. If you smell scorching, take the pot off the heat at once and do not scrape the bottom into the mugs.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cocoa should look smooth and even, not dusty with floating dry cocoa, and not covered in a thick skin if you serve it at once. You may see a little steam.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cocoa should look smooth and even, not dusty with floating dry cocoa, and not covered in a thick skin if you serve it at once. You may see a little steam.

Stir often so the milk does not scorch. The pot, steam, and mugs will be very hot. Pour slowly. Let the drink sit 1 minute so you do not burn your mouth. Refrigerate leftover cocoa within 2 hours, and reheat until steaming hot, stirring, without boiling it hard. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.
A little cinnamon or a square of chopped chocolate, stirred in at the end, makes a richer mug. See also the drinks in the Misc chapter for lemonade, iced tea, and cider.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.
