entries.title: Hummus and Pita

blocks.text: Store-bought or homemade hummus with warm pita or crackers and optional raw vegetables. For homemade hummus, see the Misc chapter. Warming the pita makes it more flexible and less likely to crack.
2 as a snack
About 10 minutes, or 5 minutes if the pita is already soft
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 cup hummus, store-bought or homemade
2 pita breads, or a handful of crackers or cut vegetables, such as carrots or cucumber
Optional: a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of paprika, for the top of the hummus
Hummus should feel smooth and thick, like a dip that holds a soft peak on a spoon, not watery and not pasty-dry. Pita should feel warm and flexible after heating, not brittle and not wet.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. Spoon the hummus into a small bowl.
Add optional oil and paprika on top.
Warm the pita in a dry skillet 30 to 60 seconds per side, or in a 350 degree F oven for 3 to 5 minutes, until it feels warm and flexible.
Crackers or raw vegetables can be used as they are.
Cut the pita into wedges if you like, on a stable board.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The hummus should look smooth, and the pita should look soft and slightly puffed, not scorched.

If you warm pita in the oven, use mitts. Keep opened hummus refrigerated, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours. If homemade or opened hummus smells sour or looks moldy, throw it out. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
This is a quieter snack than nachos and can be a lighter late-night plate. See also the Hummus Veggie Wrap in the Lunch chapter if you want a fuller meal.

Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Scoops of ice cream with simple toppings, assembled just before you eat so the ice cream does not melt. Keep the ice cream in the freezer until the toppings are ready.
1 sundae
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
2 scoops ice cream, about 1 cup
2 tablespoons chocolate sauce, caramel sauce, or fruit sauce
Optional toppings: whipped cream, sliced banana, cherries, or sprinkles
Optional crunch: 1 tablespoon chopped nuts, only if no one has a nut allergy, or crushed cookies

Ice cream that is too hard to scoop can sit on the counter 2 or 3 minutes, not longer. A warmed scoop or spoon, dipped in warm water and dried, helps. The sundae should be eaten while the ice cream still feels firm, not soupy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Set out a cold bowl and your toppings.
Scoop the ice cream into the bowl.
Spoon the sauce over the ice cream.
Add any optional toppings.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The ice cream should feel firm and very cold, and it should smell clean and creamy, not freezer-burned or off. Sauce should feel pourable. Nuts, if used, should smell fresh, not rancid.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The scoops should look rounded and still firm, with sauce on top, not already melted into a puddle.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The scoops should look rounded and still firm, with sauce on top, not already melted into a puddle.

A scoop can slip. Work over the bowl or the carton. Do not serve nuts to anyone with a nut allergy. Ice cream is perishable. Do not leave the carton out. Return it to the freezer at once. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A pinch of salt on caramel sauce makes it taste rounder. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). See also Milkshake and Root Beer Float in this chapter if you want a drinking version.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Cold leftover rice fried in a skillet with an egg, a few vegetables, and a splash of soy sauce, until everything is hot, 165 degrees F. Day-old rice works better than fresh rice, because it is drier and less likely to turn mushy. Cook the egg until it is firm, 160 degrees F if it is scrambled into the rice.
1 or 2 as a late meal
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
2 cups cold leftover cooked rice, refrigerated
1 tablespoon oil
1 large egg, beaten
1/2 cup (half a cup) frozen peas and carrots, or chopped leftover vegetables
1 or 2 green onions, sliced, optional
1 to 2 tablespoons soy sauce
Leftover cooked chicken, shrimp, or tofu, optional, already cooked

Cold rice should feel separate and a little firm, not one wet clump. Break up clumps with wet fingers or a spoon before they hit the pan. The finished rice should feel hot all the way through, 165 degrees F, and the egg should feel firm, not liquid.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Add the beaten egg.
Cook, stirring, until it is firm and in small pieces, then move it to a plate, or push it to the side of the pan.
Add the vegetables and cook 2 to 3 minutes, until they feel hot and any frozen vegetables are no longer icy.
Add the rice.
Stir and press to break up clumps, 3 to 5 minutes, until the rice feels hot, 165 degrees F, and you hear a sizzle.
Add the soy sauce, the egg, optional leftover cooked protein, and optional green onion.
Stir until everything is 165 degrees F and the egg is firm.
Taste a cooled bite, and add soy sauce if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The rice should feel hot all the way through, 165 degrees F. The egg should feel firm. You should hear a sizzle, and you should smell toasted rice and soy, not burning, and not a sour leftover smell. If leftover rice smells sour or off, throw it out and do not cook it.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The rice should look separated and slightly toasted in spots, not wet and clumped. The egg should look cooked and yellow, not raw and glossy. Vegetables should look hot and bright.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The rice should look separated and slightly toasted in spots, not wet and clumped. The egg should look cooked and yellow, not raw and glossy. Vegetables should look hot and bright.

Leftover rice should have been refrigerated within 2 hours of cooking. Reheat to 165 degrees F. Cook the egg until firm. Wash the board and your hands after handling the raw egg. The pan is very hot and can spatter. Do not leave cooked rice out on the counter overnight and then fry it. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.

This is one of the best uses for leftover takeout rice. A little sesame oil at the end is a good finish. If you do not have leftover rice, see Rice in the Misc chapter, cook it, cool it quickly in a shallow container in the refrigerator, then use it later.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A method for reheating leftover pizza so the crust firms up and the toppings reach a safe temperature. Leftovers should be reheated to 165 degrees F. A skillet or an oven works better than a microwave if you want a less soggy crust, though the microwave is fine when speed matters more than texture.
1 or more slices
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
Leftover pizza slices, kept refrigerated
A few drops of water, only if you use a covered skillet and the crust is very dry

Refrigerated pizza feels firm and the cheese is set. After reheating, the cheese should feel melted again, the crust should feel hot, and the toppings should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F in the thickest topping, especially if the pizza has meat.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Take the pizza out of the refrigerator and remove any wrapping.
For a skillet: set a skillet over medium-low heat.
Add the slice.
Cover the pan.
Heat 4 to 8 minutes, until the bottom feels crisp and the toppings are 165 degrees F.
For an oven or toaster oven: heat it to 375 degrees F.
Set the slice on a pan.
Heat 8 to 12 minutes, until the toppings are 165 degrees F and the crust feels hot and firmer.
For a microwave: set the slice on a microwave-safe plate.
Heat 30 to 60 seconds, then in short bursts, until the toppings are 165 degrees F. The crust will stay softer this way.
Let the slice sit 1 minute, then serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The toppings should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F. You should smell warmed tomato, cheese, and crust, not burning. The crust should feel hot all the way through, not icy or cold in the center of a thick slice.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look melted again, and the toppings should look hot, with a little steam. The crust should look slightly crisp in a skillet or oven, or softer in a microwave. It should not look scorched.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look melted again, and the toppings should look hot, with a little steam. The crust should look slightly crisp in a skillet or oven, or softer in a microwave. It should not look scorched.

Leftover pizza should have been refrigerated within 2 hours of the original meal. Reheat to 165 degrees F. Use mitts. Cheese and sauce can be hotter than the crust. Do not leave reheated pizza out for another long stretch. Eat it or return leftovers to the refrigerator. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.

A dry skillet is usually enough. A drop of water under the lid makes a little steam, which helps the cheese melt, but too much water softens the crust. This method is also linked from the Sheet-Pan Pizza recipe in the Supper chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A russet or similar potato cooked in the microwave until the center is soft, then topped like a baked potato. You must pierce the skin before cooking, or steam can build up and the potato can burst. For oven-baked potatoes, see Baked Potatoes in the Misc chapter.
1 potato
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A microwave-safe mug or dish
A microwave-safe cover or plate, vented
A dry mitt or thick cloth for the hot dish
1 medium russet potato, or another baking potato, scrubbed
1 teaspoon oil or butter, plus more for serving
A pinch of salt
Optional toppings: shredded cheese, sour cream, cooked bacon crumbles, or sliced green onion

The potato should feel firm and heavy for its size, with no soft or wet spots. After cooking, it should yield easily when you squeeze it gently with a mitt on your hand, and a fork should slide into the center with almost no resistance. The potato will be hotter inside than the skin suggests.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Scrub the potato and dry it.
Pierce the skin 5 or 6 times with a fork, all around, so steam can escape.
Rub the potato with a little oil or butter and a pinch of salt if you like. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Set it on a microwave-safe plate.
Microwave 4 minutes.
Turn the potato.
Microwave 3 to 5 minutes more, until a fork slides into the center easily and the potato feels soft when squeezed with a mitt.
If the center is still firm, add 1 minute at a time.
Let the potato sit 2 minutes.
Cut it open carefully.
Add butter, salt, and any toppings.
If you add leftover meat or fully cooked bacon that was chilled, the toppings should be heated until 165 degrees F, or added very hot.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A fork should slide into the center easily. The potato should feel soft when squeezed with a mitt. You should smell cooked potato, not burning. The plate and potato will be very hot. Let it sit 2 minutes so the center finishes cooking.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The skin should look slightly slack, not tight and raw, and not scorched. The inside should look fluffy and dry, not wet and hard in the center.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The skin should look slightly slack, not tight and raw, and not scorched. The inside should look fluffy and dry, not wet and hard in the center.

Pierce the skin before cooking. Use a microwave-safe plate, never metal. Use a mitt to turn and to squeeze-test the potato. Steam escapes when you cut it open, so cut slowly and keep your face back. The inside is extremely hot. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A large potato can take 10 minutes or more. Two potatoes will take longer than one. For a crispier skin, finish the microwaved potato in a 425 degree F oven for 10 minutes if you want to take that extra step.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A single-plate nacho snack made in the microwave. This is faster than oven nachos and is meant for a small serving. Microwave power varies, so start with a short time and add more in 20-second bursts.
1 or 2 as a snack
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A microwave-safe mug or dish
A microwave-safe cover or plate, vented
A dry mitt or thick cloth for the hot dish
2 large handfuls of tortilla chips, enough to cover a microwave-safe plate in a single loose layer
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) shredded cheese
Optional: drained salsa, sliced jalapenos, or leftover cooked beans
Use a microwave-safe plate, not metal. The cheese should feel fully melted, not still shredded in the center, and the plate will be hotter than you expect.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Spread the chips on a microwave-safe plate in a loose, even layer.
Sprinkle the cheese evenly over the chips.
Add any optional microwave-safe toppings.
Microwave 45 to 90 seconds, starting with 45 seconds, until the cheese is fully melted.
If the center is not melted, add 20 seconds at a time.
Stop as soon as the cheese is melted, or the chips can harden and scorch.
Let the plate sit 1 minute.
Add cold salsa or sour cream if you like, and serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cheese should feel fully melted and stretchy. The plate will feel very hot. You should smell melted cheese and corn, not burning chips or a hot-plastic smell. If you smell scorching, stop.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look melted and slightly glossy, not still shredded, and the chips should not look browned or dry at the tips.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look melted and slightly glossy, not still shredded, and the chips should not look browned or dry at the tips.

Use a microwave-safe plate, never metal or a plate with metal paint. The plate and cheese will be very hot. Use a dry mitt or a pot holder to take the plate out. Let it sit 1 minute so the heat evens out and the cheese is less likely to burn your mouth. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
This does not reheat well, so make a small plate.

Ice cream and milk blended until thick and smooth. A blender works best. A large jar and a strong spoon can work if you let the ice cream soften slightly, but the texture will be lumpier.
1 large glass
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
2 cups ice cream
1/2 to 3/4 cup (half to three-quarters of a cup) cold milk
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) vanilla extract, optional, especially with vanilla ice cream
Optional: 2 tablespoons chocolate sauce, or a banana, or a spoon of peanut butter if no one has a peanut allergy
Start with less milk. The shake should feel thick enough to drink through a straw with a little resistance, not thin like milk, and not so stiff that it will not pour.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Add the ice cream, 1/2 cup (half a cup) of the milk, and any optional flavorings to a blender.
Blend until the mix feels smooth, starting on a low speed so the blender does not splash.
If it is too thick to pour, add a little more milk and blend again.
Pour into a glass and serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The shake should feel thick, cold, and smooth. You should hear the blender change from a choppy sound to a smoother one as lumps disappear. You should smell ice cream and any mix-ins, not a burnt-motor smell from a blender that is stuck. If the blender stalls, stop and add a little milk, or stir, then start again.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The shake should look smooth and thick, with no large ice cream lumps, and it should mound slightly as it pours, not run like milk.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The shake should look smooth and thick, with no large ice cream lumps, and it should mound slightly as it pours, not run like milk.

Seat the blender lid firmly. Start on low. Never put a spoon in a running blender. Do not serve peanut butter shakes to anyone with a peanut allergy. Wash the blender soon, because dried shake is hard to clean. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
For a chocolate shake, use chocolate ice cream or chocolate sauce. For a malted shake, add 1 tablespoon malted milk powder if you have it.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Mozzarella Sticks

blocks.text: Frozen mozzarella sticks baked or air-fried until the coating is crisp and the cheese is hot and melted, but not all leaked out. Follow the package time, then use the cues here. These are messy and very hot in the center at first.
2 to 4 as a snack, about 8 to 12 sticks
About 15 to 25 minutes from frozen
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
8 to 12 frozen mozzarella sticks
Marinara sauce, warmed, for dipping, optional

Do not thaw the sticks first, or the cheese can leak before the coating crisps. The coating should feel crisp, and the cheese should feel melted and stretchy inside. If cheese is flowing out of every stick, they may have gone a little long, but they can still be eaten if the coating is not burnt.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to the package temperature, often 400 or 425 degrees F, or heat an air fryer to the package temperature, often 360 to 400 degrees F.
Arrange the frozen sticks in a single layer on a pan or in the air-fryer basket, with a little space between them.
Bake or air-fry for the package time, often 6 to 12 minutes, turning once if directed.
Check a stick: the coating should feel crisp, and the cheese should be melted.
If the cheese is still firm, add 1 or 2 minutes.
Cool 2 to 3 minutes.
Serve with warm marinara if you like.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The coating should feel crisp and should smell toasted, not burning. The cheese should feel melted and very hot. Let the sticks sit 2 to 3 minutes, because the cheese can burn your mouth.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The coating should look golden, not pale and not dark brown. A little cheese may leak at the ends. The inside of a test stick should look melted and stretchy, not still solid and cold.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The coating should look golden, not pale and not dark brown. A little cheese may leak at the ends. The inside of a test stick should look melted and stretchy, not still solid and cold.

Use mitts. The pan, basket, and cheese are extremely hot. Do not eat one the second they come out. Follow the package, and do not overcrowd, or the coating can stay soggy. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, though they are best the first time. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.

blocks.text: A small, fudgy brownie cooked in a microwave-safe mug. It should stay slightly soft in the center. Start with a short time, because a brownie can go from fudgy to dry very quickly.
1 mug
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A microwave-safe mug or dish
A microwave-safe cover or plate, vented
A dry mitt or thick cloth for the hot dish
3 tablespoons all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
2 tablespoons unsweetened cocoa powder
A pinch of salt
2 tablespoons oil or melted butter
3 tablespoons milk
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) vanilla extract
Optional: 1 tablespoon chocolate chips

The batter should feel thick and smooth, with no dry cocoa in the corners of the mug. The cooked brownie should feel set at the edges and slightly soft and fudgy in the center, not wet with raw batter, and not dry all the way through.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the flour, sugar, cocoa, and salt in a microwave-safe mug at least 12 ounces in size.
Add the oil or butter, milk, and vanilla.
Stir until the mix feels even, including in the corners.
Stir in the optional chips.
Microwave 45 to 75 seconds, starting with 45 seconds, until the edges feel set and the center feels slightly soft, not wet with raw batter.
If the center is still wet batter, add 10 seconds at a time.
Let the mug sit 1 minute, then eat with a spoon.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The edges should feel set. The center should feel slightly soft and fudgy, not wet with raw batter. You should smell chocolate, not raw flour or burning. The mug will be very hot.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The brownie should look set at the edges and slightly glossy and soft in the center, not wet and not dry and cracked all over.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The brownie should look set at the edges and slightly glossy and soft in the center, not wet and not dry and cracked all over.

Use a microwave-safe mug, never metal. Do not taste raw batter. Use a pot holder to take the mug out. Let it sit 1 minute. Melted chocolate is very hot. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.
A small scoop of ice cream on top is a good late-night finish, added after the mug has cooled 1 minute. Eat this at once.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A small vanilla cake mixed and cooked in a microwave-safe mug. Microwave cakes cook very fast and can go from done to dry in under a minute, so start with the shorter time. Do not taste the raw batter, because it contains flour and may contain egg.
1 mug
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A microwave-safe mug or dish
A microwave-safe cover or plate, vented
A dry mitt or thick cloth for the hot dish
4 tablespoons all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) baking powder
A pinch of salt
3 tablespoons milk
2 tablespoons oil or melted butter
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) vanilla extract
Optional: 1 tablespoon chocolate chips or a few berries

Use a microwave-safe mug that is at least 12 ounces, so the batter has room to rise. The batter should feel smooth and pourable, like a thin pancake batter. The cooked cake should feel set and springy on top, not wet in the center, and not dry and rubbery.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt in the mug until even.
Add the milk, oil or butter, and vanilla.
Stir until you no longer feel dry flour, including in the corners of the mug.
Stir in the optional chips or berries.
Microwave 60 to 90 seconds, starting with 60 seconds, until the top feels set and springy, and the center is not wet batter.
If the center is still wet, add 10 to 15 seconds at a time.
Stop as soon as it is set.
Let the mug sit 1 minute. The cake will finish cooking and the mug will be very hot.
Eat from the mug, or loosen the cake with a spoon and turn it out.

The cake should look risen and set on top, not wet and shiny in the center, and it should not spill over the rim if the mug was large enough. A few moist crumbs on a toothpick are all right.

entries.title: Nachos

blocks.text: Tortilla chips topped with melted cheese and simple toppings, baked just until the cheese melts. This is a shareable late-night plate. If you add leftover meat, reheat the finished nachos until the toppings are 165 degrees F.
4 as a snack, or 2 as a late meal
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
8 ounces tortilla chips, about half of a large bag
2 cups shredded cheddar or Mexican-blend cheese
Optional toppings: sliced jalapenos, drained canned black beans, leftover cooked meat, or diced tomato
Optional finishes: sour cream, salsa, or guacamole, added after baking

Use sturdy chips so they do not collapse under the cheese. The cheese should feel fully melted and stretchy, not just warm and still shredded. If you add leftover meat or beans, the center of a topped chip should feel steaming hot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Line a sheet pan with parchment, or use a broiler-safe platter.
Spread the chips in a loose, even layer.
Avoid a deep pile, or the bottom chips will stay cold and the top will overbrown.
Sprinkle the cheese evenly, including some in the middle, not only on the corners.
Add any oven-safe toppings, such as jalapenos, beans, or leftover cooked meat.
Bake 8 to 12 minutes, until the cheese is fully melted and bubbling, and any leftover meat is 165 degrees F.
Add cold finishes such as sour cream or salsa after you take the pan out.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cheese should feel fully melted and stretchy. You should smell toasted corn and melted cheese, not burning chips. Any leftover meat or beans should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cheese should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, not still shredded and not burnt. The chips at the edges may look slightly darker. That is all right if they are not black.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cheese should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, not still shredded and not burnt. The chips at the edges may look slightly darker. That is all right if they are not black.

Use mitts. The pan and cheese are very hot. Melted cheese can burn your mouth, so let the plate sit 1 or 2 minutes. Reheat leftover meat to 165 degrees F. If you use pickled jalapenos, drain them so the chips do not get soggy. Drain means pour off the liquid. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
For a smaller snack, use a microwave-safe plate and see Microwave Nachos in this chapter. Leftover nachos get soggy, so make only what you will eat.

entries.title: Oven Fries

blocks.text: Potato sticks tossed with oil and baked until they are crisp at the edges and tender inside. This is a late-night fry when you do not want a pot of hot oil. Cut the sticks as even as you can so they finish together. See also French Fries in the Misc chapter for a slightly more formal side-dish version.
2 to 3 as a snack, or 4 as a side
About 40 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 medium russet potatoes, scrubbed
1 1/2 tablespoons (one and a half tablespoons) oil
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
Optional: 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) paprika or garlic powder

Even sticks, about 1/4 to 1/3 inch (a quarter to a third of an inch) thick, cook more evenly. After baking, the edges should feel crisp, and the centers should feel tender, with no hard, raw core. A fry should bend a little, then break, not feel leathery or soggy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Line a sheet pan with parchment, or oil the pan.
Cut the potatoes into even sticks on a stable board, using a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the potato if you need it.
Toss the sticks with the oil, salt, and any optional seasoning, until they feel lightly coated.
Spread them in a single layer with space between them.
Crowding makes them steam and stay soft.
Bake 15 minutes.
Turn the sticks.
Bake 10 to 20 minutes more, until the edges feel crisp and the centers feel tender.
Taste one after a brief cool, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The edges should feel crisp. The centers should feel tender. You should smell toasted potato, not burning oil or raw potato. A test fry should have no hard, raw core.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The fries should look golden with browned edges, not pale and not burnt. They should look dry-crisp on the outside, not wet and limp.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The fries should look golden with browned edges, not pale and not burnt. They should look dry-crisp on the outside, not wet and limp.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Use mitts. The pan is very hot. Let a test fry cool a few seconds, because the inside holds heat. Do not deep-fry in this recipe. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

Soaking the cut potatoes in cold water 15 minutes, then drying them very well, can make them a little crispier. Ketchup, Ranch Dip, or the cheese sauce in the Misc chapter can go on the side. See also Chili Cheese Fries in this chapter.

blocks.text: The familiar peanut butter and jelly sandwich, written out so you can make it by feel. If you cook for someone with a peanut or nut allergy, skip this recipe entirely and see the cheese or hummus snacks in this chapter instead.
1 sandwich
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
2 slices sandwich bread
2 tablespoons peanut butter
1 to 2 tablespoons jelly or jam

Soft bread can tear if the peanut butter is very thick and cold. Let a stiff jar sit at room temperature a few minutes, or stir it. The finished sandwich should feel evenly filled, not dry in a corner and not dripping.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Lay the two slices of bread on a clean plate or board.
Spread the peanut butter evenly on one slice, all the way toward the edges.
Spread the jelly on the other slice.
If you put both on the same slice, the jelly can slide.
Press the slices together, filling sides in.
Cut the sandwich if you like, using a gentle sawing motion so the filling does not squeeze out.
Serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The sandwich should feel evenly filled. You should smell peanut butter and fruit. The bread should feel intact, not torn into holes.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The filling should look even when you cut the sandwich, with no large dry corners and no big drip of jelly.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The filling should look even when you cut the sandwich, with no large dry corners and no big drip of jelly.

Do not serve this to anyone with a peanut or nut allergy, and keep it away from other food if you are cooking for someone who cannot eat peanuts. Use a clean knife. If you rinse the knife between spreads, dry it so the bread does not get wet. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

Crunchy or creamy peanut butter both work. A ripe banana, sliced, can go on top of the peanut butter for a more filling snack. For a toasted version, toast the bread first, then add the spreads, because a filled sandwich is messy in a toaster.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A warm cheese dip, often called queso, served with tortilla chips. This stovetop version uses shredded cheese and a little milk or canned tomatoes with green chiles so the dip stays smooth. Keep it warm, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours.
4 as a snack
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 cups shredded melting cheese, such as cheddar or a Mexican blend
1/2 cup (half a cup) milk, plus more if the dip is too thick
1 can (10 ounces) diced tomatoes with green chiles, drained a little, or 1/2 cup (half a cup) salsa
A pinch of salt, if the cheese is not salty
Tortilla chips, for serving

Shredded cheese melts more evenly than cubes. The dip should feel smooth and pourable, thick enough to coat a chip, not oily and split, and not a solid clump. If it feels grainy, lower the heat and add a splash of milk, and stir.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Set a small pot over low to medium-low heat.
Add the milk and the tomatoes or salsa.
When the mix is hot and steaming, add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring until it melts before you add more.
If the dip is too thick, add milk 1 tablespoon at a time.
If it is too thin, let it cook, stirring, another minute or two.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add a pinch of salt if it needs it. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve at once with chips, or keep the pot on the lowest heat, stirring now and then.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The dip should feel smooth and hot, and it should coat a chip. You should smell melted cheese and chiles, not scorched milk. If you smell scorching, take the pot off the heat and stir, then use a lower burner.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The queso should look smooth and evenly orange or red-orange, not oily with a puddle of separated fat, and not lumpy with unmelted cheese.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The queso should look smooth and evenly orange or red-orange, not oily with a puddle of separated fat, and not lumpy with unmelted cheese.

Use low heat. Cheese sauces scorch and split on high heat. The pot and dip are very hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F, or until the dip is bubbling again, stirring often. Add a splash of milk when you reheat. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.
A pinch of cumin or chili powder is a good extra. See also Queso in the Misc chapter if you want a party-size dip, and Chips and Salsa in this chapter for a cold partner.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Instant ramen cooked in a small pot, then improved with an egg, frozen vegetables, or leftover cooked meat. The noodles are done when they feel tender but still slightly firm, not mushy. If you add an egg, cook it until the white and yolk are firm, remembering that egg dishes should reach 160 degrees F if they are stirred in.
1 bowl
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 package instant ramen noodles, with or without the seasoning packet
2 cups water, or as the package directs
Optional: 1 large egg
Optional: 1/2 cup (half a cup) frozen peas or mixed vegetables
Optional: leftover cooked chicken or tofu, for stirring in at the end
Optional extras: a splash of soy sauce, a little sesame oil, or sliced green onion

The noodles should feel tender but still slightly springy, not hard in the center and not falling apart. Frozen vegetables should feel hot all the way through. Leftover meat should feel steaming hot. An egg added to the pot should feel set, not liquid and raw.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Bring the water to a boil in a small pot, meaning large, rolling bubbles.
Add the noodles and the optional frozen vegetables.
Cook 2 to 3 minutes, or as the package directs, stirring so the noodles separate.

Reduce the heat to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Stir in the seasoning packet, or use soy sauce instead if you want less of the packet.
If you are adding an egg, crack it into a small cup first, then slide it into the simmering broth, or beat it and stir it in.
Cook until the egg is firm, or the white is set and the yolk is as firm as you want, at least 160 degrees F for a stirred-in egg dish.
Add leftover cooked meat or tofu, and heat until it is 165 degrees F if it was leftover.
Pour into a bowl.
Add any optional extras.
Let it sit 1 minute, then eat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The noodles should feel tender and slightly springy. The broth should be steaming hot. You should smell savory broth and noodles, not a sour or stale seasoning smell. Leftover meat should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The noodles should look separated and tender, not a tight brick. Vegetables should look bright and hot. An egg should look set, not raw and glossy if you wanted it firm.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The noodles should look separated and tender, not a tight brick. Vegetables should look bright and hot. An egg should look set, not raw and glossy if you wanted it firm.

Boiling water can burn you. Pour slowly. The bowl will be very hot. If you add leftover meat, reheat it to 165 degrees F. Cook eggs until they are firm, or to 160 degrees F for a stirred egg. Instant packets are high in sodium, so you can use only part of the packet. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A handful of spinach can wilt in the hot broth at the end. This is a good use for a leftover baked chicken breast, sliced and reheated in the soup.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A tall glass of root beer with a scoop of vanilla ice cream. The soda will foam, so pour slowly and use a glass with room at the top. This also works with cola or other sodas.
1 glass
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 scoop vanilla ice cream, about 1/2 cup (half a cup)
3/4 to 1 cup cold root beer

The glass should feel tall and stable. After you add the soda, the foam will rise quickly. Pause if it nears the rim. The ice cream should feel firm when it goes in, then slightly softened as you eat and drink.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the scoop of ice cream in a tall glass.
Pour the root beer slowly down the side of the glass, or over the back of a spoon, until the glass is comfortably full, leaving room for foam.
Pause if the foam rises too fast, then add more soda.
Add a straw or a long spoon, and serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: You should hear a strong fizz as the soda hits the ice cream. The drink should smell like root beer and vanilla, and it should feel very cold. If the foam threatens to spill, wait, then pour more slowly.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The foam should look tall and creamy, and the ice cream should still be visible as a scoop, not instantly melted.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The foam should look tall and creamy, and the ice cream should still be visible as a scoop, not instantly melted.

Pour slowly so the glass does not overflow and make the outside slippery. Use a stable glass on a clear counter. Caffeine and sugar can be a lot late at night if that matters for you. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Chocolate ice cream is a good change. A smaller scoop in a smaller glass is easier to manage.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

The campfire snack of graham crackers, chocolate, and a toasted marshmallow, made in an oven, toaster oven, or skillet instead of over an open fire. The marshmallow should be hot and soft, and the chocolate should be slightly melted. The filling will be extremely hot at first.
2 to 4 snacks
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
4 graham cracker sheets, broken into 8 squares
2 milk-chocolate bars, broken into 4 pieces, or 4 large pieces of chocolate
4 large marshmallows

A toasted marshmallow should feel puffed and very soft, with a slightly set or crisp outside if you browned it, not raw and firm, and not burnt and bitter. The chocolate should feel slightly softened once the hot marshmallow sits on it. The assembled snack should be cooled briefly before you eat, because the center can burn your mouth.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven or toaster oven to 400 degrees F, or set a skillet over medium-low heat.
Set 4 graham squares on a pan.
Add a piece of chocolate to each.
For the oven: set the marshmallows on the other 4 graham squares, or on a lined pan, and heat 3 to 6 minutes, until the marshmallows feel puffed and soft, and the chocolate is slightly melted.
Watch closely, because marshmallows can go from toasted to burnt quickly.
For a skillet: set the marshmallows in a dry skillet and turn them often, 2 to 4 minutes, until they feel puffed and soft and you smell toasted sugar, not burning.
Press a hot marshmallow onto each chocolate-topped cracker, then cap with the remaining graham squares.
Cool 1 minute, then eat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The marshmallows should feel puffed and very soft, and they should smell like toasted sugar, not burning. The chocolate should feel slightly melted under the marshmallow. The filling will be extremely hot.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The marshmallows should look puffed and lightly golden, not white and raw, and not black. The chocolate should look slightly softened. The crackers should still look intact, not scorched.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The marshmallows should look puffed and lightly golden, not white and raw, and not black. The chocolate should look slightly softened. The crackers should still look intact, not scorched.

Use mitts. Melted sugar and marshmallow can cause a serious burn. Cool 1 minute before you eat. If you use a broiler, do not walk away, and keep the pan a safe distance from the element. Do not toast marshmallows on a bare stovetop gas flame in this recipe. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A peanut butter smear on the cracker is a good extra if no one has a peanut allergy. These are best eaten at once.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Soft Pretzels with Mustard

blocks.text: Soft pretzels baked from store-bought dough, or reheated ready-made pretzels, served with mustard. A baking-soda bath, meaning a brief dip in hot water mixed with baking soda, can give dough pretzels a deeper brown and a more pretzel-like flavor, but it is optional.
4 to 6 pretzels with store-bought dough, or as many as the package holds
About 25 minutes with store-bought dough, or 10 minutes if you are only reheating ready-made pretzels
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 pound pizza dough, or a package of frozen soft pretzels with their own directions
2 tablespoons baking soda, optional, dissolved in 4 cups hot water, for a dip before baking dough pretzels
1 egg, beaten with 1 teaspoon water, optional, for brushing
Coarse salt, for sprinkling
Mustard, for serving

Dough should feel elastic and not ice-cold. A baked or reheated pretzel should feel set and slightly chewy, hot in the center, not doughy, and not hard as a cracker unless you prefer it very baked. Ready-made pretzels should be heated until the center is hot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
If you are reheating ready-made pretzels, follow the package, often 10 minutes at 350 or 400 degrees F, until the centers feel hot and the outside feels slightly crisp.
Serve with mustard, and skip the shaping steps.
If you are using pizza dough, heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Line a pan with parchment.
Divide the dough into 4 to 6 pieces.
Roll each piece into a long rope, then shape a pretzel, or a simple twist or stick if a pretzel shape is frustrating.
If you are using the baking-soda bath, dip each pretzel briefly in the hot baking-soda water, then set it on the pan.
If you are not, brush with the optional egg wash instead.
Sprinkle with coarse salt.
Bake 12 to 16 minutes, until the pretzels feel set and are browned, and the centers feel cooked, not doughy.
Cool 5 minutes.
Serve with mustard.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The pretzels should feel set, slightly chewy, and hot in the center, not doughy. You should smell toasted dough and salt, not raw flour or burning. Mustard should smell sharp and clean.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The pretzels should look golden to medium brown, not pale and not nearly black. The insides should look cooked and slightly chewy, not raw.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The pretzels should look golden to medium brown, not pale and not nearly black. The insides should look cooked and slightly chewy, not raw.

Do not taste raw dough. Use mitts. If you use a baking-soda bath, the water is hot. Work slowly. If you use an egg wash, wash your hands after handling the raw egg, and do not eat raw egg wash. Coarse salt can roll off the pan, so work over the sink or the pan. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.
Butter brushed on after baking is a good finish. Leftover pretzels reheat at 300 degrees F until the centers are hot.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Toast with Peanut Butter and Banana

blocks.text: Toasted bread spread with peanut butter and topped with banana slices. Toast the bread first, then add the toppings, because a filled sandwich or topped bread does not belong in a toaster. If anyone has a peanut allergy, skip the peanut butter.
1 snack
About 8 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
1 or 2 slices bread
1 to 2 tablespoons peanut butter
1 banana, sliced
A pinch of cinnamon, optional
The toast should feel dry and crisp, not soft and pale, and not burnt and brittle. The banana should feel ripe, with a little give, not rock-hard and not collapsing into mush.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Toast the bread in a toaster or in a skillet until it feels crisp and you smell toasted bread, not burning.
Let the toast sit 30 seconds so you can handle it.
Spread the peanut butter evenly on the toast.
Slice the banana on a stable board, then lay the slices on the peanut butter.
Add a pinch of cinnamon if you like. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve at once, because the toast will soften.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The toast should feel crisp and should smell toasted, not burnt. The banana should smell sweet and ripe, not fermented. The peanut butter should smell fresh, not rancid.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The toast should look evenly golden, not pale and not dark brown. The banana slices should look even and not already brown and wet.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The toast should look evenly golden, not pale and not dark brown. The banana slices should look even and not already brown and wet.

Do not put peanut butter or banana in a toaster. If anyone has a peanut allergy, skip this recipe. Use a stable board for the banana. The toaster and toast can be hot. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Honey is a good drizzle if you want more sweetness. Almond butter or sunflower seed butter can replace peanut butter if they are safe for the people eating.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A dry mix of nuts, seeds, dried fruit, and an optional sweet piece such as chocolate chips. This is a no-cook snack you can portion into small containers. If anyone has a nut allergy, skip the nuts and use seeds, pretzels, and dried fruit only, or skip this recipe.
About 10 snack servings
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 cup roasted nuts, such as peanuts, almonds, or cashews, or a mix
1 cup seeds or extra nuts, such as pumpkin seeds or sunflower seeds
1 cup dried fruit, such as raisins, cranberries, or chopped dried apricots
1 cup crunchy extras, such as pretzel pieces or cereal squares
1/2 cup (half a cup) chocolate chips or chocolate candies, optional

Everything should feel dry. If the nuts smell like old oil or paint, they are rancid. Throw them out. Dried fruit should feel slightly leathery and sticky, not wet and not rock-hard unless you like it that way.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Combine all the ingredients in a large bowl.
Toss with your hands or a spoon until the mix feels even, with no one ingredient all at the bottom.
Store in a closed container at room temperature for up to 2 weeks, or portion into small bags or cups.
Serve in small handfuls. This is rich, so a little goes a long way.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The mix should smell toasted and sweet, not rancid or stale. Everything should feel dry. Chocolate, if used, should feel firm, not melted, unless the room is very warm, in which case leave it out or store the mix in a cooler place.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The mix should look even, with visible nuts, fruit, and crunchy pieces, not a pile of the heaviest items at the bottom.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The mix should look even, with visible nuts, fruit, and crunchy pieces, not a pile of the heaviest items at the bottom.

Do not serve nuts to anyone with a nut allergy, and check labels for cross-contact if that matters for your household. Choking is a risk with whole nuts, especially if you serve this to anyone who needs softer food. Keep chocolate mixes out of a hot car or a very warm room. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Salted nuts make a sweeter-salty mix. Unsalted nuts let the dried fruit stand out. Change the ratios to suit the people eating.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A simple bowl of yogurt with granola and optional fruit. This is close to the Yogurt Parfait in the Breakfast chapter, written here as a smaller late-night snack. Add the granola just before you eat so it stays crisp.
1 bowl
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 cup plain or vanilla yogurt
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) granola, from the Breakfast chapter or store-bought
Optional: 1/2 cup (half a cup) berries or sliced banana
Optional: a drizzle of honey
The yogurt should feel cool and smooth, not watery and not lumpy in a way that suggests it has spoiled. Granola should feel crisp and dry. Fruit should feel fresh.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
Add the fruit if you are using it.
Sprinkle the granola on top, and drizzle with honey if you like.
Eat at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The yogurt should smell fresh and tangy, not sharply sour or yeasty in an off way, and it should not have a moldy smell. If the yogurt smells or looks wrong, throw it out. Granola should smell toasted, not rancid. Fruit should smell fresh.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The granola should look crisp on top, not already soaked and gray. The fruit should look fresh.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The granola should look crisp on top, not already soaked and gray. The fruit should look fresh.

Keep yogurt refrigerated, and do not leave the carton out. If anyone has a nut allergy, check the granola ingredients, because many granolas contain nuts. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Greek yogurt is thicker and more filling. See Granola in the Breakfast chapter if you want to make your own.
