entries.title: Boneless Wings

blocks.text: Boneless wings are bite-size pieces of boneless chicken, coated, cooked until crisp, and tossed in a buttery hot sauce. They are not true wings. They are closer to a sauced chicken tender or nugget, which makes them easier to cut, easier to eat, and easier to check with a thermometer.

This version is baked, which is the safer teaching method. You still get a crunchy coating and a familiar buffalo-style sauce, without a pot of hot oil on the stove. A stovetop fry is described later as a variation, with extra safety notes, for when you want that style.
4 as an appetizer, or 2 as a main dish
About 50 minutes, including 15 minutes of prep and 16 to 20 minutes in the oven. Add 20 minutes if you chill the breaded chicken before baking, which helps the coating stay put.
Intermediate. You will cut raw chicken, work with a two-bowl breading setup, and use a hot oven. A thermometer is required for doneness.
A cutting board used only for raw poultry, or a board you will wash with soap and hot water before it touches anything else
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the chicken
Two shallow bowls, pie plates, or a bowl plus a large zip-top bag
A rimmed baking sheet
A wire rack that fits in the baking sheet, if you have one (this lets hot air move under the chicken and makes the coating crisper)
Parchment paper or foil, to line the pan
Cooking spray or a little oil and a pastry brush
A talking or instant-read meat thermometer
A tactile or talking timer
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator, for the milk if you use it, and for leftover sauce
A small saucepan, for the sauce
A large mixing bowl, for tossing the cooked chicken with sauce
Tongs or a fork
Long oven mitts
A splatter screen, if you use the fried variation
A fry or probe thermometer that can read oil temperature, if you use the fried variation
Chicken and coating
1 pound boneless, skinless chicken breasts (or boneless, skinless chicken thighs)
2 large eggs
1 cup all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt, divided (use 1/2 teaspoon, which is half a teaspoon, in the flour, and keep the rest for the chicken)
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) paprika
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) to 1/2 teaspoon cayenne pepper, optional, depending on how much heat you want in the coating
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper
Oil spray, or about 1 tablespoon neutral oil
Buffalo-style sauce
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) cayenne hot sauce, such as Frank's RedHot or a similar vinegar-based sauce
3 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 teaspoon honey or a pinch of sugar, optional, to soften the sharp edge of the sauce
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) Worcestershire sauce, optional
For serving, optional
Ranch or blue cheese dressing, for dipping
Celery sticks or carrot sticks

Chicken breasts feel smooth, slightly damp, and firm, with a tapered end. If a breast is very thick in the middle, you will slice it horizontally or pound it so the pieces cook evenly. Keep the package on a plate so juices do not run onto the counter.

Flour feels fine, dry, and silky, and it has almost no smell. Salt feels crystalline and heavier in the spoon. Garlic powder smells clearly of garlic. Paprika is a little coarser and smells sweet and slightly smoky. Cayenne smells sharper and can irritate your nose if you lean in close, so measure it carefully and wash your hands after you touch it.
Crack each egg into a small bowl of its own before adding it to the dipping bowl. That way, if a piece of shell falls in, you can fish it out with a spoon by feeling for the hard fragment.

Hot sauce is thin, sharp-smelling, and vinegary. Butter is firm when cold and is usually wrapped; unwrap it over the saucepan so it cannot slide away. If you measure hot sauce in a liquid cup, set a liquid level indicator on the rim so it beeps as the liquid rises.
To measure flour, spoon it into a dry measuring cup and level the top with a straight edge, feeling for the rim of the cup. Do not pack it down.

Set the oven rack in the middle position before you turn the oven on. Line the baking sheet with parchment or foil, and set the wire rack on it if you are using one. Lightly oil the rack or the lined pan so the coating does not stick.

Set out two zones on the counter: a raw-chicken zone for cutting and breading, and a clean landing zone for the finished baking sheet. Put a damp towel under the cutting board. Put on the cut-resistant glove. Decide where the hot pan will land when it comes out of the oven, and clear that space now.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Pat the chicken dry with paper towels. This helps the coating stick and reduces sputtering later.

On the raw-poultry board, use the claw grip: tuck your fingertips under, curl your fingers, and let the side of the knife rest against your knuckles. Cut the chicken into pieces about 1 1/2 to 2 inches long (one and a half to two inches). A useful tactile guide is the length of the first two joints of an adult index finger. Try to keep the pieces close to the same size so they finish together. If a breast is much thicker in the center than at the end, slice that thick part in half horizontally so you do not have a dense middle that stays undercooked.
Sprinkle the chicken lightly with the remaining salt.
In one shallow bowl, beat the eggs with a fork until the mixture feels even, with no large pockets of unmixed white.

In the second bowl or a large zip-top bag, combine the flour, 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, garlic powder, paprika, black pepper, and cayenne if you are using it. Stir or shake until the seasonings are mixed through the flour. You should no longer feel clumps of spice sitting on top.
Working with a few pieces at a time, set the chicken in the egg and turn it until it is wet all over.
Lift a piece and let the extra egg drip back into the bowl.
Place it in the flour and press the flour on so the piece feels dry and sandy on all sides, with no slick, bare spots.
Shake off the loose flour. Set the coated pieces on the prepared rack or pan in a single layer, with a little space between them so the edges can crisp.
If you have time, refrigerate the breaded chicken for 20 minutes. The coating firms up and is less likely to slide off.
Spray the tops of the pieces lightly with oil, or brush on a thin film. You want the coating barely moistened, not soaked.
Wear long oven mitts. Place the pan on the middle rack. Set a talking timer for 10 minutes.
At 10 minutes, pull the rack partly out and turn each piece with tongs so the other side can brown. The coating should already feel drier and a little firm, not wet and pasty.
Return the pan and bake 6 to 10 minutes more.

Check the doneness cues in the next section. The chicken is safely done when a talking or instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of the thickest piece reads 165 degrees F. Check two or three pieces, especially any that felt larger when you cut them. Do not let the thermometer tip touch the pan, or the reading can run high. If any piece is under 165 degrees F, return the whole pan to the oven for 2 to 3 minutes and check again.
While the chicken bakes, add the hot sauce, butter, and optional honey and Worcestershire to a small saucepan.

Warm over low to medium-low heat, stirring, until the butter melts and the sauce feels smooth and even. You should hear only a faint, lazy bubble, not a hard boil. If the sauce spatters, the heat is too high. Take it off the heat and keep it warm.
Transfer the cooked chicken to a large bowl.
Pour on enough warm sauce to coat, then toss or fold with a spoon until the pieces feel evenly slick. Fold means turn the pieces over themselves gently.
Serve right away, with dressing and celery if you like. The coating is at its crispest in the first few minutes.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A thermometer in the center of the thickest piece must read 165 degrees F. The pieces feel firm when pressed with tongs, with a slight spring, not soft or squishy in the middle. The juices, if any, run clear, not thick and raw-feeling. The coating sounds dry and faintly crisp if you tap two pieces together, and it smells like cooked chicken and toasted flour, not raw meat. If you cut one thick piece open, use a clean knife, and the interior should feel set and fibrous, not pasty or gelatinous.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The coating should look dry and lightly golden, not wet and pasty, and not dark brown or burnt. The interior of a test piece should look white and opaque, not pink and raw, and the juices should look clear. A thermometer in the thickest piece should read 165 degrees F.
These visual cues are for a sighted partner. They do not replace the thermometer or the non-visual cues in the steps. Call them out loud so both of you are working from the same information.

The breaded chicken should turn a light to medium golden brown, not pale and pasty and not dark brown or black in spots. When you cut a thick piece, the meat should be opaque and white or very light tan all the way through, with no raw pink or glassy look, and the juices should run clear. The sauce should coat the pieces evenly and look glossy, not watery in the bottom of the bowl.

Raw chicken can carry bacteria. Use a dedicated board, keep juices on a plate, and wash your hands, knife, tongs, and the board with soap and hot water after you finish breading, before you touch the sauce, the serving bowl, or any ready-to-eat food. Do not use the same tongs for raw and cooked chicken unless you wash them in between.
Use the claw grip and a cut-resistant glove when you cut. Confirm the knife's sharp edge faces down by feeling the spine (the dull top) first.

The baking sheet and the oven rack are hot enough to burn. Use long oven mitts, pull the rack partly out rather than reaching deep into the oven, and set the pan on a surface you cleared in advance. Turn off the oven when you are finished.
Hot sauce can splash and sting eyes and small cuts. Stir the sauce gently, and wash your hands after handling cayenne or hot sauce.
If you use the fried variation below, treat hot oil as a serious burn and fire hazard. See those notes before you start.
Oven-crisp coating: A wire rack is worth using if you have one. If you do not, turn the pieces once, as written, so the bottoms do not steam.

Mild or hot: For a milder sauce, use more butter or a little more honey. For more heat, add a pinch of cayenne to the sauce or use a hotter sauce. Taste a cooled drop of sauce on a clean spoon before you toss the chicken.
Other sauces: The same baked pieces work with barbecue sauce, a mild garlic-butter sauce, or a honey-mustard sauce. Warm thick sauces slightly so they coat evenly.
Thighs instead of breasts: Boneless thighs stay moist and are forgiving. They still need 165 degrees F in the center.
Air fryer: Cook in a single layer at 375 to 400 degrees F, turning once, until the thickest piece is 165 degrees F. Time varies by basket, often 12 to 16 minutes. Do not crowd the basket.
Stovetop fried variation (higher risk):
This is closer to many restaurant boneless wings, but it uses hot oil. Skip it until you are comfortable with the baked method and with thermometer use.

Refrigerate the breaded pieces for at least 20 minutes so the coating stays on. In a deep, heavy pot, add enough oil to come about 2 inches up the sides, leaving plenty of empty space above the oil. Heat the oil slowly over medium heat to 375 degrees F, measured with a fry or probe thermometer clipped or held so the tip is in the oil and not on the bottom of the pot. The oil should smell hot and faintly toasty, not sharp or acrid. If it smokes, it is too hot. Turn the heat off and let it cool.

Fry a few pieces at a time so the oil temperature does not drop hard and so the pot cannot bubble over. The oil will hiss and sizzle when the chicken goes in. Use long tongs, wear rolled-up sleeves, and keep a splatter screen handy. Cook about 5 to 7 minutes, turning once, until the coating feels firm and a thermometer in the center of a piece reads 165 degrees F. If the sizzle fades to almost nothing too quickly, the oil may have cooled; let it return to temperature between batches. Drain on a rack, then toss with sauce.

Never leave hot oil unattended. Keep a lid nearby. If the oil catches fire, turn off the heat and slide a lid over the pot. Do not throw water on oil, and do not try to carry a flaming pot. Keep water, ice, and wet chicken away from the oil, because water makes hot oil pop and spatter.

Refrigerate leftover chicken within 2 hours, in a shallow container, for 3 to 4 days. The coating will soften in the refrigerator. Reheat in a 375 degree F oven or air fryer until the center reaches 165 degrees F. Microwaving works for safety but leaves the coating soft.

entries.title: Jalapeno Poppers

blocks.text: This recipe was on the original request list for the book.

Jalapeno poppers are jalapeno peppers halved, seeded, filled with a cream cheese mix, and baked until the peppers are tender and the filling is hot. This is an oven method, which is safer than deep frying. Wear gloves when you cut jalapenos, and do not touch your eyes or face. The peppers are spicy, even after the seeds are out.
4 to 6 as an appetizer, about 16 popper halves
About 40 minutes
Intermediate, because of pepper cutting and hot filling
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A spoon, for scooping seeds
Disposable or reusable kitchen gloves
A small knife or teaspoon
An air fryer, optional
8 jalapeno peppers, about 3 to 4 inches long
8 ounces cream cheese, softened at room temperature for about 20 minutes
1/2 cup (half a cup) shredded cheddar or Monterey Jack cheese
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) garlic powder
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
2 green onions, thinly sliced, optional
8 slices bacon, raw, optional, if you want bacon-wrapped poppers
Oil spray, or 1 teaspoon oil, for the pan

A jalapeno is a smooth, firm, tapered pepper, smaller than a bell pepper, with a stem at the wide end. After you cut it in half the long way, the seeds and pale ribs inside feel slippery and are the most spicy part. Softened cream cheese should give easily when pressed, like soft butter, not like a cold block. Bacon, if you use it, feels slippery and should stay raw only until it is wrapped and baked.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Line a baking sheet with foil and oil it lightly.
Put on gloves.
Cut each jalapeno in half from stem to tip.
Leave the stem on if you want a little handle, or trim it off.
Use a spoon to scrape out the seeds and pale ribs.
Drop them in the trash. Do not touch your face.
In a bowl, mix the cream cheese, shredded cheese, garlic powder, salt, and optional green onion until even.
Spoon the filling into each pepper half.
Fill them full but not overflowing.
If you are using bacon, wrap a half slice around each stuffed pepper and set it seam-side down.
Raw bacon is a raw-meat product, so keep it on a separate plate until it is wrapped, then wash your hands.
Set the poppers on the pan, filling-side up, with a little space between them.
Bake 15 to 20 minutes, until the peppers feel tender when pierced with a fork and the filling is hot in the center.
If you used bacon, it should feel firm and cooked, not raw and soft, and the filling should still be hot.
Bake a few minutes more if needed.
Let the pan rest 5 minutes. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat. The filling will be molten at first.
Serve warm.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The pepper walls should feel tender, not crisp and raw, when you pierce them. The filling should feel hot all the way through, not cool in the middle. You should smell cooked peppers and melted cheese, and cooked bacon if you used it. Let them cool a few minutes so the filling does not burn your mouth.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The peppers should look slightly wrinkled and duller, not raw and tight. The filling should look bubbly and set, not icy-cold in the center. Bacon, if used, should look browned and cooked, even if some cured bacon stays a little pink. The filling may be lightly browned on top.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The peppers should look slightly wrinkled and duller, not raw and tight. The filling should look bubbly and set, not icy-cold in the center. Bacon, if used, should look browned and cooked, even if some cured bacon stays a little pink. The filling may be lightly browned on top.

Wear gloves when you cut jalapenos. Capsaicin, the spicy oil, can burn your skin and eyes. Do not touch your face. Wash the board, knife, and your hands with soap after you finish cutting, even if you wore gloves. If you wrap with bacon, treat it like raw meat and cook it thoroughly. Use long mitts. The filling can be hotter than it feels on the outside. If you want a fried version, skip it until you are very comfortable with hot oil, and use the baked method first. An air fryer can cook a single layer at 375 degrees F for about 8 to 12 minutes, until the same doneness cues are met. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

For milder poppers, scrape the ribs very clean, or use mini sweet peppers instead of jalapenos. For spicier poppers, leave a few seeds in. You can mix a little cooked, crumbled bacon into the filling instead of wrapping. Serve with ranch dip from the Misc chapter if you like.

Refrigerate within 2 hours. Reheat in a 350 degree F oven or air fryer until the center is 165 degrees F. The microwave works, but the peppers will be softer. Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Applesauce

blocks.text: Apples cooked until they fall apart, then mashed into a sauce. You can peel them for a smoother sauce, or leave the peels on for more texture and then mash or blend carefully. This is a side for pork, a snack, or a topping for pancakes and pork chops.
4 to 6 as a side, about 3 cups
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 pounds apples, peeled if you want a smoother sauce, cored and cut into chunks
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) water, or apple juice
2 tablespoons sugar, or to taste, or skip if the apples are very sweet
1 teaspoon lemon juice
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) cinnamon, optional

Apple chunks should become very soft and collapse under a spoon when they are done. The sauce should feel like a thick puree, either smooth or lightly chunky, not watery and not like raw, firm pieces in syrup.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the apples, water or juice, lemon juice, optional sugar, and optional cinnamon in a pot.
Cover and cook over medium-low heat 15 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the apples feel very soft and fall apart when pressed.
If the pot looks dry before the apples are soft, add 1 or 2 tablespoons water.
Mash with a potato masher or a large fork for a chunky sauce, or puree carefully once it is not piping hot if you want it smooth.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add sugar or lemon if it needs it.
Serve warm or chilled.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The apples should feel completely soft before you mash. The sauce should smell like cooked apple and optional cinnamon, not burning. A cooled spoonful should feel thick and tender, not starchy and raw.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sauce should look even and golden or pale, depending on the apples, not brown and scorched, and not watery with floating firm pieces unless you left some chunks on purpose.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look even and golden or pale, depending on the apples, not brown and scorched, and not watery with floating firm pieces unless you left some chunks on purpose.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife to core and cut the apples. The pot and steam are hot, and bubbling fruit can spatter. Cool a spoonful before you taste. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot if you want them warm, or serve chilled. Refrigerate within 2 hours. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A mix of sweet and tart apples tastes better than one kind alone. This freezes well.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Baked Beans

blocks.text: A sweet-savory pot of beans baked with onion, a little mustard, and a sweetener, until the sauce is thick and the beans are hot, 165 degrees F in the center. This version starts with canned beans to keep the time reasonable. It is a classic picnic and supper side.
6 as a side
About 1 hour with canned beans, or much longer if you start from dried beans
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
2 cans (15 ounces each) navy beans or pinto beans, drained and rinsed, or 3 cups cooked beans
1/2 onion, diced
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) ketchup or tomato sauce
2 tablespoons brown sugar or molasses
1 tablespoon mustard
1 tablespoon vinegar
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) water or broth, plus more if the pot looks dry
Optional: 2 slices cooked bacon, crumbled, for stirring in at the end

The sauce should feel thick enough to coat the beans, not watery, and not pasty and dry. The beans should feel tender and hot. If you add leftover bacon, it should already be fully cooked, then heated through in the pot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F, or plan to simmer the beans on the stove. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Mix the beans, onion, ketchup or tomato sauce, brown sugar or molasses, mustard, vinegar, salt, and water in a baking dish or in a pot.

Cover and bake 45 to 60 minutes, stirring once, until the sauce feels thick and the beans are bubbling and 165 degrees F, or simmer on the stove over low heat 25 to 35 minutes, stirring often so they do not scorch.
Add a splash of water if the mix gets too thick before the onion is soft.
Stir in optional cooked bacon.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add salt or vinegar if it needs it.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The beans should feel tender and steaming hot, 165 degrees F. The sauce should feel thick and should coat a spoon. You should smell tomato, sweet molasses or brown sugar, and onion, not scorching.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sauce should look thick, dark, and glossy, coating the beans, not watery, and not dried to the edges in a hard crust unless you like a little browned edge.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look thick, dark, and glossy, coating the beans, not watery, and not dried to the edges in a hard crust unless you like a little browned edge.

Use mitts if you bake the dish. The pot and sauce are very hot, and a sugar-tomato sauce can scorch on the bottom if you stop stirring on the stove. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Molasses gives a deeper flavor than brown sugar. These are good with cornbread from the Baked Goods chapter, and with pulled pork from the Supper chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Baked Potatoes

blocks.text: Whole russet potatoes baked until the skins are dry and the insides are fluffy. Pierce the skins before they go in the oven so steam can escape. For a faster method, see Microwave Baked Potato in the Midnight Snacks chapter.
4 as a side or a simple meal
About 1 hour 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
4 medium russet potatoes, scrubbed
1 tablespoon oil
1 teaspoon salt
Butter, sour cream, cheese, or other toppings, for serving

The potatoes should feel firm and heavy, with no soft or wet spots. After baking, a potato should yield when you squeeze it gently with a mitt on your hand, and a fork should slide into the center with almost no resistance.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Scrub the potatoes and dry them.
Pierce each one 5 or 6 times with a fork, all around.
Rub with oil and salt.
Set them on a pan or directly on the oven rack, with a pan on a lower rack to catch drips if you use the rack.
Bake 45 to 60 minutes, until a fork slides into the center easily and the potato feels soft when squeezed with a mitt.
Let them sit 5 minutes.
Cut open carefully, fluff the insides with a fork, and add toppings.
If you add leftover meat or chilled cooked bacon, those toppings should be heated to 165 degrees F, or added very hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A fork should slide into the center easily. The potato should feel soft when squeezed with a mitt. You should smell baked potato, not burning. Steam will escape when you cut one open.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The skins should look dry and slightly crisp, not tight and raw, and not scorched. The insides should look fluffy and dry, not wet and hard in the center.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The skins should look dry and slightly crisp, not tight and raw, and not scorched. The insides should look fluffy and dry, not wet and hard in the center.

Pierce the skins before baking. Use mitts to squeeze-test and to cut the potatoes open. Keep your face back from the steam. The inside is extremely hot. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A large potato can take longer than 1 hour. For crispier skin, do not wrap the potatoes in foil. Foil makes a softer, steamed skin.

blocks.text: Cubed bread mixed with cooked onion and celery, broth, and eggs, then baked until the top is crisp and the center is set and hot, 165 degrees F. This is baked in a dish, not inside a bird, which is a safer and more even method. Dry or slightly stale bread works better than very fresh, soft bread.
8 as a side
About 1 hour
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
10 cups cubed sturdy bread, about 3/4 inch (three-quarters of an inch) pieces, left out to dry for a few hours, or lightly toasted
6 tablespoons unsalted butter
1 onion, diced
2 celery stalks, diced
2 teaspoons dried sage, or 1 tablespoon chopped fresh sage, plus 1 teaspoon dried thyme or poultry seasoning
1 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) black pepper
2 to 2 1/2 cups (two to two and a half cups) broth
2 large eggs, beaten

The bread cubes should feel dry at the edges, not soft and squishy, before you mix. After mixing, the cubes should feel moistened, not swimming in broth, and not dry in the middle of the bowl. After baking, the center should feel set and steaming hot, 165 degrees F, and the top should feel crisp.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees F.
Butter a 9 by 13 inch baking dish, or a similar 3 quart dish.
Melt the butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Add the onion and celery, and cook until they feel soft, 6 to 8 minutes.
Stir in the herbs, salt, and pepper.
Put the bread cubes in a large bowl.
Add the onion mix and toss.
Mix 2 cups of the broth with the eggs.
Pour over the bread and toss until the cubes feel evenly moist.
Add more broth if dry pockets remain.
Spread the mix in the dish.
Cover with foil.
Bake 25 minutes.
Uncover and bake 20 to 25 minutes more, until the top feels crisp and the center is 165 degrees F and set, not wet and liquid.
Cool 10 minutes, then serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The center should be 165 degrees F and feel set and steaming hot. The top should feel crisp. You should smell toasted bread, butter, onion, and sage, not raw egg or burning.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look golden and crisp. The center, when you scoop it, should look moist and set, not soupy and not dry as crumbs.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look golden and crisp. The center, when you scoop it, should look moist and set, not soupy and not dry as crumbs.

Do not taste the raw mix. It contains eggs. Use mitts. The dish is very hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F. This recipe is for a baking dish, not for stuffing the cavity of a bird, where the center can stay too cool. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.

If you want a softer stuffing, leave the foil on for more of the bake. Sausage stuffing starts with cooked, drained sausage, cooked to 160 degrees F for pork sausage or 165 degrees F for poultry sausage, then mixed in with the bread.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A pan gravy made from butter or pan drippings, flour, and broth. Drippings are the juices and fat left in a pan after you cook meat. A roux, which is fat and flour cooked together, thickens the gravy. The gravy should come back to a bubble and feel smooth. Reheat leftover gravy to a boil, 165 degrees F.
About 2 cups, 6 to 8 servings
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
4 tablespoons butter, or 4 tablespoons pan drippings, or a mix
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) all-purpose flour
2 cups broth, beef or chicken, warmed
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, or to taste, less if the drippings or broth are salty
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper
The roux should feel smooth and smell toasty, not raw and pasty, and not burnt. The finished gravy should feel smooth and thick enough to coat a spoon, not watery, and not lumpy and pasty.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Melt the butter, or heat the drippings, in a saucepan over medium heat.
Stir in the flour.
Cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the mix smells toasty and looks a shade darker. This is the roux.
Add the warm broth a little at a time, whisking so there are no lumps. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk.
Simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles, 3 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the gravy feels smooth and coats a spoon. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Add salt and pepper to taste.
If it is too thick, add a splash of broth.
If it is too thin, simmer 1 or 2 minutes more.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The gravy should feel smooth and should coat a spoon. You should smell toasted flour and broth, not raw flour or burning. If you used drippings, you should also smell the meat they came from.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The gravy should look smooth and brown, not pale and pasty, and not dark and speckled with burnt bits unless you strained it. It should coat a spoon, not run off like broth.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The gravy should look smooth and brown, not pale and pasty, and not dark and speckled with burnt bits unless you strained it. It should coat a spoon, not run off like broth.

The pan and bubbling gravy are very hot and can spatter. Whisk with a long-handled tool. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftover gravy to a boil, 165 degrees F, stirring, and add a little broth if it has thickened. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.

If you get lumps, pour the gravy through a strainer. A splash of Worcestershire sauce or a pinch of dried thyme is a good extra. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). This is the usual partner for Mashed Potatoes and for roast meats in the Supper chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Brown Rice

blocks.text: A pot of brown rice, which still has the bran layer and takes longer than white rice. Use the package water amount if it differs from this page. The rice should be tender, with a slight chew, not hard in the center.
4 as a side, about 3 cups cooked
About 50 minutes, plus a 10-minute rest
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 cup brown rice
2 1/4 cups (two and a quarter cups) water, or as the package directs
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 teaspoon oil, optional

Brown rice feels a little harder and more elongated than white rice when raw. After cooking and resting, the grains should feel tender with a slight chew, not chalky and hard in the center, and not mushy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Rinse the rice in a fine strainer, unless the package says not to.
Put the rice, water, salt, and optional oil in a pot with a tight lid.

Bring to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles, then stir once, cover, and reduce the heat to a low simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cook 40 to 45 minutes, or as the package directs, without lifting the lid.
Take the pot off the heat.
Let it rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Fluff with a fork, meaning gently loosen the grains.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The grains should feel tender with a slight chew, not hard in the center. You should smell a nutty, cooked-rice smell, not scorching.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The rice should look separate and slightly nutty-brown, with steam rising, not wet and not a hard, dry crust unless the heat was too high.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The rice should look separate and slightly nutty-brown, with steam rising, not wet and not a hard, dry crust unless the heat was too high.

The pot and steam are very hot. Tilt the lid away from you. Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Reheat to 165 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
If the rice is still firm, add 2 tablespoons water, cover, and cook 5 minutes more, then rest again. Brown rice keeps well and is a good base for the Rice and Bean Bowl in the Lunch chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Toasted bread topped with a fresh mix of tomato, oil, salt, and basil or parsley. The topping should go on just before you serve, so the bread stays crisp. Bruschetta is toasted bread with a topping, often tomato.
8 to 12 pieces
About 25 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 baguette, cut into 1/2 inch (half inch) slices, about 12 slices
2 tablespoons olive oil, divided
3 ripe tomatoes, diced and drained of extra juice
1 small garlic clove, minced, plus 1 whole clove for rubbing the toast, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
2 tablespoons chopped fresh basil or parsley

Dice means cut into small, even cubes. Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces. The toast should feel crisp at the edges. The tomato mix should feel juicy but not watery, after a brief drain, and it should smell fresh. Drain means pour off the liquid.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Set the bread slices on a pan.
Brush them with 1 tablespoon of the oil.
Bake 6 to 10 minutes, until the edges feel crisp and the centers feel lightly toasted, not hard as a cracker unless you prefer them very crisp, and not burnt.
Cool 1 or 2 minutes.
If you like, rub a cut garlic clove lightly on the warm toast.
Mix the tomatoes, remaining 1 tablespoon oil, minced garlic, salt, and basil or parsley. Mince means cut into very small pieces.
Taste a little, and add salt if it needs it.
Spoon the tomato mix onto the toast just before you serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The toast should feel crisp at the edges and should smell toasted, not burnt. The tomato mix should smell fresh, tomatoey, and herby, not fermented. The bread will soften after it is topped, so serve at once.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The toast should look lightly golden, not pale and not dark brown. The topping should look moist and red, with visible herbs, not watery and puddled on the plate if you drained the tomatoes a little.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The toast should look lightly golden, not pale and not dark brown. The topping should look moist and red, with visible herbs, not watery and puddled on the plate if you drained the tomatoes a little.

Use mitts. Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly, for the bread and tomatoes. Mince garlic on a stable board. Tomato topping left on bread gets soggy, so top only what you will eat soon. Keep leftover topping refrigerated, and use within 2 days. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A little balsamic vinegar in the tomato mix is a good extra. If tomatoes are out of season, this will taste dull, and you may prefer a caprese-style topping with better tomatoes, or skip to Caprese Skewers in this chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A hot dip of cooked, shredded chicken mixed with cream cheese, a buffalo-style hot sauce, and cheese, baked until bubbling, 165 degrees F in the center. Use already-cooked chicken, such as a leftover baked breast, reheated in the dip to 165 degrees F. This is a party cousin of the Boneless Wings in this chapter.
8 as an appetizer
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
2 cups cooked, shredded chicken
8 ounces cream cheese, softened
1/2 cup (half a cup) buffalo-style hot sauce, or to taste
1/2 cup (half a cup) ranch dressing or sour cream, or Ranch Dip from this chapter
1 cup shredded cheddar or a cheddar-jack mix, divided
The mix should feel thick and even before it bakes, with visible shreds of chicken. After baking, the center should feel steaming hot, 165 degrees F, and creamy, not watery, and not oily.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease a small baking dish.
Mix the cream cheese, hot sauce, and ranch or sour cream until even.
Stir in the chicken and 3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) of the cheese.
Spread the mix in the dish.
Sprinkle the remaining cheese on top.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until the dip is bubbling and the center is 165 degrees F.
Cool 5 minutes, then serve with celery, chips, or crackers.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The center should be 165 degrees F and feel steaming hot. You should smell chicken, hot sauce, and melted cheese, not scorching. The dip should feel creamy and thick.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look melted and bubbling, with a little orange oil from the sauce, which is common, not dried and dark brown.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look melted and bubbling, with a little orange oil from the sauce, which is common, not dried and dark brown.

Use already-cooked chicken. The finished dip must reach 165 degrees F. Use mitts. Cool 5 minutes, because bubbling sauce and cheese can burn your mouth. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F. Wash the board after handling the chicken, even though it is cooked, if you also cut raw vegetables on it later, or use a clean board. Cook all poultry to 165 degrees F. Measure in the thickest part. Do not let the thermometer tip touch bone or the pan.
Rotisserie chicken, skin and bones removed, works well. Start with less hot sauce if you are not sure about the heat, then add more.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Plain pasta tossed with butter, salt, and optional cheese. This is a simple side, or a mild main dish for a night when you want something easy. See the Pasta Primer in the Supper chapter for the basic boiling method. Save a little pasta water so the butter coats the noodles.
4 as a side
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
12 ounces egg noodles or any short or long pasta
1 tablespoon salt, for the pasta water
3 tablespoons unsalted butter
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) grated Parmesan cheese, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper, optional

The pasta should feel tender but still slightly firm in the center, not hard, and not mushy. The dressed noodles should feel evenly coated and slightly glossy, not dry, and not swimming in melted butter.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cook the pasta in salted boiling water until it is tender but still slightly firm in the center.
Save 1/2 cup (half a cup) of the pasta water, then drain. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Return the pasta to the pot.
Add the butter and a splash of pasta water.
Toss until the butter is melted and the noodles feel coated, adding more pasta water if they are tight.
Add optional Parmesan and pepper.
Taste a cooled noodle, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The pasta should feel tender with a slight firmness. You should smell butter and pasta, and optional cheese, not a starchy, undercooked smell.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The noodles should look glossy and evenly coated, not dry and clumped, and not sitting in a puddle of butter.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The noodles should look glossy and evenly coated, not dry and clumped, and not sitting in a puddle of butter.

Boiling water can burn you. See the Pasta Primer for draining safety. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F with a splash of water. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A little garlic, cooked briefly in the butter before you add the pasta, is a good extra. Peas or leftover chicken, reheated to 165 degrees F, can turn this into a fuller plate.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

Small skewers of tomato, mozzarella, and basil, finished with oil, salt, and optional balsamic vinegar. This is a no-cook appetizer. Use ripe but still firm tomatoes so they stay on the skewer.
About 12 skewers
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
12 small mozzarella balls, or 8 ounces mozzarella, cut into 12 cubes
12 cherry or grape tomatoes
12 fresh basil leaves, or as many as you have, folded if they are large
1 tablespoon olive oil
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt
Optional: 1 teaspoon balsamic vinegar, or a thick balsamic glaze, for drizzling
12 small skewers or sturdy toothpicks

The mozzarella should feel moist and slightly springy, not slimy. The tomatoes should feel ripe but still firm, not collapsed. A finished skewer should feel stable, with the basil tucked so it does not slip off.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Drain the mozzarella if it is packed in water, and pat it dry. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Thread a tomato, a basil leaf, and a mozzarella ball or cube onto each skewer, in any order you can handle easily.
Repeat if the skewers are longer.
Arrange the skewers on a plate.
Drizzle with oil and optional vinegar, and sprinkle with salt.
Serve at once, or cover and refrigerate for up to 2 hours, then add the oil and salt just before serving if you want them to stay fresh-looking.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The mozzarella should feel moist and fresh, and it should smell clean and milky, not sour or ammonia-like. Tomatoes should smell fresh and sweet. Basil should smell green and fragrant, not black and slimy.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The skewers should look neat and colorful, with shiny oil, not watery and not wilted if you serve them soon.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The skewers should look neat and colorful, with shiny oil, not watery and not wilted if you serve them soon.

Skewer points are sharp. Work slowly, and set a guard or a cork on the point if you are passing a platter among children or anyone who might grab the point. Keep the platter refrigerated until serving, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
If you do not have basil, a little dried oregano in the oil is an acceptable stand-in, though the plate will be less fragrant. See also Caprese Salad in the Lunch chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A smooth sauce of milk thickened with a butter-and-flour roux, then finished with shredded cheese. A roux is fat and flour cooked together. This is the sauce for vegetables, oven fries, or a quick stovetop pasta. Use low heat after the cheese goes in so the sauce does not split, meaning the fat and liquid separate.
About 2 cups, 4 to 6 servings
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 tablespoons butter
2 tablespoons all-purpose flour
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) milk
1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups) shredded cheddar cheese, or a mix of cheddar and American
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) paprika or mustard powder, optional

The roux should feel smooth and smell slightly toasty. The milk sauce, before cheese, should feel smooth and slightly thick, like heavy cream. The finished sauce should feel smooth and pourable, thick enough to coat a spoon, not grainy, and not oily and split.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat.
Stir in the flour and cook 1 minute.
Whisk in the milk slowly until the mix feels smooth. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk so there are no lumps.
Cook, stirring, until the sauce is slightly thick and you see small bubbles, 3 to 5 minutes.
Take the pot off the heat.
Stir in the cheese, salt, and optional paprika or mustard, until the cheese is melted and the sauce feels smooth.
If it is too thick, add a splash of milk.
If the cheese has not fully melted, return the pot to very low heat and stir, without boiling.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The sauce should feel smooth and should coat a spoon. You should smell melted cheese and milk, not scorched milk or a grainy, split sauce. If you smell scorching, take the pot off the heat and stop scraping the bottom into the serving dish.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sauce should look smooth and evenly yellow or orange, not lumpy, and not oily with a pool of separated fat.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look smooth and evenly yellow or orange, not lumpy, and not oily with a pool of separated fat.

Stir often so the milk does not scorch. The pot and sauce are very hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftover cheese sauce to 165 degrees F, or until it is bubbling again, on low heat, stirring, with a splash of milk. Do not boil it hard, or it can split. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.

This is a close cousin of the sauce in Stovetop Mac and Cheese in the Lunch chapter. A pinch of cayenne is a good extra. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Chocolate Frosting

blocks.text: A chocolate buttercream made with cocoa powder, butter, and powdered sugar. Use this on Chocolate Cake or Chocolate Cupcakes in the Baked Goods chapter. The cake must be fully cool before you frost it.
About 2 cups, enough for 12 cupcakes or a thin layer on a 9 by 13 inch cake
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, softened
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsweetened cocoa powder
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) powdered sugar, plus more if the frosting is too thin
3 tablespoons milk, plus more as needed
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
A pinch of salt

Softened butter should give like cool clay. Cocoa and powdered sugar are dusty, so add them slowly. The finished frosting should feel smooth, fluffy, and spreadable, not dry and crumbly, and not soupy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Beat the butter until it feels smooth and slightly fluffy.
Add the cocoa, 1 cup of the powdered sugar, and 1 tablespoon of the milk.
Mix slowly, then more firmly, until combined.
Add the remaining powdered sugar, the remaining milk, the vanilla, and the salt.
Beat until the frosting feels fluffy and spreadable.
If it is too thick, add milk 1 teaspoon at a time.
If it is too thin, add powdered sugar 2 tablespoons at a time.
Spread on a fully cooled cake or cupcakes.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The frosting should feel smooth, fluffy, and spreadable. You should smell chocolate, butter, and vanilla, not raw, dusty cocoa once it is fully mixed.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The frosting should look smooth and evenly chocolate-colored, not streaky with dry cocoa, and not oily or soupy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The frosting should look smooth and evenly chocolate-colored, not streaky with dry cocoa, and not oily or soupy.

Mix slowly at first so cocoa and sugar do not puff into the air. There are no raw eggs in this frosting. The cake must be cool, or the frosting will melt. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

A pinch of espresso powder, if you have it, deepens the chocolate flavor and will not make the frosting taste like coffee. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: A cold, sharp ketchup-and-horseradish sauce for shrimp cocktail and other seafood. Prepared horseradish is very strong. Start with less, then add more. See Shrimp Cocktail in this chapter.
About 3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup)
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/2 cup (half a cup) ketchup
1 to 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish, starting with 1 tablespoon
1 teaspoon lemon juice
A dash of hot sauce or Worcestershire sauce, optional
Prepared horseradish feels wet and fiery in the nose as well as on the tongue. The sauce should feel thick and scoopable, like a loose ketchup, and it should smell sharp and tomatoey, not only sweet.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the ketchup, 1 tablespoon horseradish, lemon juice, and any optional hot sauce or Worcestershire in a bowl.
Taste a tiny amount, and add more horseradish if you want more heat.
Chill until you serve it, then serve cold.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The sauce should feel thick and should smell sharp, tomatoey, and a little peppery from the horseradish. It should not smell fermented or off.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sauce should look thick and red, evenly mixed, not watery.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look thick and red, evenly mixed, not watery.

Taste a very small amount when you adjust the horseradish, because it can sting. Keep the sauce refrigerated, and use within 1 week. Do not leave it out more than 2 hours at a party, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A little extra lemon on the shrimp, not only in the sauce, makes the plate brighter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Coleslaw

blocks.text: Shredded cabbage in a creamy dressing, served cold. This is the slaw to go with Fish Tacos, pulled pork, or fried-style foods in this book. You can start with a bag of shredded coleslaw mix to skip the knife work.
6 as a side
About 15 minutes, plus 15 minutes of rest
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
6 cups shredded cabbage, or one 14 ounce bag of coleslaw mix
1 carrot, shredded, if your mix does not already include it
1/2 cup (half a cup) mayonnaise
1 tablespoon vinegar or lemon juice
1 teaspoon sugar, or to taste
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper

Shredded cabbage should feel crisp and dry before you dress it. The dressing should feel smooth and pourable, like a thick cream, not pasty and not watery. After a short rest, the slaw should feel slightly softened but still crisp, not soupy. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
If you are shredding your own cabbage, cut it into thin shreds on a stable board, using a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the cabbage if you need it.
Shred the carrot.
Mix the mayonnaise, vinegar or lemon juice, sugar, salt, and pepper in a large bowl until smooth.
Add the cabbage and carrot.
Toss until the shreds feel evenly coated.
Taste a piece, and add salt, sugar, or vinegar if it needs it.
Rest 15 minutes in the refrigerator, then toss again and serve cold.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cabbage should feel crisp at first, then slightly softened after the rest. The dressing should taste balanced, tangy and a little creamy. You should smell fresh cabbage and vinegar, not a sour, off smell. If bagged mix smells sour or sulfurous in an off way, throw it out.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The slaw should look moist and evenly coated, not dry and not sitting in a puddle of dressing. The cabbage should still look fairly crisp and pale, not dull and limp if you serve it the same day.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The slaw should look moist and evenly coated, not dry and not sitting in a puddle of dressing. The cabbage should still look fairly crisp and pale, not dull and limp if you serve it the same day.

Keep the slaw refrigerated. Do not leave it out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Because it contains mayonnaise, treat it as a perishable side. Wash the board and grater after use. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A spoon of Dijon mustard or a pinch of celery seed is a good extra. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). For a vinegar slaw without mayonnaise, toss the cabbage with 3 tablespoons vinegar, 1 tablespoon oil, 1 teaspoon sugar, and salt.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.totalTime: About 15 minutes, plus 15 minutes of rest

blocks.text: Whole ears of corn cooked in simmering water until the kernels are tender and hot. You can also steam the ears or cook them in the microwave. Butter and salt at the table are plenty.
4 ears
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
4 ears corn, husks and silk removed
Butter and salt, for serving

Husk means the leafy outer layers. Silk means the fine threads under the husk. After cooking, a kernel should feel tender and release a little juice when you press it, not hard and starchy, and not mushy and collapsed.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles.
Add the corn.
When the water returns to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles, cook 4 to 8 minutes, until a kernel feels tender. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Lift the ears out with tongs.
Let them sit 1 minute.
Serve with butter and salt.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A kernel should feel tender and juicy. You should smell sweet corn, not sour or fermented corn, which should be thrown out before cooking. The ears will be very hot and wet.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The kernels should look bright yellow and plump, not dull and shrunken, and not still pale and raw if the corn was very young and pale to start, though some varieties stay paler.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The kernels should look bright yellow and plump, not dull and shrunken, and not still pale and raw if the corn was very young and pale to start, though some varieties stay paler.

Boiling water can burn you. Use tongs, not your fingers, to lift the ears. Let them sit 1 minute. Butter can make the cob slippery, so use corn holders or a fork if you need a better grip. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

For a microwave ear, leave the husk on, microwave 3 to 4 minutes, then let it sit 2 minutes, and husk carefully, because steam will escape. For a skillet version, cook shucked ears in a little butter over medium heat, turning, until some kernels feel browned and all feel tender.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Couscous

blocks.text: A very fast grain-like side made from tiny pasta pellets, usually sold as couscous. Most packaged couscous is precooked and only needs to sit in boiling water or broth until it is tender. This is faster than rice and is a good weeknight side.
4 as a side, about 3 cups cooked
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 cup couscous
1 cup water or broth, or as the package directs
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, or less if the broth is salty
1 tablespoon olive oil or butter

Uncooked couscous feels like tiny dry pellets. After it sits in the hot liquid, it should feel tender and fluffy, not hard in the center, and not wet and clumped. Fluff means loosen the grains with a fork.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Bring the water or broth, salt, and oil or butter to a boil in a small pot, meaning large, rolling bubbles.
Stir in the couscous.
Take the pot off the heat and cover it.
Let it sit 5 minutes, or as the package directs, until the liquid is absorbed and the couscous feels tender.
Fluff with a fork.
Taste a cooled bite, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot, or cool and use in a salad.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The pellets should feel tender, not hard. You should smell a mild wheat and butter or oil smell, not raw, starchy pasta, and not scorching from a pot left on the heat.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The couscous should look fluffy and separate, not wet and not a tight cake, though it will pack together until you fluff it.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The couscous should look fluffy and separate, not wet and not a tight cake, though it will pack together until you fluff it.

The pot and steam are very hot. Tilt the lid away from you. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F with a splash of water, or serve cold and keep refrigerated. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A squeeze of lemon, chopped herbs, or leftover roasted vegetables can be folded in after fluffing. This is a good base for a quick lunch bowl.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.servings: 4 as a side, about 3 cups cooked

blocks.text: Fresh cranberries simmered with sugar and a little water until they burst and the sauce thickens. The sauce will thicken more as it cools. This is the usual partner for roast turkey or turkey breast in the Supper chapter.
8 as a side, about 2 cups
About 20 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
12 ounces fresh or frozen cranberries, about 3 cups
3/4 to 1 cup sugar, depending on how tart you like it
1 cup water
Optional: 1 teaspoon orange zest, or 2 tablespoons orange juice

Zest is the fragrant orange outer skin, not the bitter white pith, if you use it. Raw cranberries feel firm and very tart. After simmering, most of the berries should have burst, and the sauce should feel slightly thick, like a loose jam, and it will thicken more as it cools.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the cranberries, sugar, and water in a pot.
Add optional zest or juice.
Bring to a simmer over medium heat, meaning small, gentle bubbles, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cook 8 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until most of the berries have burst and the sauce feels slightly thick.
Take the pot off the heat.
Cool at least 30 minutes. The sauce will thicken as it cools.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add a little sugar if it is too tart, stirring until it dissolves.
Serve at room temperature or chilled.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: Most of the berries should feel burst. The sauce should feel slightly thick in the pot and thicker after it cools. You should smell cranberry and sugar, not burning sugar.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The sauce should look glossy and deep red, with some whole and some burst berries, not watery and pale, and not dark and scorched.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look glossy and deep red, with some whole and some burst berries, not watery and pale, and not dark and scorched.

The pot and bubbling sugar-fruit mix are very hot and can spatter. Stir with a long-handled spoon. Cool before you taste for sweetness. Refrigerate leftovers, and use within 1 week, or freeze. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
This can be made 2 or 3 days ahead. If you want a smoother sauce, mash the berries more as they cook, or puree after cooling, carefully, once they are not hot.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.
