entries.title: Cream Cheese Frosting

blocks.text: A tangy frosting made with cream cheese, butter, and powdered sugar. This is the usual frosting for Carrot Cake in the Baked Goods chapter, and it also works on cupcakes. Because it contains cream cheese, keep frosted cakes refrigerated.
About 2 cups, enough for a 9 by 13 inch carrot cake or 12 cupcakes
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
8 ounces cream cheese, softened
4 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened
2 1/2 cups (two and a half cups) powdered sugar, plus more if needed
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
A pinch of salt

Softened cream cheese and butter should feel smooth and spreadable, not cold and lumpy, and not melted and oily. The finished frosting should feel smooth, thick, and spreadable, a little looser than vanilla buttercream, not soupy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Beat the cream cheese and butter together until the mix feels completely smooth, with no lumps.
Add the powdered sugar 1 cup at a time, mixing slowly at first, then more firmly.
Add the vanilla and salt.
Beat until the frosting feels smooth and spreadable.
If it is too thin, add more powdered sugar 2 tablespoons at a time, or chill the frosting 15 minutes, then beat again.
If it is too thick, add milk 1 teaspoon at a time.
Spread on a fully cooled cake.
Refrigerate the frosted cake.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The frosting should feel smooth and thick, and it should smell like cream cheese, butter, and vanilla, not sour in an off way. If the cream cheese smelled or looked wrong before you mixed, throw it out.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The frosting should look smooth and pale, not lumpy with bits of cold cream cheese, and not soupy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The frosting should look smooth and pale, not lumpy with bits of cold cream cheese, and not soupy.

The cake must be fully cool. Keep frosted cake refrigerated because of the cream cheese, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Let a slice sit out a few minutes before you eat it if you like the frosting softer. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot.

A little lemon zest is a good extra on carrot cake. This frosting is softer than vanilla buttercream, so a thick layer on a warm day can slump. Chill the cake briefly after frosting if you need neater slices.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Corn kernels heated in a creamy sauce of milk, butter, and a little flour or cornstarch until the mix is thick and bubbling hot. Frozen corn works well and does not need to be thawed first.
4 as a side
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
3 cups corn kernels, frozen or fresh, or two 15 ounce cans, drained
2 tablespoons butter
1 tablespoon flour, or 1 teaspoon cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon cold water
1/2 cup (half a cup) milk, plus more if the sauce is too thick
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper, optional
1 teaspoon sugar, optional, if the corn is not very sweet
The sauce should feel smooth and thick enough to coat the corn, not watery, and not pasty. The corn should feel tender and hot. Frozen kernels will go from icy to hot in a few minutes.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat.
Stir in the flour and cook 1 minute if you are using flour.
Whisk in the milk until the mix feels smooth. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk so there are no lumps.
Add the corn, salt, optional pepper, and optional sugar.
Cook, stirring, 5 to 8 minutes, until the corn is hot and the sauce feels slightly thick and is bubbling.
If you are using cornstarch instead of flour, stir it in now and cook 1 minute more.
If the mix is too thick, add a little milk.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The corn should feel tender and hot. The sauce should feel smooth and slightly thick, and it should bubble gently. You should smell sweet corn, butter, and milk, not scorched milk.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The mix should look creamy and pale gold, coating the kernels, not watery, and not scorched at the edges of the pan.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The mix should look creamy and pale gold, coating the kernels, not watery, and not scorched at the edges of the pan.

Stir often so the milk does not scorch. The pot and sauce are very hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F, or until the sauce bubbles again, stirring, with a splash of milk if it has thickened. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.
A pinch of paprika or a little grated cheddar at the end makes a richer side. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.title: Deviled Eggs

blocks.text: Hard-boiled eggs halved and filled with a creamy yolk mix. Cook the eggs until the whites and yolks are firm, as in Hard-Boiled Eggs in the Breakfast chapter. Cool them fully before you peel and fill them. Keep the finished eggs cold.
12 halves, 6 appetizer servings
About 30 minutes, including the time to hard-boil and cool the eggs
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
6 large eggs, hard-boiled and cooled, from the Breakfast chapter
3 tablespoons mayonnaise
1 teaspoon mustard
1 teaspoon vinegar or pickle juice, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
Paprika or chopped chives, for a topping, optional

A well-cooked yolk should feel firm and dry-crumbly, not wet and liquid, and not with a gray-green dry ring if you can help it, though that ring is a sign of a longer cook, not unsafety, once the egg was fully cooked and then cooled. The filling should feel smooth and pipeable or spoonable, not stiff and dry, and not runny.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Peel the cooled eggs.
Cut each egg in half lengthwise on a stable board.
Scoop the yolks into a bowl.
Set the whites on a plate, cut-side up.
Mash the yolks with the mayonnaise, mustard, optional vinegar, and salt until the mix feels smooth.
Taste a little, and add salt if it needs it.
If the filling is too stiff, add mayonnaise 1 teaspoon at a time.
Spoon or pipe the filling into the whites.
Add optional paprika or chives.
Serve cold, or cover and refrigerate until you serve them.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The filling should feel smooth and creamy. You should smell cooked egg, mayonnaise, and mustard, not a sulfur smell so strong it seems off, and not a sour mayonnaise smell. The whites should feel firm and cool, not slimy.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The filling should look smooth and pale yellow, mounded neatly in the whites, not watery, and not dry and crumbly. The whites should look intact, not badly torn.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The filling should look smooth and pale yellow, mounded neatly in the whites, not watery, and not dry and crumbly. The whites should look intact, not badly torn.

Use fully cooked, firm hard-boiled eggs that were cooled and refrigerated. Keep deviled eggs refrigerated, and do not leave them out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Eat within 3 to 4 days. Wash the board after cutting the eggs. Cook eggs until the yolk and white are firm. Cook egg dishes to 160 degrees F.

A little pickle relish or a pinch of paprika in the filling is a good extra. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon). If the shells are hard to peel, try older eggs, and peel them under a thin stream of cold water.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: An oven-baked side of potato sticks, similar to the Oven Fries in the Midnight Snacks chapter, written here as a supper side. Cut the sticks even so they finish together. This page does not use a pot of hot oil.
4 as a side
About 40 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
2 pounds russet potatoes, scrubbed
2 tablespoons oil
1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
Optional: 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) paprika
Even sticks, about 1/4 to 1/3 inch (a quarter to a third of an inch) thick, cook more evenly. After baking, the edges should feel crisp, and the centers should feel tender, with no hard, raw core.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F.
Line two sheet pans with parchment, or oil the pans.
Cut the potatoes into even sticks on a stable board, using a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the potato if you need it.
Toss with oil, salt, and optional paprika, until they feel lightly coated.
Spread in a single layer with space between the sticks.
Use two pans if you need to.
Bake 15 minutes.
Turn the sticks.
Bake 10 to 20 minutes more, until the edges feel crisp and the centers feel tender.
Taste a cooled fry, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The fries should look golden with browned edges, not pale and not burnt, and not wet and limp.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The fries should look golden with browned edges, not pale and not burnt, and not wet and limp.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Use mitts. Let a test fry cool a few seconds. Do not deep-fry in this recipe. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Soaking the cut potatoes in cold water 15 minutes, then drying them very well, can make them a little crispier. Serve with ketchup or Ranch Dip from this chapter.

A larger, shareable version of the Cheese and Crackers snack in the Midnight Snacks chapter, with fruit added. Keep the cheese and any cut fruit cold until you plate them, then serve soon. Arrange items with a little space so people can find each one by touch.
6 as an appetizer
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
8 ounces cheese, such as a mix of cheddar, Swiss, and a softer cheese, sliced or cubed
2 cups fruit, such as apple slices, grapes, or berries
1 handful of crackers, about 16 to 20
Optional: a small bowl of nuts, only if no one has a nut allergy, or a small bowl of olives

Cheese straight from the refrigerator is firmer and easier to slice. Fruit should feel fresh and ripe, not fermented or mushy. Keep wet fruit, such as cut melon, in a small bowl so it does not sog the crackers.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Slice or cube the firmer cheeses on a stable board, using a cut-resistant glove on the hand that holds the cheese if you need it.
Leave a very soft cheese in a small bowl with a knife.
Wash the fruit.
Slice apples just before serving, or toss them with a little lemon juice so they brown more slowly.
Arrange the cheese, fruit, and crackers on a large plate or board, with a little space between groups, and put any nuts or olives in small bowls.
Serve soon, or cover and refrigerate for up to 1 hour, then bring it out just before people eat.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cheese should feel cool and clean-cut, not slimy, and it should smell as you expect, not of ammonia or sourness. Fruit should smell fresh. Crackers should feel crisp. Nuts, if used, should smell toasted, not rancid.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The plate should look uncrowded, with distinct groups of cheese, fruit, and crackers, not a jumble, so each item is easy to pick up.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The plate should look uncrowded, with distinct groups of cheese, fruit, and crackers, not a jumble, so each item is easy to pick up.

Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Do not serve nuts to anyone with a nut allergy. Keep perishable cheese and cut fruit refrigerated until serving, and do not leave the plate out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A small bowl of honey or jam is a good extra with a sharper cheese. Label the cheeses if they look or feel similar, so people can choose by name as well as by taste.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. A simple, nonalcoholic punch of fruit juices and cold water or a clear soda, served in a pitcher or a bowl over ice. Keep it cold. If you add cut fruit, treat the punch as perishable and do not leave it out more than 2 hours.
About 3 quarts, 12 servings
About 15 minutes, plus chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
4 cups unsweetened pineapple juice, or a mix of pineapple and orange juice
2 cups cranberry juice
2 cups cold water, or a clear lemon-lime soda, added just before serving if you want bubbles
2 tablespoons lemon or lime juice, optional
Ice, and optional orange or lemon slices, for serving

The punch should feel cold and taste fruity and balanced, not only sweet, and not watery once the ice starts to melt, which is why you should not add all the ice to the pitcher hours ahead if you can add it to the glasses instead.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the pineapple or mixed juice, cranberry juice, and optional lemon or lime juice in a pitcher or a punch bowl.
Add the water now, or wait and add the soda just before serving if you are using soda.
Chill the punch.
Serve over ice, with optional fruit slices.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The punch should smell fruity and clean, not fermented. It should taste balanced. If a juice smelled or tasted off before you mixed, throw it out.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The punch should look bright and clear or only slightly cloudy, depending on the juices, not dull and brown from sitting out a long time with cut fruit in a warm room.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. The punch should look bright and clear or only slightly cloudy, depending on the juices, not dull and brown from sitting out a long time with cut fruit in a warm room.

Keep the punch refrigerated. If you add cut fruit or soda is not the only perishable concern, do not leave the bowl out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Frozen fruit can stand in for some of the ice and will dilute the punch less as it thaws. This is a party drink, not a cocktail, in this book.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. About 15 minutes

Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids

A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath

A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 baguette or small Italian loaf, or 8 slices sturdy bread
4 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened
2 garlic cloves, minced, or 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, if the butter is unsalted
Optional: 1 tablespoon chopped parsley, or 2 tablespoons grated Parmesan cheese

Softened butter should spread without tearing the bread. Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces. The finished bread should feel crisp at the edges and soft in the middle, and it should smell toasty and garlicky, not burnt.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Mix the butter, garlic, salt, and any optional parsley or Parmesan until even.
Split the loaf, or slice the bread.
Spread the garlic butter on the cut sides.
Set the bread on a pan, buttered side up.
Bake 8 to 12 minutes, until the edges feel crisp and the butter is melted and bubbling.
For a slightly crisper top, you can switch to a brief broil, but do not walk away.
Cool 1 minute, then cut into pieces if you used a whole loaf, and serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The edges should feel crisp. You should smell toasted bread, butter, and garlic, not burning garlic or burning bread. The bread will be very hot.

About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 pound carrots, peeled and sliced into 1/2 inch (half inch) coins, or 1 pound baby carrots
2 tablespoons butter
1 tablespoon brown sugar or honey
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/3 cup (a third of a cup) water

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the carrots, water, butter, sugar or honey, and salt in a skillet or wide pot.
Bring to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cover and cook 8 to 12 minutes, until a fork slides in easily.
Take off the lid.
Cook, stirring, 2 to 4 minutes more, until most of the liquid has thickened into a glaze that coats the carrots.
Taste a cooled piece, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot.

2 ripe avocados
1 tablespoon lime juice, plus more to taste
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
Optional: 2 tablespoons diced onion, 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) diced tomato, 1 tablespoon minced jalapeno, or 1 tablespoon chopped cilantro

A ripe avocado should yield to gentle pressure, not feel rock-hard, and not feel mushy and hollow. After you cut it, the flesh should feel creamy, not fibrous and brown all the way through. If the flesh is brown only in a thin layer under the peel, you can scoop away that layer. The finished guacamole should feel creamy, with some small chunks if you like them, not watery, and not stiff as paste.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Cut each avocado in half lengthwise, around the pit, on a stable board.
Twist the halves apart.
Remove the pit by scooping it out with a spoon, or by carefully easing it out. Do not strike the pit with a knife.
Scoop the flesh into a bowl.
Add the lime juice and salt.
Mash with a fork until the mix feels as smooth or as chunky as you like.
Stir in any optional add-ins.
Taste a little, and add salt or lime if it needs it.
Serve at once.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The mix should feel creamy. You should smell avocado, lime, and salt, and any optional onion or cilantro. It should not smell rancid or fermented. If an avocado is brown, stringy, and off-smelling inside, throw it out.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The guacamole should look creamy and green, maybe with a few yellow-green chunks, not gray-brown all the way through, and not watery. A little browning on the surface after it sits is common.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. Use a stable board and a sharp knife, slowly. Do not strike the pit with a knife, because the knife can slip. Wear gloves if you mince a chili, and do not touch your eyes. Mince means cut into very small pieces. Press plastic wrap onto the surface of leftovers, refrigerate, and eat within 1 day. Do not leave guacamole out more than 2 hours. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
A ripe avocado can be ripened at room temperature and then kept in the refrigerator for a day or two. This is the usual partner for tacos and for Chips and Salsa in the Midnight Snacks chapter.

Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Apple cider or apple juice heated with a few warm spices, served in a mug. This is not hard cider, and it is not alcoholic in this recipe. Heat it until it is steaming hot, but do not boil it hard, or the flavor can taste duller and the pot can scorch.
4 mugs
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
4 cups apple cider or apple juice
2 cinnamon sticks, or 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) ground cinnamon
2 whole cloves, optional, or a pinch of ground cloves
1 thin orange slice, optional
Optional: 1 to 2 teaspoons brown sugar or maple syrup, if the cider is very tart
The cider should feel steaming hot and should smell like apple and cinnamon, not scorched. If you use whole spices, they should stay in the pot or be strained out so no one bites a clove by surprise.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the cider, cinnamon, optional cloves, and optional orange slice in a pot.
Heat over medium-low heat, stirring now and then, until the cider is steaming hot and you see small bubbles at the edge, not a rolling boil.
Taste a cooled sip, and add optional sugar or syrup if it needs it.
Strain out whole spices if you used them, or ladle carefully around them.
Pour into mugs.
Let it sit 1 minute, then drink.

A chickpea dip blended with tahini, which is sesame paste, plus lemon, garlic, and oil. A food processor or blender makes it smooth. If you do not have tahini, a little extra oil and a pinch of cumin still make a good dip, though the flavor will be lighter. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
About 2 cups, 6 to 8 snack servings
About 15 minutes

Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 can (15 ounces) chickpeas, drained and rinsed, with 2 tablespoons of the liquid reserved
3 tablespoons tahini, or 2 tablespoons extra oil if you do not have tahini
2 tablespoons lemon juice, plus more to taste
1 small garlic clove, minced, or 1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) garlic powder
2 tablespoons olive oil, plus more for serving
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) cumin, optional
2 to 4 tablespoons reserved chickpea liquid or water, as needed

Tahini feels thick, oily, and a little bitter on its own, then tastes nutty and creamy in the dip. The finished hummus should feel very smooth and thick, like a dip that holds a soft peak on a spoon, not pasty and dry, and not runny. Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the chickpeas, tahini or extra oil, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt, and optional cumin in a food processor or blender.
Blend until the mix feels smooth, stopping to scrape the sides.
Add reserved liquid or water 1 tablespoon at a time, and blend again, until the hummus feels creamy and thick but spreadable.
Taste a little, and add salt or lemon if it needs it.
Spoon into a bowl.
Add a little olive oil on top if you like.
Serve with pita, crackers, or vegetables, or see Hummus and Pita in the Midnight Snacks chapter.

entries.title: Iced Coffee

blocks.text: Coffee served cold over ice, either by cooling a strong brew or by steeping coffee in cold water overnight, which is called cold brew. Steep means let the coffee sit in water so the flavor comes out. If you pour hot coffee straight over a lot of ice, brew it stronger than usual, or the ice will dilute it.
2 glasses
About 10 minutes, plus time to brew and cool the coffee, or overnight for a cold brew
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
2 cups strong coffee, cooled, or 1/2 cup (half a cup) coarsely ground coffee plus 2 cups cold water, for a small cold brew
Ice, for serving
Milk or cream, optional
Sugar or simple syrup, optional, meaning sugar dissolved in an equal amount of hot water, then cooled

Cooled coffee should smell like coffee, not scorched or stale. Cold brew, after straining, should feel smooth and less sharp than a hot brew that was cooled, and it should not feel sludgy if you strained it well.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
For cooled coffee: brew coffee at about twice your usual strength if you will pour it over ice, or brew it as usual if you will cool it fully first and use less ice.
Cool it, then refrigerate.
For a small cold brew: mix the ground coffee and cold water in a jar.
Cover and refrigerate 12 to 18 hours.
Strain through a fine strainer or a coffee filter, slowly.
Fill two glasses with ice.
Pour the coffee over the ice.
Add optional milk and optional sugar or syrup.
Stir and serve.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The coffee should smell like coffee, not scorched or rancid, and it should taste strong enough after the ice. If the coffee smells stale or oily in an off way, throw it out and start with fresh beans or grounds.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The coffee should look dark and clear or only slightly cloudy, not muddy with a thick layer of grounds if you strained it.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The coffee should look dark and clear or only slightly cloudy, not muddy with a thick layer of grounds if you strained it.

If you brew with hot water, the pot and steam are very hot. Cool hot coffee within 2 hours and refrigerate it. Keep milk cold, and do not leave a milky iced coffee out for a long time. Use cold brew or cooled coffee within 3 to 4 days, kept refrigerated. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
Sweetening works better with a syrup than with dry sugar in a very cold glass, because dry sugar can sit undissolved at the bottom.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Black tea brewed strong, then cooled and served over ice, with optional lemon and sugar. Do not brew the tea for a very long time, or it can taste bitter and astringent, meaning dry and puckery. Cool the tea before you add a lot of ice, or the ice will melt and dilute it more than you want, unless you make an extra-strong brew on purpose.
About 2 quarts, 8 servings
About 20 minutes, plus cooling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
8 cups water, divided
4 to 6 tea bags, or 2 tablespoons loose black tea in a strainer
1/4 to 1/2 cup (a quarter to half a cup) sugar, optional, or to taste
Lemon slices, optional
Ice, for serving

The hot tea should smell fragrant, like black tea, not scorched. After steeping, it should taste strong, because it will be diluted a little by ice. Steep means let the tea sit in hot water so the flavor comes out.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Bring 4 cups of the water to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles, then take the pot off the heat.
Add the tea bags or loose tea.
Steep 3 to 5 minutes, then remove the tea.
If you are using sugar, stir it in now, while the tea is hot, until it dissolves.
Add the remaining 4 cups of cold water.
Cool the tea to room temperature, then refrigerate until it is cold.
Serve over ice, with optional lemon.

entries.title: Lemonade

blocks.text: A simple drink of lemon juice, sugar, and water. Dissolving the sugar in a little hot water first, which makes a syrup, keeps the sugar from sitting in a grit at the bottom of a cold pitcher. Taste as you go, because lemons vary.
About 1 1/2 quarts (one and a half quarts), 6 servings
About 15 minutes, plus chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 cup lemon juice, from about 5 to 7 lemons, or bottled juice if you need a shortcut
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) sugar, plus more to taste
1/2 cup (half a cup) hot water, for dissolving the sugar
4 cups cold water, plus more if the lemonade is too strong
Ice, and optional lemon slices, for serving

Fresh lemon juice should smell bright and sharp, not fermented. The finished lemonade should feel smooth, not gritty with undissolved sugar, and it should taste bright and balanced, not only sour, and not only sweet.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Stir the sugar and hot water in a pitcher until the sugar dissolves completely. This is a simple syrup, meaning sugar dissolved in water.
Add the lemon juice and the cold water.
Stir well.
Taste a little, and add more sugar, more lemon, or more water if it needs it.
Stir until any added sugar dissolves, or dissolve it in a little hot water first and then add it.
Chill, then serve over ice, with optional lemon slices.

Cook the pasta in salted boiling water until it is tender.
See the Pasta Primer in the Supper chapter for the basic method.
Drain, then rinse under cold water until the pasta feels cool. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Drain very well.
Mix the mayonnaise, vinegar or pickle juice, optional sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt in a large bowl.
Add the pasta and the vegetables.
Toss until evenly coated.
Taste a piece, and add salt or vinegar if it needs it.
Chill at least 30 minutes before serving.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The pasta should feel tender and cool. You should smell mayonnaise, vinegar, and pasta, not a sour, off smell. The vegetables should feel crisp.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The salad should look creamy and evenly mixed, not dry, and not sitting in a puddle of dressing.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The salad should look creamy and evenly mixed, not dry, and not sitting in a puddle of dressing.

Boiling water can burn you. Cool and refrigerate the salad within 2 hours. Because of mayonnaise, keep it cold, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Eat within 3 to 4 days. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

If the salad dries out in the refrigerator, fold in a spoon of mayonnaise before serving. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air. A little mustard in the dressing is a good extra.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A simple tomato sauce with garlic, oil, and dried herbs. This is the sauce to keep for pasta, pizza, chicken Parmesan, and baked ziti in the Supper chapter. Simmer means cook with small, gentle bubbles so the sauce thickens and the raw tomato taste cooks off.
About 4 cups, 6 to 8 servings
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 tablespoons olive oil
3 garlic cloves, minced, or 1 teaspoon garlic powder
1 can (28 ounces) crushed tomatoes, or whole tomatoes you crush with a spoon
1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
1 teaspoon dried oregano or Italian seasoning
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) sugar, optional, if the tomatoes taste very sharp
A pinch of red pepper flakes, optional

Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces. The finished sauce should feel slightly thick, like a loose puree that coats pasta, not watery like tomato juice, and not a stiff paste. It should smell cooked and round, not raw and tinny.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oil in a pot over medium heat.
Add the garlic and optional red pepper flakes, and cook 30 seconds, until the garlic smells fragrant, not brown and bitter.
Add the tomatoes, salt, oregano or Italian seasoning, and optional sugar.
Bring to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles.
Reduce the heat to low. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
Simmer 15 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce feels slightly thick and the raw tomato smell is gone.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add salt or a pinch of sugar if it needs it. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve hot, or cool and store.

The sauce should look red and slightly thick, with a little oil on the surface, not watery, and not dark and scorched at the edges of the pot.

The pot and bubbling sauce are very hot and can spatter. Use a lid that is slightly ajar if it spatters a lot. Mince garlic on a stable board. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F, or until the sauce bubbles again. The sauce also freezes well. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

A little chopped basil at the end is a good finish. If you want a meat sauce, see Spaghetti with Meat Sauce in the Supper chapter, instead of adding raw meat to this page. For pizza, you can use this sauce as it is, or see Pizza Sauce in this chapter for a thicker, no-simmer option.

Potatoes boiled until tender, then mashed with butter and milk until they are smooth and fluffy, or left a little lumpy if you prefer. This is a standalone side to go with beef tips, meatloaf, or roasted meats in the Supper chapter.
4 to 6 as a side
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 pounds russet or Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into even chunks
1 tablespoon salt, for the cooking water, plus more to taste
4 tablespoons unsalted butter
1/2 to 3/4 cup (half to three-quarters of a cup) warm milk
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper, optional

Even chunks cook at the same rate. A fork should slide into a chunk with no resistance when the potatoes are done. The finished mash should feel smooth and fluffy, or softly lumpy, not watery and not stiff as paste.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the potatoes in a pot.
Add cold water to cover them by about 1 inch, and add the 1 tablespoon salt.

Bring to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles, then reduce to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cook 12 to 18 minutes, until a fork slides into a chunk easily.
Drain the potatoes well in a colander. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Return them to the hot pot for 1 minute so extra steam can escape.
Add the butter.
Mash until the butter is mixed in.
Add 1/2 cup (half a cup) of the warm milk.
Mash or beat until the potatoes feel fluffy.
Add more milk if they are too stiff.
Add salt and optional pepper to taste.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A fork should slide into the boiled chunks easily before you mash. The finished mash should feel fluffy and hot. You should smell potato and butter, not a raw, starchy smell or scorching.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The mash should look fluffy and even, not gluey and shiny, and not dry with lumps of unmashed potato unless you left them on purpose.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The mash should look fluffy and even, not gluey and shiny, and not dry with lumps of unmashed potato unless you left them on purpose.

The pot, steam, and colander are very hot. Drain slowly, away from your body. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F with a splash of milk. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

Do not overmash, especially with a blender or food processor, or the potatoes can turn gluey. For garlic mashed potatoes, simmer a few peeled cloves with the potatoes and mash them in. See Beef Tips and Mashed Potatoes in the Supper chapter for a combined plate.

Small sausages wrapped in dough and baked until the dough is golden and the sausages are hot. Use cocktail wieners, or cut regular hot dogs into short pieces. If the sausages are already fully cooked, you are heating them through, often to 165 degrees F to be safe if they were leftover or chilled, or until they are steaming hot. The dough should be cooked, not raw on the inside.
24 pieces, 8 appetizer servings
About 30 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
1 package refrigerated crescent-roll dough, or 1 pound pizza dough, thawed if frozen
24 cocktail wieners, or 6 hot dogs, each cut into 4 pieces, patted dry
1 egg, beaten with 1 teaspoon water, optional, for brushing
Mustard or ketchup, for serving

The dough should feel soft and easy to wrap, not sticky and not dry and cracked. After baking, the dough should feel set and golden, not doughy next to the sausage, and the sausage should feel steaming hot.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F, or to the temperature on the dough package if it is different.
Line a pan with parchment.
If you are using crescent dough, separate it into triangles and cut each triangle into smaller strips if needed.
If you are using pizza dough, roll it thin and cut it into 24 small strips.

Wrap each sausage in a strip of dough, leaving the ends slightly visible if you like, and pinch the seam shut. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Set the pieces seam-side down on the pan.
Brush with the optional egg wash.
Bake 12 to 18 minutes, until the dough feels set and golden, and the sausages are steaming hot, 165 degrees F if they were leftover or if you want a clear target.
Cool 5 minutes.
Serve with mustard or ketchup.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The dough should feel set and lightly crisp in spots, not doughy. The sausages should feel steaming hot. You should smell toasted dough and sausage, not raw flour or burning.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The dough should look golden, not pale and not dark brown. A little grease may leak, which is common. The dough next to the sausage, if you break one open to test, should look cooked, not raw and doughy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. A little grease may leak, which is common. The dough next to the sausage, if you break one open to test, should look cooked, not raw and doughy.

Use mitts. The pan, filling, and steam are very hot. Cool 5 minutes. If you use an egg wash, wash your hands after handling the raw egg. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F. Do not taste raw dough. For pork chops, ribs, and roasts, the USDA minimum is 145 degrees F, then a 3-minute rest. For ribs or pulled pork, also cook until the meat is tender.
A pinch of everything-bagel seasoning on the egg wash is a good extra. These are best eaten warm.

entries.title: Pizza Sauce

blocks.text: A thick, no-cook or barely cooked tomato sauce for the Sheet-Pan Pizza in the Supper chapter. Because it does not simmer long, it should start with a thick canned tomato product, such as tomato puree or thick crushed tomatoes, and enough salt and herbs to taste good even before it bakes. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
About 1 1/2 cups (one and a half cups), enough for 2 sheet-pan pizzas
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 can (15 ounces) tomato puree or thick crushed tomatoes
1 tablespoon olive oil
1 teaspoon dried oregano
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder, or 1 small garlic clove, minced
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) sugar, optional
The sauce should feel thick enough to spread on dough without running off, like a loose paste, not watery. Mince means cut the garlic into very small pieces if you use fresh garlic.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Mix the tomato puree, oil, oregano, salt, garlic, and optional sugar in a bowl until even.
Taste a little, and add salt or a pinch of sugar if it needs it. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The sauce should look thick and even, red and slightly glossy from the oil, not watery.

If you use fresh garlic, mince it on a stable board. Refrigerate the sauce, and do not leave it out more than 2 hours. If you want a fully cooked sauce, simmer this mix 10 minutes instead, then cool, and reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.
This is intentionally thicker than marinara. If it seems thin, stir in 1 tablespoon tomato paste.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. entries.title: Polenta

blocks.text: A creamy cornmeal porridge, served soft as a side, often under meats or vegetables, or cooled and later sliced. Stir often so it does not scorch. Instant polenta is faster, and you should follow the package liquid amount if it differs. This is similar in comfort to the Grits in the Breakfast chapter, but usually made with a finer cornmeal.
4 as a side
About 30 minutes for regular polenta, or about 10 minutes for instant
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 cup regular or instant polenta or yellow cornmeal, not self-rising
4 cups water or a mix of water and milk, or as the package directs
1 teaspoon salt
2 tablespoons butter
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) grated Parmesan cheese, optional

The cooked polenta should feel smooth and creamy, like a thick porridge, not gritty and raw, and not so stiff that it tears away from the sides in a hard mass unless you want it firm enough to slice later. A spoon should stand for a moment, then slowly fall.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Bring the water or water-and-milk and the salt to a boil in a heavy pot, meaning large, rolling bubbles.
Whisk in the polenta slowly, so it does not clump. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk as you pour.
Reduce the heat to low. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
For regular polenta, cook 20 to 30 minutes, stirring often, until it feels creamy and the raw cornmeal taste is gone.
For instant polenta, cook 3 to 5 minutes, or as the package directs, stirring.
Stir in the butter and optional Parmesan.
If it is too thick, add a splash of water or milk.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve at once, because soft polenta firms as it sits.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The polenta should feel creamy and smooth, not gritty. You should smell cooked corn, butter, and optional cheese, not raw meal or scorching. If you smell scorching, take the pot off the heat and stop scraping the bottom into the serving bowl.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The polenta should look smooth and golden, not lumpy, and not scorched and brown at the edges of the pot. Soft polenta should look pourable but thick, like a loose mash.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The polenta should look smooth and golden, not lumpy, and not scorched and brown at the edges of the pot. Soft polenta should look pourable but thick, like a loose mash.

Bubbling polenta can spatter and is very hot, like thick lava. Stir with a long-handled spoon, and keep your face back. Use a heavy pot and low heat. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F with extra liquid, stirring, or slice cooled polenta and brown the slices in a skillet until they are hot in the center. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

For firm, sliceable polenta, spread the cooked mix in a greased dish, chill until set, then cut and brown. Soft polenta is a good bed for the Garlic Butter Shrimp or the Chickpea Curry in the Supper chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

blocks.text: Cooked potato chunks mixed with a creamy dressing, often with celery, onion, and chopped hard-boiled egg. Cool the potatoes until they are just warm before you dress them, then chill the salad. If you add eggs, they should be fully cooked, firm hard-boiled eggs, as in the Breakfast chapter.

About 40 minutes, plus chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
2 pounds waxy potatoes, such as red or Yukon Gold, cut into 3/4 inch (three-quarters of an inch) chunks
1 tablespoon salt, for the cooking water, plus 3/4 teaspoon (three-quarters of a teaspoon) for the dressing, or to taste
1/2 cup (half a cup) mayonnaise
1 tablespoon mustard
1 tablespoon vinegar or pickle juice
2 celery stalks, diced
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) diced onion, or 2 sliced green onions
2 hard-boiled eggs, chopped, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper

Waxy potatoes hold their shape better than russets in a salad. A fork should slide into a chunk when they are done, but the chunks should not fall apart. The dressed salad should feel creamy and cohesive, with tender potato pieces, not watery and not mashed.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the potatoes in a pot.
Cover with cold water, add the 1 tablespoon salt, and bring to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Cook 8 to 12 minutes, until a fork slides in and the chunks still hold their shape.
Drain well. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Let the potatoes cool until they are just warm, about 15 minutes, stirring once so they cool more evenly.
Mix the mayonnaise, mustard, vinegar or pickle juice, 3/4 teaspoon (three-quarters of a teaspoon) salt, and pepper in a large bowl.
Add the potatoes, celery, onion, and optional eggs.
Toss gently until coated.
Taste a cooled bite, and add salt or vinegar if it needs it.
Chill at least 1 hour before serving.

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The potatoes should feel tender and hold their shape. You should smell potato, mayonnaise, and a little vinegar or pickle, not a sour, off leftover smell. The salad should feel cool and cohesive after chilling.

Use hard-boiled eggs that were cooked until firm and then chilled. Reheat is not the usual path here. Serve cold, and throw the salad out after 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator. Cook egg dishes to 160 degrees F. There should be no liquid raw egg left.

A little chopped pickle or fresh dill is a good extra. If the salad seems dry after chilling, fold in 1 tablespoon mayonnaise. Fold means gently turn the mixture over itself so you do not knock out the air.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

A party-size warm cheese dip, similar to the Queso and Chips in the Midnight Snacks chapter, written here for a larger platter. Keep the pot on very low heat, and do not leave the dip out more than 2 hours. Reheat leftovers until bubbling, 165 degrees F, stirring, with a splash of milk.
8 as an appetizer, about 3 cups
About 20 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
3 cups shredded melting cheese, such as cheddar or a Mexican blend
3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) milk, plus more if the dip is too thick
1 can (10 ounces) diced tomatoes with green chiles, drained a little, or 3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup) salsa
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, if the cheese is not salty
Tortilla chips, for serving

Shredded cheese melts more evenly than cubes. The dip should feel smooth and pourable, thick enough to coat a chip, not oily and split, and not a solid clump. If it feels grainy, lower the heat and add a splash of milk, and stir.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Set a pot over low to medium-low heat.
Add the milk and the tomatoes or salsa.
When the mix is hot and steaming, add the cheese a handful at a time, stirring until it melts before you add more.
If the dip is too thick, add milk 1 tablespoon at a time.
If it is too thin, cook, stirring, another minute or two.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add a pinch of salt if it needs it. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Serve warm with chips, and keep the pot on the lowest heat, stirring now and then.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The dip should feel smooth and hot, and it should coat a chip. You should smell melted cheese and chiles, not scorched milk.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The queso should look smooth and evenly orange or red-orange, not oily with a puddle of separated fat, and not lumpy with unmelted cheese.

Use low heat. Cheese sauces scorch and split on high heat. The pot and dip are very hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F, or until the dip is bubbling again, stirring often. Add a splash of milk when you reheat. Do not leave the dip out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F, or until a sauce or gravy returns to a boil.

A pinch of cumin is a good extra. A slow cooker on the warm setting can hold the dip for a party if you stir now and then and still follow the 2-hour guidance for food sitting in the temperature danger zone, or keep it above 140 degrees F if you are holding it hot.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. entries.title: Quinoa

blocks.text: A pot of quinoa, which is a small seed cooked like a grain. Rinse it first, unless the package says it is pre-rinsed, because the natural coating can taste bitter. The grains are done when they look slightly popped and feel tender, and the water is absorbed.
4 as a side, about 3 cups cooked
About 25 minutes, plus a 5-minute rest
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 cup quinoa
2 cups water or broth
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, or less if the broth is salty

Uncooked quinoa feels small, dry, and slightly oval. After cooking, the grains should feel tender, not chalky, and you may feel a little ring or tail on each grain, which is normal. The pot should feel fluffy, not watery, and not dry and stuck.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Rinse the quinoa in a fine strainer under cold water, unless the package says it is pre-rinsed.
Put the quinoa, water or broth, and salt in a pot.
Bring to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles.

Cover, reduce to a low simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles, and cook 12 to 15 minutes, until the water is absorbed and the grains feel tender. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Take the pot off the heat.
Rest, covered, 5 minutes. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Fluff with a fork, meaning gently loosen the grains.
Serve hot, or cool and use in a salad.

Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The quinoa should look fluffy, with visible little rings or tails, and no puddle of water in the pot. It should not look dry and crusted unless the heat was too high.

A squeeze of lemon and a little oil turn leftover quinoa into a simple salad base. This is a good partner for the roasted vegetables in this chapter.

entries.title: Ranch Dip

blocks.text: A cold, creamy dip with herbs, good for raw vegetables, oven fries, and wings. You can use a mix of mayonnaise and sour cream or yogurt. The flavor improves if the dip sits in the refrigerator for 30 minutes so the dried herbs soften.
About 1 cup, 6 to 8 snack servings
About 10 minutes, plus an optional 30-minute rest
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/2 cup (half a cup) mayonnaise
1/2 cup (half a cup) sour cream or plain yogurt
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) garlic powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) onion powder
1 teaspoon dried parsley, or 1 tablespoon chopped fresh parsley
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) dried dill, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1 tablespoon milk, if the dip is too thick
The dip should feel smooth and thick enough to cling to a carrot stick, not watery, and not pasty. Dried herbs will feel slightly rough at first and will soften as the dip rests.

Mix the mayonnaise, sour cream or yogurt, garlic powder, onion powder, parsley, optional dill, and salt in a bowl until even.
If the dip is too thick, add milk 1 teaspoon at a time.
Taste a little, and add salt if it needs it.
Cover and refrigerate 30 minutes if you have time, then stir and serve cold, with vegetables or chips.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Fresh chives are a good extra. This is the usual partner for Boneless Wings in this chapter and for Oven Fries in the Midnight Snacks chapter.

blocks.text: Canned or leftover pinto or black beans mashed and heated with a little oil or butter until they are thick, creamy, and steaming hot, 165 degrees F. These are a side for tacos, burritos, and rice bowls.
4 as a side
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large skillet or saute pan
A heat-safe spatula or wooden spoon
A splatter screen
2 cans (15 ounces each) pinto or black beans, drained, with 1/2 cup (half a cup) of the liquid reserved, or 3 cups cooked beans plus a little broth
1 tablespoon oil or butter
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) ground cumin, optional
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste

Heat the oil or butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook the optional onion until it feels soft.
Add the beans, cumin if using, and salt.
Add a splash of the reserved liquid or broth.
Cook, mashing with a spoon or a potato masher, 5 to 8 minutes, until the beans are thick, creamy, and 165 degrees F.
Add more liquid if they get too thick, or cook a minute more if they are too loose.
Taste a cooled spoonful, and add salt if it needs it.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

entries.title: Rice

blocks.text: A basic pot of white long-grain rice. The rice simmers in a measured amount of water, then rests off the heat so it can finish steaming. Simmer means cook in liquid with small, gentle bubbles, not a hard boil. Do not lift the lid during the simmer and rest if you can help it.
4 as a side, about 3 cups cooked
About 25 minutes, plus a 10-minute rest
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 cup long-grain white rice
1 3/4 cups (one and three-quarters cups) water, or as the package directs, because brands vary
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt
1 teaspoon butter or oil, optional
Uncooked rice feels hard and dry. After cooking and resting, the grains should feel tender, not chalky in the center, and not mushy, and they should be separate, not a wet clump.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Rinse the rice in a fine strainer under cold water until the water runs less cloudy, unless the package says not to rinse.
Put the rice, water, salt, and optional butter or oil in a small pot with a tight lid.

Bring to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles, then stir once, cover, and reduce the heat to low so the pot stays at a gentle simmer. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens.
Cook 15 to 18 minutes, or as the package directs, without lifting the lid.
Take the pot off the heat.
Let it rest, still covered, 10 minutes. Rest means let cooked meat sit so the juices settle back into the meat.
Uncover and fluff the rice with a fork, meaning gently loosen the grains.
Serve hot.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Do not leave cooked rice out overnight. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

If the rice is still firm after the rest, add 2 tablespoons water, cover, and return to low heat for 3 to 5 minutes, then rest again. For fried rice, cool this rice, refrigerate it, then see Leftover Fried Rice in the Midnight Snacks chapter.

About 35 minutes

A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath

A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food

A reserved landing space for hot pans

2 tablespoons oil
3/4 teaspoon (three-quarters of a teaspoon) salt
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper

Shrimp simmered just until they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled, then chilled and served with Cocktail Sauce from this chapter. Shrimp cook very fast. They should curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean they are overcooked. Keep them cold after cooking.
4 as an appetizer
About 20 minutes, plus chilling
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 pound large raw shrimp, peeled and deveined, tails on if you like, for a handle
1 tablespoon salt, for the water
Optional: a slice of lemon, or 1 bay leaf, for the water
1 recipe Cocktail Sauce, for serving
Lemon wedges, for serving

Raw shrimp feel slightly translucent and soft. Deveined means the dark vein along the back has been removed. Done shrimp feel firm and springy, not mushy, and not tough as rubber, and they should be opaque. After chilling, they should feel cold and firm.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.

Bring a pot of water, the salt, and any optional lemon or bay leaf to a boil, meaning large, rolling bubbles, then reduce to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Reduce means boil gently until some of the liquid evaporates and the sauce thickens. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Add the shrimp.
Cook 2 to 4 minutes, until they are opaque, firm, and loosely curled.
Drain, then cool the shrimp quickly in an ice bath, meaning a bowl of ice and water, or under cold running water, until they feel cold. Drain means pour off the liquid.
Drain well and pat dry.
Refrigerate until you serve them, at least 20 minutes if they are not already fully cold.
Serve cold with cocktail sauce and lemon wedges.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The shrimp should feel firm, springy, and cold, and they should smell sweet and briny, not ammonia-like or sour. If they smell off before cooking, throw them out.

Visual cues for a sighted helper: The shrimp should look opaque and pink or pearly, not gray and translucent, and they should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. They should look moist, not dry and stringy.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The shrimp should look opaque and pink or pearly, not gray and translucent, and they should curl into a loose C, not a tight O. They should look moist, not dry and stringy.

Keep raw shrimp cold, then wash the board, knife, and your hands. Do not leave cooked shrimp out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Keep the platter on ice if it will sit out at a party. Ice-bath water is messy. Work near the sink. Cook shrimp until the flesh is pearly, opaque, and firm. It should curl into a loose C shape, not a tight O, which can mean it is overcooked.

You can also buy already-cooked chilled shrimp and skip the simmer, then still serve them very cold with sauce. Taste one after cooking and cooling so you can adjust the time next time, because size changes the minutes a lot.

entries.title: Simple Vinaigrette

blocks.text: A basic oil-and-vinegar dressing for green salads. The usual starting ratio is about 3 parts oil to 1 part vinegar, plus salt and an optional dab of mustard to help the dressing stay mixed. A vinaigrette is a dressing made from oil and an acid such as vinegar or lemon juice. Shake or whisk it again just before you use it, because it will separate as it sits. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk until the mixture looks even.
About 3/4 cup (three-quarters of a cup), enough for several salads
About 5 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/2 cup (half a cup) olive oil, or another oil you like
3 tablespoons vinegar, such as red wine, white wine, or cider vinegar, or lemon juice
1 teaspoon mustard, optional, to help it stay mixed
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) black pepper
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) honey or sugar, optional

The mixed dressing should feel smooth and slightly thick if you used mustard, and thinner if you did not. It should taste bright and balanced, not only oily, and not only sharp. It will separate as it sits, which is normal.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put the vinegar, optional mustard, salt, pepper, and optional honey or sugar in a jar or a small bowl.
Add the oil.
Close the jar and shake until the dressing looks even, or whisk it in the bowl. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk.
Taste a little on a piece of lettuce if you can, and add salt or a little more vinegar or oil if it needs it.
Shake or whisk again just before you dress a salad.
Start with less dressing than you think you need, then add more.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The dressing should feel smooth and should taste bright. You should smell vinegar or lemon, oil, and optional mustard. If the oil smells rancid, like old crayons or paint, throw it out and start over with fresh oil.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: Just after shaking, the dressing should look even and slightly cloudy, not a layer of oil sitting on a layer of vinegar, though it will separate again as it sits.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. Just after shaking, the dressing should look even and slightly cloudy, not a layer of oil sitting on a layer of vinegar, though it will separate again as it sits.

A glass jar can slip. Work over the sink or a bowl when you shake it. Store the dressing in the refrigerator if it contains fresh garlic or if you will keep it more than a day, and use within 1 week. Oil may thicken in the refrigerator. Let the jar sit at room temperature a few minutes, then shake again. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

This is the usual dressing for Garden Salad and Spinach Salad in the Lunch chapter. A small minced garlic clove is a good extra if you will use the dressing within a day or two. Mince means cut into very small pieces.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.
