blocks.text: A hot dip of chopped spinach, artichoke hearts, cream cheese, and melted cheese, baked until it is bubbling, 165 degrees F in the center. Squeeze the spinach very dry, or the dip will be watery. Serve with pita, crackers, or cut vegetables.
8 as an appetizer
About 35 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A stable cutting board with a damp towel underneath
A sharp chef's knife
A cut-resistant glove for the hand that holds the food
A rimmed baking sheet or the baking dish named in the ingredients
Parchment paper or foil, when useful
Long oven mitts
A reserved landing space for hot pans
A talking or instant-read food thermometer
8 ounces cream cheese, softened
1/2 cup (half a cup) sour cream or mayonnaise
1 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, plus 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) for the top
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) grated Parmesan cheese
1 package (10 ounces) frozen chopped spinach, thawed and squeezed very dry, or 10 ounces fresh spinach, wilted, cooled, and squeezed dry
1 can (14 ounces) artichoke hearts, drained and chopped
1 garlic clove, minced, or 1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) garlic powder
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt

Squeezed spinach should feel damp but not dripping. Softened cream cheese should feel smooth and spreadable. The baked dip should feel hot and bubbling in the center, 165 degrees F, and creamy, not watery, and not oily and split.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 375 degrees F.
Grease a small baking dish, about 1 quart, or an 8 inch square dish.
Mix the cream cheese, sour cream or mayonnaise, 1 cup mozzarella, Parmesan, garlic, and salt until even.
Stir in the spinach and artichokes until they are evenly distributed.
Spread the mix in the dish.
Sprinkle the remaining mozzarella on top.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until the dip is bubbling at the edges and the center is 165 degrees F and hot.
Cool 5 minutes, then serve with dippers.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The center should be 165 degrees F and feel steaming hot and creamy. You should smell cheese, spinach, and garlic, not scorching. The dip should feel thick, not watery.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The top should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, not pale and still, and not dark brown and dried out.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The top should look melted and bubbling, with a few light brown spots, not pale and still, and not dark brown and dried out.

The dish and dip are very hot, and bubbling cheese can burn your mouth. Cool 5 minutes. Use mitts. Squeeze spinach in a clean towel. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours, and reheat to 165 degrees F. Cook casseroles to 165 degrees F in the center.

A fresh jalapeno, minced, with gloves on, adds heat. Mince means cut into very small pieces. This can be mixed ahead, refrigerated, and baked just before serving, adding a few minutes if it goes in cold.

Broccoli cooked over simmering water until it is tender-crisp, meaning it is hot and slightly bent but not mushy. You can use a steamer basket, or a colander that sits above the water in a pot without touching the water, with a lid on top.
4 as a side
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A large pot with a lid
A wooden spoon or ladle
1 large bunch broccoli, cut into florets, or 6 cups florets, or a 12 ounce bag of florets
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste
1 tablespoon butter or olive oil, optional
Lemon wedges, optional

Florets are the tree-like heads, cut into even, bite-size pieces. Stems can be peeled and sliced and cooked with the florets if you like them. Done broccoli should feel bright and tender-crisp, not raw and squeaky, and not dull and mushy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Pour about 1 inch of water into a pot.
Set a steamer basket in the pot, making sure the water does not sit above the bottom of the basket.
Bring the water to a simmer, meaning small, gentle bubbles. Simmer means cook just below a boil, with small, gentle bubbles.
Add the broccoli to the basket.
Sprinkle with salt.
Cover the pot.
Steam 5 to 8 minutes, until a stem feels tender-crisp when pierced, not hard and not collapsing.
Move the broccoli to a bowl.
Add optional butter or oil, and more salt if it needs it.
Serve with optional lemon.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: A stem should feel tender-crisp when pierced. You should smell fresh, cooked broccoli, not sulfur from a long overcook, and not raw vegetable. The florets should feel hot and slightly springy.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The broccoli should look bright green, not olive-drab and mushy, and not still dusty and raw-looking. The stems should look a little translucent at the cut ends.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The broccoli should look bright green, not olive-drab and mushy, and not still dusty and raw-looking. The stems should look a little translucent at the cut ends.

Steam can burn you. Tilt the lid away from you. Use mitts or tongs to lift the basket. The water and pot are very hot. This dish has no raw meat. Still keep perishable ingredients cold. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F.

If you do not have a basket, microwave the florets in a microwave-safe dish with 2 tablespoons water, covered, 3 to 5 minutes, then check and add time as needed. Do not overcook. A sprinkle of grated Parmesan is a good finish.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Mushroom caps filled with a breadcrumb, cheese, and herb mix, then baked until the mushrooms are tender and the filling is hot. Pull the stems out and chop them for the filling so nothing is wasted.
About 16 mushrooms, 6 to 8 appetizer servings
About 35 minutes

16 medium white or cremini mushrooms, stems pulled out and chopped, caps left whole
2 tablespoons oil or butter, divided
2 tablespoons minced onion or shallot
1 garlic clove, minced
1/2 cup (half a cup) breadcrumbs
1/4 cup (a quarter cup) grated Parmesan cheese
2 tablespoons chopped parsley, optional
1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt, plus more to taste

After you pull the stems, the caps should feel intact, like little bowls. The filling should feel moist enough to mound, not dry and sandy, and not wet. After baking, the caps should feel tender, and the filling should feel hot and slightly crisp on top.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Heat the oven to 400 degrees F.
Line a pan with parchment, or oil the pan.
Toss the caps with 1 tablespoon of the oil and a pinch of salt. A pinch is a small amount you can hold between two fingers, about 1/8 teaspoon (an eighth of a teaspoon).
Set them cavity-side up on the pan.
Heat the remaining oil or butter in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook the chopped stems and the onion until they feel soft, about 5 minutes.
Add the garlic for the last 30 seconds.
Take the skillet off the heat.
Stir in the breadcrumbs, Parmesan, optional parsley, and 1/4 teaspoon (a quarter teaspoon) salt.
If the mix feels dry, add 1 teaspoon oil or water.
Mound the filling in the caps.
Bake 15 to 20 minutes, until the caps feel tender and the filling is hot and lightly crisp on top.
Cool 3 minutes, then serve.

blocks.text: A cold yogurt and cucumber dip with garlic and lemon, often served with pita, roasted meats, or falafel. Squeeze the cucumber dry, or the dip will be watery. This is a good partner for the Falafel Pita in the Lunch chapter and for lamb in the Supper chapter.

A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork

1/2 cucumber, peeled if the skin is thick, grated or finely diced, then squeezed dry

1 tablespoon olive oil

entries.title: Vanilla Frosting

blocks.text: A simple buttercream, meaning a frosting of butter and powdered sugar beaten until it is fluffy, flavored with vanilla. The cake or cupcakes must be fully cool before you frost them, or the frosting will melt and slide. See Yellow Cake and Vanilla Cupcakes in the Baked Goods chapter.
About 2 cups, enough for 12 cupcakes or a thin layer on a 9 by 13 inch cake
About 15 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1/2 cup (half a cup) unsalted butter, softened
3 cups powdered sugar, plus 1/4 cup (a quarter cup) more if the frosting is too thin
2 to 3 tablespoons milk
2 teaspoons vanilla extract
A pinch of salt

Softened butter should give like cool clay, not feel melted. Powdered sugar is very fine and can puff into the air, so add it slowly. The finished frosting should feel smooth, fluffy, and spreadable, not stiff as paste, and not soupy.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Beat the butter in a bowl until it feels smooth and slightly fluffy.
Add the powdered sugar 1 cup at a time, mixing slowly at first so it does not puff out of the bowl, then more firmly, until it is combined.
Add 2 tablespoons milk, the vanilla, and the salt.
Beat until the frosting feels fluffy and spreadable.
If it is too thick, add more milk 1 teaspoon at a time.
If it is too thin, add more powdered sugar 2 tablespoons at a time.
Spread or pipe the frosting on a fully cooled cake or cupcakes.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

Do not taste raw frosting if you are concerned about raw flour on shared spoons from a baking project. There are no raw eggs in this frosting. Powdered sugar can puff. Mix slowly at first. If the kitchen is very warm, chill the frosting 10 minutes, then beat again. Do not taste raw dough or batter that contains eggs or raw flour. Bake until the doneness cues in the steps are met. For a thinner glaze, add more milk until it is pourable, and spoon it over a cooled loaf, such as the Lemon Loaf in the Baked Goods chapter.

Refrigerate perishable leftovers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Use shallow containers so the food cools faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within 3 to 4 days. Reheat leftovers to 165 degrees F. Bring leftover soups, sauces, and gravies back to a boil.

entries.servings: About 2 cups, enough for 12 cupcakes or a thin layer on a 9 by 13 inch cake

blocks.text: Cold cream beaten until it is fluffy and holds a shape, then lightly sweetened. This is the topping for pies, shortcake, cocoa, and sundaes in this book. Stop beating when the cream holds a soft or firm peak, or it can turn grainy and then become butter.
About 2 cups, 6 to 8 servings
About 10 minutes
Beginner
Measuring cups and spoons with tactile markings
A liquid measuring cup and a liquid level indicator when you are measuring liquids
A tactile or talking timer
A mixing bowl
A whisk or fork
1 cup heavy cream, very cold
1 to 2 tablespoons powdered sugar, or to taste
1/2 teaspoon (half a teaspoon) vanilla extract, optional

A soft peak means a ridge of cream stands up and then slightly folds over. A firm peak means the ridge stands up and holds. The cream should feel cold, smooth, and fluffy, not grainy, and not so stiff that it looks and feels like wet butter, which means it has gone too far.

Read the whole recipe once before you turn on the heat. Set out the equipment and ingredients. Clear a landing space for hot pans. If you will be cutting, put a damp towel under the cutting board. If you are cooking with a helper, decide who will handle knives, the stove, and the thermometer before you start.
Put a mixing bowl and beaters or a whisk in the refrigerator for 10 minutes if you have time. Whisk means beat with a fork or a whisk until the mixture looks even.
Pour in the cold cream.
Beat on medium speed, or whisk by hand, until the cream thickens and you see soft tracks.
Add the sugar and optional vanilla.
Beat until the cream holds a soft or firm peak, then stop at once.
Use at once, or cover and refrigerate for a few hours, then whisk once more if it has loosened.

sections.title: How to Tell When It Is Done

blocks.text: Non-visual cues: The cream should feel cold, smooth, and fluffy, and it should hold a soft or firm peak. You should smell cream and vanilla, not a sour cream smell. If you hear the beaters change to a heavy slosh and then a slap, and the cream looks grainy, stop. You are close to making butter.
Visual cues for a sighted helper: The cream should look smooth and fluffy, with soft or firm peaks, not grainy and yellow, and not still liquid and bubbly only at the surface.

Say what you see out loud, especially color and browning. Share any thermometer reading with your partner. Do not skip the temperature checks in the steps. Visual cues help, but they do not replace a thermometer for meat, poultry, egg dishes, or leftovers. The cream should look smooth and fluffy, with soft or firm peaks, not grainy and yellow, and not still liquid and bubbly only at the surface.

Do not leave whipped cream out more than 2 hours, or more than 1 hour if the room is hotter than 90 degrees F. Keep it cold. A splash guard or a deep bowl helps, because cream splatters as it thickens. If you overwhip and it just starts to look grainy, you can sometimes save it by gently folding in a few tablespoons of unwhipped cream. Serve cream and cheese sauces hot.
